The dome removes 3 whole machines from the chain, and it can only do that because a triangulated shell does not care whether its sticks are rectangular.

chapters.title: What a shelf price is made of
chapters.promise: Almost none of it is the tree.
narration: When you buy a stud you are not mostly buying wood. You are buying the sawing, the drying, the planing, the grading, the log truck, the flatbed, the warehouse that held it and the yard that sold it.
None of those people are villains and none of that work is fake. But every one of those steps exists to turn a round local thing into a standard shippable thing.
A dome does not need it to be standard, and I do not need it to be shipped, because the tree was already here.
equations: 15 hands between the tree and the rack

chapters.title: Fifteen sets of hands
chapters.promise: Listed, because a round number is easy to say and hard to check.
narration: Claiming you have cut out about fifteen middle men is the sort of thing that deserves a list rather than a wave, so here is the list. Every one of them took a margin, and every one of those margins is in the price on the rack, along with the tax on top of all of it.
The wedge path in full is three steps: fell the tree, rip the trunk, use the wood.
equations: a stud on a rack has been sold and handled this many times:
1. timber broker        sells the standing timber
2. logging contractor   fells and skids it
3. log haulier          trucks it to the mill yard
4. log scaler           measures and grades the log
5. headrig sawyer       breaks the log down
6. edger operator       squares the waney sides
8. kiln operator        dries it to a moisture spec
9. lumber grader        stamps a grade on it
10. planing mill         surfaces four sides to dimension
11. bundler              packs and wraps a unit
14. distributor          holds stock and breaks bulk
15. retail yard          sells you one stick
then sales tax: $8.88 on the rack becomes $10.00 paid
every one of the 15 took a margin, and every margin is in that price
the wedge path is: fell the tree, rip the trunk, use the wood
Cutting your own wedges removes 15 separate parties from between the tree and the wall, none of whom did anything to the wood that a geodesic shell needed done.

chapters.title: What the saw actually does
chapters.promise: Two sittings, timed, with the fuel written down.
narration: Everything so far could be argued. This part was measured.

One sitting produced twelve wedges in two hours and burned ten dollars of fuel and bar oil. A separate sitting cut forty-two feet of rip at six inches of depth in one hour, on two tanks of fuel and two of bar oil, including a chain sharpening.

Those two sessions counted different things, which is what makes them worth having. Divide one by the other and you get feet of cut per finished wedge, and the geometry can predict that number independently.

chapters.title: Do the two sessions agree?
chapters.promise: A prediction the geometry can make without being told.
narration: Splitting a round into eight sectors takes seven passes down the whole length of the section. That is a pure geometric statement and it gives feet of cut per wedge without any timing at all.

Set it beside the number the two timed sessions imply and they land close. The gap between them is rolling the log, setting up and sharpening, which is exactly the sort of thing that should be the difference.
Planning then uses a rate below both, because an afternoon is not a timed sprint.
equations: $10.00 of fuel and bar oil = $5.00/hour, the only cash spent
6 passes at 7 ft = 42 ft of rip in 1 h, at 6 in+ of depth
2 tanks of fuel and 2 of bar oil, one sharpening
the two sessions measured different things, so divide them:
42 ft/h / 6.0 wedges/h = 7.00 ft of rip per wedge
and the geometry predicts the same number independently:
8 sectors takes 7 passes down a 7 ft section
the pure cutting is 88 % of the measured time; the other 12 % is rolling the log, setting up and sharpening
planning uses 5.0 wedges/hour, 17 % below the measured rate
Two independent measurements and a geometric prediction agree to within 12 percent, which is why the rate below is worth anything at all.

chapters.title: What one wedge is worth
chapters.promise: Priced against the sticks it would take to replace it.
narration: A wedge is not one two-by-four. It is thicker, so comparing them piece for piece would quietly build a weaker dome and call it cheaper.

The honest comparison is by cross-section: how many dressed studs you would have to lay alongside one wedge to match the wood in it. At the trunk diameter I actually cut, that number is close to three, and the estimate I have been using for planning is two.

chapters.title: The rule of thumb, checked
chapters.promise: Two ways to price a wedge, and how far apart they land.
narration: The rule of thumb multiplies a conservative section factor by the price of an eight-foot stud section. The strict version uses the computed section and also corrects for the fact that a six-foot wedge is shorter than an eight-foot stud.
They should not agree as closely as they do. The conservative multiplier and the generous length happen to cancel almost exactly, which is a piece of luck rather than a method.
Either way, an afternoon of ripping produces a specific number of dollars of wood I would otherwise have had to buy.
equations: a 2x4x16 untreated pine is $8.88 on the rack, $10.00 with tax
one 1/8 wedge of a 12 in trunk has 14.14 in2 of section
the estimate on site was 2.5 x
the multiplier actually used for planning was 2.0 x -- lower than both
STRICT, counting section AND the length difference:
at 5 wedges an hour that is $50.00/hour gross, $45.00 after fuel
one 6-hour afternoon: 30 wedges, $300 of wood, $30 of fuel
A conservative multiplier and a generous length cancel almost exactly, so both methods say the same thing: about $45 an hour, in wood you would otherwise have had to buy.

chapters.title: The part nobody counts
chapters.promise: Culls, trips, hours and the boards that never make it.
narration: A shelf price is not what lumber costs you. There is the drive there and back, the time picking through a rack for boards that are not bowed, the queue, the loading and the unloading.
There are the boards you buy and then reject anyway, and the ones that split or soak between the yard and the site. You paid for those too.
My chainsaw's fuel bill sits roughly where the truck's fuel bill would have been, so it is not the consumables that differ. It is everything attached to them.

chapters.title: The same frame, bought
chapters.promise: Enough studs to match the section, plus everything attached.
narration: This prices the store-bought route properly: enough dressed studs to match the cross-section the wedges provide, not one stud per member, because those are not the same building. Then the culls, the transit losses, the truck runs and the hours those runs take.
Every one of those is an estimate and every one is on the side of the comparison I am arguing against. The cutting column is the measured rate and the measured fuel, and it contains no trips at all.
equations: to match the section 120 wedges provide you would need 2.69 dressed studs alongside each one
/ 16 ft = 121 sticks of actual wood needed
10 % bought and rejected -- bowed, twisted, wet, split
3 % lost to handling and weather on the way
so you buy 139 sticks, 18 of which become firewood ($176)
4 truck loads x 40 mi = 160 mi at $0.55/mi = $88
and 6.0 h of driving, picking, queuing, loading and unloading = $150 of time
CUT: 24 h of ripping, $120 of fuel and oil, no trips at all
The chainsaw's fuel bill roughly replaces the truck's, so the real difference is $1356 of cash that never leaves, and a stack of wood that was already on the property.

chapters.title: The number that depends on the tree
chapters.promise: The one figure that could sink all of this.
narration: A raw sector is literally one eighth of the tree. Whether that is a stronger stick than a two-by-four is not a yes or a no; it is a question about diameter.

Cross-section grows with the square of the radius and bending stiffness grows with the cube, so there is a trunk diameter where the sector overtakes the stud, and below it the sector loses. I am going to give you that crossover diameter rather than a slogan, because it is the one number that could sink this whole method and it deserves to be said out loud.
equations: the trees being cut are 12-15 in

chapters.title: Section properties, and the crossover
chapters.promise: Area, second moment and section modulus, at both diameters.
narration: These are not looked up. The sector outline comes out of the same code that builds the dome, and the area and second moments are integrated around that polygon, checked against the closed form for a circular sector.
At the eight-inch trunk the simulator defaults to, one wedge is the weaker stick in bending. At the twelve-inch trunks I actually cut, it is comfortably the stronger one.
The crossover is solved for rather than asserted. None of this is an engineer's design check.
A real build needs species, grade, moisture and somebody who will sign it. This is the geometry underneath that conversation.
equations: a raw sector is literally 1/8 of the tree, and how strong that is depends entirely on how big the tree was.
= 120 % of a dressed 2x4's area but only 67 % of its bending
AT THE 12 IN TRUNKS ACTUALLY BEING CUT:
= 269 % of a dressed 2x4's area and 226 % of its bending
section grows with the square of the radius and bending with the
cube, so there is a diameter where the sector overtakes the stud:
more area than a dressed 2x4 above 7.31 in
stiffer than a dressed 2x4 above 9.14 in
stiffer than a FULL 2x4 above 11.00 in
and neighbouring panels never share a stick, so all 55 interior edges carry TWO sectors:
539 % of a stud's area, 452 % of its bending
Under 9.1 inches of trunk the wedge is the weaker member and this argument fails. The trees being cut are 12 to 15 inches, which is why it does not.

chapters.title: Four ways up, one of them free
chapters.promise: The wedge is not symmetric, so which way it faces is a decision.
narration: A sector has a point, two flat sawn faces and a curved bark back. Rotate it about its own long axis and you have four distinct positions in the wall.

The way to read them is to look at a pair either side of one seam. The points can face into the dome together, out at the sky together, apart into their own panels, or in toward each other across the seam.
It costs nothing to choose. Same stick, same wood, turned before it goes down.
But the choice changes how deep the section is in the direction the shell actually bends.
equations: points in, points out, points apart, points together
same wood, different depth under load

chapters.title: A panel that cannot fall through
chapters.promise: Point the wedge outward and the opening tapers.
narration: Here is the part that made me stop thinking of these as struts and start thinking of them as a chassis. Turn every member so its pith faces out and its fat bark faces in.

The opening in the middle of each triangle is now wider at the outside than the inside, because each member gets wider as it goes inward. A panel dropped in from outside seats on that taper and is physically stopped.
It is a keystone. Which means a panel is not cladding.
It is a swappable module. You want an air conditioner: you attach one to a panel and swap the panel.
Shelving, glazing, a vent, a whole fitted appliance -- all of it becomes something you pop in and out.

chapters.title: A vein through the whole shell
chapters.promise: The same rotation leaves a duct along every seam.
narration: That rotation does something else for free. With the points facing out, the two sawn faces either side of a seam open away from each other, and they leave a continuous V running the length of every seam in the dome.
Every seam meets every other one at a vertex, so it is not a set of grooves. It is one connected network through the entire shell.
Fill it with key and it is a joint. Leave some of it and it is a duct: air moved between outside and inside, water, wire, pipe, run anywhere on the building without cutting into anything structural.

chapters.title: Four rotations, four buildings
chapters.promise: Where the panel is caught, where the services run, what the saw does.
narration: Stiffness was one axis of this choice and it is already covered. Here are the others, measured off the same cross-section.
Point out and a panel is caught from outside with the conduit in the weather. Point in and it is caught from inside with the services in the warm.

Turn it sideways and the opening goes parallel: no lip, panels held by fixings, but the sawn faces come much closer to flat, which is what sheathing wants to land on. And one of the four does something I did not expect until the solve printed it.
Turned sideways with the points facing each other across the seam, the butt cut's bevel goes to zero. The hardest cut in the build becomes a plain mitre.
equations: stiffness is one axis of the choice and it is already covered.
here is what each rotation does to the BUILDING:
S  2.05 in3   depth 4.00 in   butt bevel +22.50 deg
lip -1.53 in -- panel goes in from INSIDE and cannot fall out
seam V 22.5-27.0 deg, 3.3 in2 -> 7.1 cu ft of continuous conduit
sawn faces sit 67.5 deg off the dome surface
S  1.63 in3   depth 3.06 in   butt bevel -67.50 deg
no lip: opening is parallel-sided, panels held by fixings
seam opens to 153-157 deg: a shallow dish, not a duct
sawn faces sit 22.5 deg off the dome surface
S  2.05 in3   depth 4.00 in   butt bevel -22.50 deg
lip +1.53 in -- panel drops in from OUTSIDE and cannot fall through
seam V 63.0-67.5 deg, 7.3 in2 -> 15.6 cu ft of continuous conduit
sawn faces sit 67.5 deg off the dome surface
S  1.63 in3   depth 3.06 in   butt bevel  +0.00 deg
no lip: opening is parallel-sided, panels held by fixings
seam opens to 153-157 deg: a shallow dish, not a duct
sawn faces sit 22.5 deg off the dome surface
so: DOME-OUT catches a panel from OUTSIDE like a keystone, and puts 16 cu ft of conduit out there too
DOME-IN catches it from INSIDE and runs the services in the warm
PANEL-IN and PANEL-OUT present the flattest wood to sheathing, 22.5 deg off the surface
PANEL-OUT makes the hardest cut in the build a plain mitre, bevel 0.0 deg
Four rotations, four different buildings out of one stick: where the panel is caught, which side the services run, what sheathing lands on, and how hard the one difficult cut is.

chapters.title: What the rotation is worth
chapters.promise: The same area, turned four ways, measured each time.
narration: A shell member is pushed in and out along the dome's own radius, so the stiffness that matters is measured in that direction. Turn the sector and the area does not move by a thousandth of an inch, because rotating a shape does not add wood to it.
The section modulus moves a great deal. Pointing the wedge at the centre of the dome, bark out at the weather, is the position that puts the most depth where the bending is.
It also puts the densest outer wood on the wet side and leaves both flat sawn faces where the seam key wants them.
equations: the wedge is not symmetric, so which way it faces is a decision.
turn it about its own long axis and the SHAPE stays the same
while the STIFFNESS does not, because bending in a shell is
radial: in and out along the dome's own radius.
a pair at one seam: both points inward, toward the centre of the dome
a pair at one seam: points apart, each into the middle of its own triangle
a pair at one seam: both points outward, away from the centre, at the sky
a pair at one seam: points toward each other, across the seam
area is 6.28 in2 in all four -- rotation moves no wood
but S runs 1.63 to 2.05 in3, a factor of 1.25
Pointing the wedge at the dome's centre puts 1.25 times the bending stiffness under the same wood, for free, by turning the stick before it goes down.

chapters.title: A dome from whatever the woodlot gives
chapters.promise: I need a house, not a reference standard for symmetry.
narration: Everything so far assumed one trunk diameter. Trees do not sort themselves, and mine run ten to fifteen inches.
So solve the same dome at both ends of that range. What moves is much less than you would think, and what does move lands somewhere harmless.
Not one angle changes. The fold between panels is a property of the subdivision and has never heard of the log.

What changes is how far each member sits back from its ideal edge, and therefore how wide the key between two panels has to be -- which is the one part that was already variable. The surface ends up slightly restless where a thin member meets a fat one.
I am building somewhere to live, not something a friend can hold a straightedge against.
equations: 10-15 in logs, not one angle changes

chapters.title: What actually moves
chapters.promise: The same shell solved at both ends of the range.
narration: The fold angles come out identical to six decimal places at both ends, which is the whole argument in one line: the geodesic solution does not know what a log is. The blank length barely shifts.

The offset and the key take up the rest, and the key was already absorbing the dihedral spread, so it is doing one more job it was already shaped for. And the strength question is settled by the thinnest member on the building, not the average.
At ten inches a sector still clears the crossover, so every log in the range is stiffer than the stud it replaces.
equations: the rest of this film assumes one trunk diameter. Real trees run 10 to 15 in and do not sort themselves.
solve the same dome at both ends of that range and see what moves:
fold angles: 18.029 to 22.459 deg at 10 in
fold angles: 18.029 to 22.459 deg at 15 in
IDENTICAL. not one angle in the shell depends on the log size,
because the dihedral is a property of the subdivision
member sits back from its ideal edge, further by 0.96 in on the fat logs
key base 1.95-2.33 in thin, 2.93-3.50 in fat
blank length shifts by 0.76 in across the whole range
outer surface steps by up to 2.50 in where a thin member meets a fat one
and the strength question is settled by the THINNEST member present:
= 187 % of a dressed 2x4's area and 131 % of its bending
and 10 in clears the 9.14 in crossover, so the whole range does
Mixing 10 to 15 inch logs changes no angle, moves the blank by 0.76 in, and lands the rest in the key. You get a shell with a slightly restless surface and a house that is entirely sound.

chapters.title: Why there is a key in every seam
chapters.promise: Put the variation somewhere it is cheap to be wrong.
narration: Neighbouring triangles in a geodesic shell meet at an angle, and it is not the same angle everywhere. That fold is what makes the thing a dome instead of a floor.

Because each panel carries its own member, a seam is two raw sawn faces looking at each other with a gap between them, and the gap changes seam by seam. You can close it by shaving the wood to suit each neighbour, which is a different bevel every time.
Or you can leave the structure alone and put the variation into a small tapered part that is not holding the building up.

chapters.title: The angle nobody wants to cut
chapters.promise: Better in a cheap part than in every stick.
narration: Here is the fold at every interior seam, and what is left over after two forty-five degree faces have folded toward each other. The spread is small in degrees and enormous in workshop terms, because it is a setup change on a saw, repeated once per seam, cut into structural members that are then not interchangeable.
Moving that variation into the key means the wood stays generic and the fussy part is small, cheap and replaceable.
equations: two panels meeting along one edge are not in the same plane.
the fold between them runs 18.03 to 22.46 deg
a spread of 4.43 deg across 55 interior seams
each panel brings its own member, so a seam has two raw sawn
faces 45 deg apart before anything folds
after folding, the gap left between them runs 22.54 to 26.97 deg
which is exactly 45 deg minus the fold
there are only two ways to close a gap that is never the same:
shave the wood to suit each seam -- a different bevel, 55 times
or leave the wood alone and fit a key that varies instead
the key's base runs 1.56 to 1.87 in
one part, cut on a taper, doing what would otherwise be a setup change per seam
The key exists so the 4.43 degrees of dihedral variation live in a small replaceable part instead of in every structural member of the building.

chapters.title: One flat board, forty panels
chapters.promise: The jig is not a drawing aid. It is what makes them identical.
narration: The fixture is a flat board with the panel's triangle struck on it once, three rails, six little plates and some clamps. The rails set each member across the panel by its sawn point line, never by its bark, because the bark is the part of a log that is different every time.
The red and green plates do something a drawing cannot. A sector dropped in rotated ninety degrees still looks plausible; against these plates it physically will not seat.
The fixture refuses the mistake instead of relying on someone noticing it.
equations: rails on the sawn point, not the bark

chapters.title: The cut that is never measured
chapters.promise: One end arrives finished. The other arrives too long, on purpose.
narration: The two ends of a member are made in completely different places. The butt is cut before assembly, off the jig, to the angle its neighbour presents.
It is the same cut for every member of a family, so it batches. The head is not cut at all.

It arrives long, hangs off the board, and stays long while all three butts are pulled up tight and the pinwheel closes. Only then does a saw run flat along the fence and take the head off at the plane the neighbouring member has already established.
Nothing is measured, and every error in stock length or butt angle walks away in the offcut instead of accumulating around the triangle.

chapters.title: What the fixture is enforcing
chapters.promise: Twelve steps, three constraints, and the offcut that buys accuracy.
narration: The fixture holds three things and nothing else: where the member sits across the panel, which way up it is turned, and the plane its head will be cut to. It is worth being precise about what the offcut buys.
Every stick has some error in it. Cut both ends to a measurement and those errors add up around the triangle until the last corner does not close.
Cut one end in place, against the neighbour, and the error has nowhere to accumulate. It leaves in the piece that falls on the floor.
equations: 40 triangles, 120 members, 120 corner joints -- all off one flat board
the fixture comes in 12 steps and holds three things:
a RAIL per member, set to the sawn point-axis, not the bark
a RED and a GREEN plate that make a wrongly-turned wedge physically refuse to seat
a FENCE at each head end, which is the plane the saw runs on
each member arrives with ONE cut already made:
the butt, cut to the angle its neighbour presents, batched
and one deliberate error: the head is left 6 in too long
three butts are pulled up, the loop closes, and only then is
each head sawn against its fence -- unmeasured, in place
the offcut is 60 ft per dome = 8.3 % of raw length
and 40 panels need only 4 physically different fixtures
Leaving 8.3 percent of the length as offcut is what buys the accuracy: error in stock length or butt angle leaves in the offcut instead of accumulating around the triangle.

chapters.title: What two trees make
chapters.promise: The building at the end of all of that.
narration: So this is what the arithmetic buys. Two pines off the property, converted with a chainsaw and a flat board, become a shell you can stand up in.

The floor area, the height and the member count all fall out of the longest useful piece the trees give, rather than the other way round. The building is sized by the wood, not the wood by the building.
That inversion is the part I would most like to hand to somebody else, because it is what makes the whole thing available to anyone with a saw and some trees.

chapters.title: The dome the trees size
chapters.promise: Solved backwards from the longest member the wood gives.
narration: Normally you pick a dome diameter and then go and find members long enough for it. This is the same solve run the other way: start from the piece the tree actually yields and ask what shell that makes.
The chord factors do not change, so the radius, the floor area and the member count all follow from one length.
equations: the tree sets the strut length, so it also sets the dome:
12 ft section, cut once = 6 ft members
the longest pinwheel member is 72.0 in
solve for the radius that makes that true:
160 - 120 = 40 left for the floor and the fit-out
timber standing in the frame = 672 ft of member
Two trees, 120 members, a 22 foot dome with 380 square feet of floor -- and 40 sticks still spare.

chapters.title: The shape is doing the work
chapters.promise: None of this is a claim that split wood is better wood.
narration: A wedge from a small tree is not a stronger stick than a stud. It is a cheaper stick, a faster stick, a stick that leaves far more of the tree standing as structure instead of as shavings, and a stick that can be made without owning a factory.
From a big enough tree it is also simply the stronger stick, and I gave you the diameter where that flips. But what makes it sufficient either way is the building.
A triangulated shell puts its members mostly in axial load, doubles every interior edge, and asks only that the ends can be made to meet. So the honest version is not that I found a better board.
It is that I picked a building that does not need one.

chapters.title: The whole argument on one page
chapters.promise: Wood, machines, hands, rate, value, cost, strength, angle and cuts.
narration: This is everything the film just showed, in the order it showed it, with the number attached to each line. One line still carries a condition rather than a boast: below about nine inches of trunk the single wedge is the weaker member and this stops working.
That stays on the page. Change the assumptions and the money moves.
Change the log or the dome and the geometry moves with it, because all of it is computed and none of it is typed in.
equations: WOOD     88 % of the tree kept split, 45 % sawn -- 1.95x
MACHINE  3 fewer: SAWMILL, EDGER, PLANING MILL
HANDS    15 middle men removed between tree and wall
RATE     6 wedges/hour measured, 5 used for planning
VALUE    $10.00 of wood per wedge, $45/hour net of fuel
COST     $120 to cut this dome's frame against $1476 to buy it
STICK    226 % of a dressed stud in bending at 12 in trunk; under 9.1 in it would lose
EDGE     every interior edge carries two, 539 % of a stud's section
ANGLE    4.43 deg of dihedral variation lives in the key, not the timber
CUTS     one batched butt per member, one flush cut in place, 4 fixtures for 40 panels
Not one of those lines works on a rectangular building. They work because a triangulated shell will take any stick whose ends can be made to meet, and a split log is already that stick.

chapters.title: Two trees
chapters.promise: The whole woodpile is standing up.
narration: It will take me 2 whole pine trees to harvest all of the wood a 300 square foot house needs. No lumber yard and no delivery truck, just the trees already standing on the property, and one small chainsaw.

chapters.title: The fell line
chapters.promise: The hinge steers the tree. The saw only sets it free.
narration: It starts with a notch, cut into the side I want it to fall toward, and then a back cut from the other side, a little higher. The strip of wood left between the two is the hinge. It steers the tree all the way over, and it is why felling gets a chapter of its own before any of this is safe to try. The saw is a 38.2 cc hardware-store model with a 16 inch bar.

chapters.title: All at once
chapters.promise: Every section splits at the same time.
narration: Then everything happens at once. The crown comes off, the trunk is cut into 8 sections, 6 feet each, and every section splits into 8 wedges. That is 64 struts from one tree. With 3 trees it is 192, for a frame that needs 120.

chapters.title: Why split it
chapters.promise: Split, the log keeps most of itself.
narration: Why split it instead of milling it square? Because the only wood a split loses is the width of the cut. Of the 318 board feet in this trunk, the saw takes 40 and the wedges keep 278, which is 87.4 percent of the tree standing in the frame. The honest cost is the stick itself. From a small log, a single wedge is the weaker stick in bending, and it is the triangulated shell, not the wedge, that makes it enough.

chapters.title: Measured, and guessed
chapters.promise: What the next figures rest on.
narration: Before the days and the fuel, here is what those figures rest on. The fuel rate was measured, in one timed sitting with the tanks counted. The ripping hours come from the cutting rate, which was also measured. The day plan is a decision, not a result. And the size of the saw's tank is an estimate, because the listings disagree and nobody has checked this saw, so the fuel comes out as a range.
equations: MEASURED   fuel while ripping: 2 tanks an hour, one timed sitting
MEASURED   cutting rate: 30 struts in a 4-hour afternoon
DERIVED    ripping time: 120 struts at 7.5 an hour = 16 hours
DECIDED    the plan: felling days 1-2, bucking days 3-4, ripping days 5-8
ESTIMATED  the saw's tank: 0.28 to 0.37 L; the listings disagree
NOT METERED  fuel for felling and bucking: left out, not guessed
So the fuel is a range, and it is the ripping only

chapters.title: What it took
chapters.promise: 8 days of saw work, and a few gallons.
narration: The whole harvest takes 8 days: 2 of felling, 2 of bucking, and 4 of ripping. Ripping is the part that was timed with the fuel written down: 2 tanks an hour, for 16 hours. That is 32 tanks, and at 0.28 to 0.37 litres a tank, somewhere between 2.4 and 3.1 US gallons. Felling and bucking were never metered, so they are not in that number.

chapters.title: What the house numbers rest on
chapters.promise: Published, the author's, decided, estimated.
narration: Now the question every build gets asked: what is it worth? Before a single house figure, here is what they rest on. The published ones come from the home builders' association's cost survey, the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the builders' survey is a small one, which its own authors say. The 200,000 dollar house, the 100,000 dollar trailer, the 40 percent labor share and the 80 hours of shell work are my own round figures. The tax bracket is a decision. Everything else is an estimate, and it is labelled as one.
equations: PUBLISHED  NAHB 2024 cost survey: who gets a house's price, and 37 line items of building it (41 builders; not representative)
PUBLISHED  Census: 7.6 months, start to finish; BLS wages, May 2025
PUBLISHED  Lumber peak: $1,500 per 1,000 bd ft; +$35,872 on an average home
PUBLISHED  Manufactured homes: $86.62 a sq ft; factory split from 2002
THE AUTHOR'S  $200,000 house, $100,000 trailer, 40% labor, 80 hours of shell work
DECIDED    the 12% federal bracket; state tax left out
ESTIMATED  dealer 25%, labor by item, run share 35%, curve +25%
So every estimate below is a guess that can be changed, and says so

chapters.title: Where a house's time goes
chapters.promise: 7.6 months, most of it inside.
narration: A new house takes 7.6 months on average, from the first shovel to finished, by the Census Bureau's count, and 15.1 months when its owner builds it. One builder's week by week schedule shows where that time goes. 15 percent is the ground and the foundation. 10 percent is framing. 7.5 percent is pipes, wires and ducts. 27.5 percent is the inside: insulation, drywall, floors, trim, paint and fixtures. 10 percent is the outside, 15 percent the driveway, yard and clean up, and the last 15 percent is inspection and closing.

chapters.title: Where a house's money goes
chapters.promise: The land, the building, and the people who sell it.
narration: Now the money, in the shares the builders' survey found. Of a 200,000 dollar new house, 27,400 dollars is the land. 128,700 is the building itself. 33,400 is the builder's overhead and profit, and 10,500 is the commission, marketing and financing it takes to sell it. At the survey's national average, that much new house is only about 796 square feet.

chapters.title: Labor is not most of it
chapters.promise: Even at the record lumber price, labor is about a quarter.
narration: So is labor most of what you pay for? Not in a new house. Take my 40 percent of the building as labor, and it is 25.7 percent of the price. Then put the lumber at its record. In the spring of twenty twenty one, framing lumber topped 1,500 dollars a thousand board feet, and the builders worked out it added 35,872 dollars to an average new home. Price this house that way and it comes to 214,800: 82,200 in materials, 51,500 in labor, 9,800 in permits, fees and design, 27,400 for the land, 33,400 to the builder and 10,500 to sell it. Labor is 24 percent. About a quarter.

chapters.title: The trailer is built the other way
chapters.promise: A factory's labor is a smaller share still.
narration: A new manufactured home splits another way. Of a 100,000 dollar home, about 20,000 is the dealer's share. 46,000 is what the factory spends on materials, 16,800 is its payroll, and 17,200 is its overhead and profit. Factory labor is only 16.8 percent of the price. At the Census average of 86.62 dollars a square foot, that buys about 1,154 square feet, set up, without the land. The factory split is from the two thousand two Economic Census, the newest published in that detail, so read it as a shape more than a figure.

chapters.title: What the fortnight is worth
chapters.promise: Two weeks of one person, against buying the frame.
narration: Now the frame this film has been building. Framing is 16.6 percent of what it costs to build a new house, which is 10.7 percent of its price. For 300 square feet, bought at the national rate with the builder's share, the frame costs 9,798 dollars. The fortnight spends 492 dollars: the saw, the fuel, the hardware, and the two trees at what a timber buyer would pay for them standing. That keeps 9,306 dollars, for 80 hours of hands-on work. 116 dollars an hour. Against a manufactured home's cheaper rate it is 59. A carpenter's median wage is 29.12 an hour, and a typical worker takes home 19.69, so buying that frame would cost 498 hours of ordinary pay.

chapters.title: Every part of the house
chapters.promise: The same sum, stage by stage.
narration: Here is every part of the house, done the same way for 300 square feet: what it costs to buy, what the dome way still pays in money, and how many hours of a typical worker's take-home pay the difference is worth. Fees stay fees. The foundation is shorter, because a circle has the least edge for its floor. The skin is smaller but harder to finish, and the pipes and wires run from a central column instead of around the walls. The last line is the whole floor, if every hour of the work is yours.
equations: Site work: buy $4,973 · dome $3,708 · 64 h of pay
Foundations: buy $6,801 · dome $1,816 · 253 h of pay
Framing: buy $10,788 · dome $841 · 505 h of pay
Exterior: buy $8,741 · dome $3,788 · 251 h of pay
Pipes, wires, HVAC: buy $12,511 · dome $3,759 · 444 h of pay
Interior: buy $15,714 · dome $7,420 · 421 h of pay
Yard, driveway: buy $4,212 · dome $1,771 · 124 h of pay
Other: buy $1,343 · dome $631 · 36 h of pay
All: buy $65,082, dome way $23,733, if every hour of the work is yours

chapters.title: Where the saving comes from
chapters.promise: Most of it is building your own, not the shape.
narration: Stack it all up and the saving has four sources. Bought whole, the floor costs 65,100 dollars. 16,600 of that is the builder's and the seller's share, which anyone who builds their own house keeps, whatever its shape. 17,300 is labor you do yourself, paid in hours instead of money. 3,200 is lumber from your own trees instead of a yard. And 4,300 is the shape itself: 55 percent less framing, 40 percent less skin, a 12 percent shorter foundation, and runs 44 percent shorter from the central column. That leaves 23,700 dollars to pay.

chapters.title: What this does not show
chapters.promise: The half of the sum that does not flatter the dome.
narration: And what it does not show. 37 percent of what a house costs to build does not care about its shape: fees, windows, cabinets, appliances, floors, the driveway. Only the frame's hours were measured; the rest of that labor is weeks more of somebody's time, and wiring, plumbing and gas usually need a licensed trade and an inspection. A triangle is harder to finish than a flat wall, and the dome's laminate skin is its most expensive material. Against a manufactured home the gap is small: 300 square feet at a trailer's average price is 25,986 dollars, and the dome way pays 16,439 for the same parts, before your hours. And the biggest saving here, the builder's share and the labor, belongs to anyone who builds their own house, whatever its shape.

chapters.title: How much shelter does an hour buy
chapters.promise: Not how cheap the house is. How much shelter an hour buys.
narration: The case for this dome is not that it makes a house cheap. It is that it changes the trade between a person, their time, raw wood and shelter. This is one shell, 300 square feet, from 2 trees. The question worth asking is not how cheap the house is, but how much shelter one hour of your life can buy, and this way of building changes the answer.

chapters.title: A long chain, and a short one
chapters.promise: Income, tax, store, contractor, loan. Or tree, wedge, jig, shell.
narration: Conventional housing asks you to join a long chain. You sell hours for money, pay tax on it, buy lumber that was sawn, dried, shipped, stocked and marked up, hire the labor to put it together, and very often borrow for all of it for decades. This system shortens the chain. A tree is split into wedges, the wedges go into a jig, and the jig makes the shell. Part of your labor turns straight into structure, without passing through a paycheck, a tax bill, a store and a loan on the way.

chapters.title: The tree is the product
chapters.promise: Split, not sawn: the round log keeps its wood.
narration: A sawmill forces a round tree into rectangles. The wedge does not. An 8 inch log splits into 8 sectors, and each one keeps 6.28 square inches of wood, against 5.25 in a dressed two by four. That does not make every wedge stronger than every board; from a log that small, a single wedge is the weaker stick in bending. What it means is that very little happens between the tree and the frame: 8 operations, where a graded board takes 14.

chapters.title: The geometry does some of the work
chapters.promise: A wedge arrives with its angle already in it.
narration: An eighth of a log arrives with two split faces 45 degrees apart. The dome's panels fold at only 2 angles, 18.03 and 22.46 degrees. The wedge does not match them exactly, but it starts with useful angle already in it, and a shaped key takes up the rest, so nobody has to manufacture every angle out of a rectangle. That is the rule the whole system runs on: do not make every piece perfect; make the system force imperfect pieces into the right relationship.

chapters.title: Locate first, cut second
chapters.promise: The jig solves the geometry once, not for every stick.
narration: Custom timber work means measuring, transferring angles, fitting, checking and trimming, again and again. Here the jig decides where each member belongs and which way it turns. The members are left long, their ends hang past the triangle, and once the jig holds all three in their true relationship, the excess is cut flush. Locate accurately first; cut accurately second. The hard geometry is solved once, in the jig, and a complicated dome becomes 40 repeats of one job.

chapters.title: The figures this rests on
chapters.promise: The author's round numbers, beside the published ones.
narration: Now the money, and first what it rests on. These are my own round figures: bought space at 100 dollars a square foot, framing as 16 percent of it, 80 hours of hands-on shell work, and a 6.5 percent mortgage over 30 years. Beside them are the published ones. A new manufactured home averages 86.62 dollars a square foot, and a new site-built house about 217 without the land. My figures sit on the cautious side of both.
equations: THE AUTHOR'S  $100 a sq ft; framing 16% of it; 80 hours of shell work
THE AUTHOR'S  6.5% for 30 years; $25 an hour take-home; $800 cash
PUBLISHED  new manufactured home: $86.62 a sq ft (Census)
PUBLISHED  new site-built house: $216.94 a sq ft without land (NAHB)
PUBLISHED  framing 16.6% of building cost; median take-home $19.69 an hour (BLS)
So the author's figures sit on the cautious side of the published ones

chapters.title: What an hour produces
chapters.promise: Not a paycheck. Value you no longer have to buy.
narration: 300 square feet in 80 hours is 3.75 square feet an hour. At 100 dollars a square foot, that floor is worth 30,000 dollars finished, but framing did not create all of it; plumbing, wiring, windows and finishes are still to come. So take only the framing, 16 percent of it: 4,800 dollars. Divided by 80 hours, that is 60 dollars an hour. Nobody hands me that as a wage. A wage is what someone pays you for your hour; this is what your hour saves you from having to buy.

chapters.title: Why the hour beats a wage
chapters.promise: It replaces the wood as well as the work.
narration: Of that 4,800 dollars, the labor is 40 percent: 1,920 dollars, and over the same 80 hours that is 24 dollars an hour. That is the framing labor alone. The dome way produces 60, which is 2.5 times as much, an index of 250 where framing labor alone scores a hundred. Be clear about where that comes from: it is one over the labor share. You supply the labor, and you also replace the wood you would have bought. That second part is exactly what a wage comparison leaves out.

chapters.title: Debt makes it larger
chapters.promise: An avoided dollar can be an avoided interest-bearing dollar.
narration: Now suppose that framing would otherwise ride on a 30 year mortgage at 6.5 percent. Then 4,800 dollars does not stay 4,800; it becomes 10,922 dollars of payments. Spread over the same 80 hours, that is 137 dollars an hour. That is not a wage, and it is not today's money: it is payments that never have to be made, stretched across 30 years. Today's value is still 60 dollars an hour. But a dollar avoided before it enters a mortgage is a dollar that never collects interest.

chapters.title: Interest builds nothing
chapters.promise: No bedroom, no wall, no square foot.
narration: Take a 100,000 dollar mortgage at the same rate. Over 30 years you pay 127,544 dollars of interest on it, 227,544 in all. At 100 dollars a square foot, the interest alone would buy 1,275 square feet. Interest builds no bedroom, no workshop, no wall. It is the price of having the house before you have the money. Building directly does something else: effort becomes equity. Hours become members, members become panels, and panels become square feet.

chapters.title: Count it in hours of your life
chapters.promise: Money is stored labor.
narration: Here is the comparison that matters most. Buying that 4,800 dollar frame, at 25 dollars an hour take-home, takes 192 hours of work. Building it takes 80 hours, plus 32 more to earn its 800 dollars of cash, 112 hours in all. That keeps 80 hours of your life, 2 full working weeks, on one shell. And the typical worker takes home less than 25, about 19.69 an hour, which makes buying cost 244 hours instead.

chapters.title: When to build, and when to buy
chapters.promise: Build while your hour creates more than it earns.
narration: This is a rule, not an ideology. What building earns per hour is the money it avoids, less the cash it still costs, over the hours it takes. 4,800 less 800 is 4,000, and over 80 hours that is 50 dollars an hour. If you take home less than that, those hours are worth more building than working extra to buy the same frame. If you take home a good deal more, buying may be the better use of your time. Build while the value your hour creates beats what it earns after tax.

chapters.title: Out of the commodity chain
chapters.promise: Every member from a nearby tree is one less price shock.
narration: A conventional house also runs a long critical path, about 33 weeks from start to finish, carrying financing, weather, scheduling and overhead the whole way. And it rides on commodity lumber. In the spring of twenty twenty one, framing lumber topped 1,500 dollars a thousand board feet and added 35,872 dollars to an average new home. A dome still needs fasteners, glazing, wiring, plumbing and a foundation. But every structural member cut from a nearby tree instead of bought at a yard is one less exposure to that market. A tree on the land stops being scenery and becomes inventory.

chapters.title: The economic score
chapters.promise: One shell, on one sheet.
narration: Put one cycle on a single sheet. 300 square feet of shell in 80 hours. 4,800 dollars of commercial framing displaced. 60 dollars an hour of production value, 2.5 times the framing labor alone. 10,922 dollars of mortgage payments avoided, 137 an hour, and not a wage. 80 hours of life kept. A break-even of 50 dollars an hour. And one shell a year for 30 years is 144,000 dollars of framing and 9,000 square feet.
equations: 300 sq ft of shell in 80 hours: 3.75 sq ft an hour
$60 an hour production value; 2.5x the framing labor alone
$10,922 of 30-year payments avoided: $136.53 an hour, not a wage
80 hours of life kept, against earning $25 an hour to buy it
Worth building while your take-home is under $50 an hour
One shell a year for 30 years: $144,000 of framing, 9,000 sq ft
One hour: $60 of shelter today, $137 of payments never made

chapters.title: What the model does not promise
chapters.promise: A model, not a guarantee.
narration: None of this is a guarantee; it is a model. The 60 dollars an hour is money not spent, not money earned, and it only counts if you would otherwise have bought the frame. The frame is 16.6 percent of what a new house costs to build, and permits, wiring, plumbing, windows and finishes are still ahead, some of it needing a licensed trade and an inspection. The house labor budget I once compared against was 80,000 dollars; the builders' survey puts that house's labor nearer 51,491, about 39.01 dollars per working hour of the build, so the dome's 60 is 154 percent of it, not the same. And my 4,800 dollar frame is cheaper than either published price, 5,186 at a manufactured home's rate and 9,798 at a new house's, so the case is made at its weakest.

chapters.title: The why
chapters.promise: More shelter from each hour of a finite life.
narration: So the reason to build this way is not that domes look different, or that ordinary houses are bad, or that lumber is useless. It is that conventional housing is built around buying highly processed materials and buying specialized labor, and this asks whether the owner can take back part of both. If the answer is yes, the rest follows: less processing, less bought lumber and labor, less financing, less interest, less exposure to prices and schedules, and more use of what is already standing on the land. The question is not how cheap the house is, but how much shelter an hour of your life can buy. On these numbers, this way of building changes that exchange rate. That is the reason.

chapters.title: What is a pine worth
chapters.promise: Not one price. A ladder of them.
narration: What is a pine tree worth? Ask a timber buyer, a firewood dealer, a sawmill and a builder, and each gives a different answer, because a tree has no single value. It has a ladder of them, and the rung it reaches depends on what somebody does to it, and on how much of it they keep. Take one representative pine, the log the wedge film is built on: 60 feet of usable stem, 15 inches across at the butt and 5.5 at the top. Let us climb its ladder, one rung at a time.

chapters.title: What the ladder rests on
chapters.promise: Measured, published and mine, kept apart.
narration: Every rung rests on a figure, so here they all are before any of them is used. The tree is my representative pine, the wedge film's own log. Some figures are published: a sawmill's price for common pine, what standing pine sells for, and the size of a cord. Some are mine: a mill keeps 60 percent of the stem as the lumber it wants, splitting keeps 88, and the sawing rate and the cord price are mine too. The simulator checks both recoveries. Sawn into two by fours, this log keeps only 45 percent; split, it keeps 88.4 before any trimming. So the mill gets the benefit of the doubt, and the wedge gets no more than the model allows.
equations: THE AUTHOR'S  a representative pine: 60 ft of stem, 15 in to 5.5 in
THE AUTHOR'S  60% kept by a mill; 88% by splitting; 90 cu ft of wood a cord
THE AUTHOR'S  sawing $0.60/bd ft; a cord $275 picked up, $300 delivered
THE AUTHOR'S  $4,800 of framing for the shell; it uses 1.5 trees, 2 felled
PUBLISHED  pine $1.50/bd ft; stumpage $23.23/ton; a cord 128 cu ft stacked
CHECK  this log in the simulator: sawn to 2x4s 45%, split 88.4% before trimming
So the mill gets the benefit of the doubt, not the wedge

chapters.title: The stem, in board feet
chapters.promise: 442 board feet, and about $24 standing.
narration: The usable stem is a long, tapering cone: 36.8 cubic feet of solid wood. A cubic foot holds 12 board feet, so that is 442 board feet, the most that any method could ever get out of it. Green, it weighs about 1.01 tons, and at the published stumpage of $23.23 a ton, it sells standing for about 24 dollars. That is the twenty-dollar pine. Every rung above this one is something somebody does to it.

chapters.title: Burned, it is heat
chapters.promise: Burned, it is worth its heat: $113.
narration: The first rung up is fire. This stem is 36.8 cubic feet of solid wood. A cord is 4 feet high, 4 deep and 8 long, 128 cubic feet stacked, but air fills the gaps, and only about 90 of those cubic feet are wood. So the stem makes 0.41 of a cord. At 275 dollars a cord picked up, that is 113 dollars, or about 123 delivered. That values the tree for its heat. Every rung above this one values it for its shape.

chapters.title: Split, not sawn
chapters.promise: A mill wants rectangles. A wedge takes the log as it is.
narration: Now shape. A sawmill has to turn a round log into rectangles, and everything outside them leaves as slabs, edgings and sawdust. The picture is the simulator's, packing this log with two by fours, and it keeps only 45 percent. A good mill cutting mixed sizes does better, so I give it 60 percent. Splitting follows the round log instead of fighting it. From the same stem it keeps 88 percent, 389 board feet, where the mill keeps 265. That is 124 more board feet of usable wood from one tree, because the corners of a log are not bad wood. They are only not rectangular.

chapters.title: Almost half as much again
chapters.promise: 46.7% more wood, 70% less thrown away.
narration: Put the two recoveries side by side. 88 percent over 60 is 1.467, so splitting gets 46.7 percent more usable wood out of the same tree. Now look at what is left behind. The mill leaves 40 percent of the stem, 177 board feet of it. Splitting leaves 12 percent, 53. That is 70 percent less of the tree thrown away, from the same tree, with the same saw.

chapters.title: The same wood from fewer trees
chapters.promise: 2 trees split give as much wood as 2.93 sawn.
narration: A 300 square foot shell needs 2 of these trees felled. Each one, split, gives 389 board feet, so the pair gives 778. A mill keeping 60 percent gets 265 from a tree, so to match the pair it would need 2.93 trees. Put the other way round, the mill's way needs almost half as many trees again, and a tree not cut is a tree still standing, or a tree left for the next building.

chapters.title: Priced as lumber
chapters.promise: Priced as wood, splitting is worth $186 more a tree.
narration: Now put a price on the wood. The split yield, 389 board feet, at one sawmill's list price for common pine of $1.50 a board foot, is worth 584 dollars. The sawn yield, 265 board feet, is worth 398. That is 186 dollars more from one tree, and 372 from the shell's 2. And the sawn path still has to pay for the sawing: at my rate of $0.60 a board foot, about 159 dollars for this tree.

chapters.title: Built, it replaces framing
chapters.promise: Not what the wood would sell for. What it does.
narration: The next rung is not a price for wood at all. In the dome, these trees become a shell of 300 square feet. At 100 dollars a square foot, with framing 16 percent of it, the framing that shell replaces is worth 4,800 dollars, the figure the last film built. The frame uses 90 feet of trunk, 1.5 trees' worth, but 2 are felled, so I divide by 2: each tree's share is 2,400 dollars. That is use value: not what the wood would fetch, but what you no longer have to buy, because the wood is doing the job.

chapters.title: Carried on a mortgage
chapters.promise: What the same framing costs when it is borrowed.
narration: Most framing is not paid for in cash. It rides on a mortgage. On a 30 year loan at 6.5 percent, 4,800 dollars of framing becomes 10,922 dollars of payments, and this tree's half of that is 5,461. Read this rung carefully. It is nominal dollars, paid a month at a time for 30 years, not money in your hand today. But it is money a household never has to send to a lender, because a tree did the job instead.

chapters.title: The ladder
chapters.promise: One tree, every rung.
narration: Now put the rungs together. Standing, about 24 dollars. Burned, 113. Sawn into lumber, 398. Split into wedge stock, 584. Built into structure, 2,400. And as the mortgage payments that structure avoids, 5,461, nominal, over 30 years. It is the same tree on every rung. What changes is how much of it is kept, and how far along the chain it travels before anyone has to pay for the next step.

chapters.title: The wood did not get better
chapters.promise: It got used.
narration: Compare the structure rung with the ones below it. 2,400 dollars is 21 times what the tree brings as firewood, 6 times its sawn lumber, and 4.1 times its split stock. The wood did not get better between those rungs. The same fibres, from the same tree, stopped being sold as a commodity and started doing a job. The biggest step on this ladder is not from the woods to the mill. It is from material to function.

chapters.title: What the tree is worth to me
chapters.promise: What it replaces, less what it costs me to make it do so.
narration: So here is the valuation that matters to a builder. A tree is worth to me what it can replace, less the cash it costs to process, less what my own hours could have earned instead. This tree replaces 2,400 dollars of framing. Its share of the work is 40 hours, and at 25 dollars an hour take-home, that is 1,000 dollars of my time. Its share of the cash is half the shell's 800, 400 dollars. That leaves 1,000 dollars. A pine that sells for 24 dollars standing is worth 1,000 to the person who builds with it, after paying for their own time. With the fortnight's actual receipts of 492 dollars, it is 1,154.

chapters.title: The household as the whole chain
chapters.promise: Logger, mill, yard, framer and lender, kept at home.
narration: This is vertical integration, at the scale of one household. A commercial house pays every hand between the stump and the wall: the logger, the hauler, the mill, the kiln, the yard, the framer, and very often the lender. Each one takes a margin, and every margin is inside the price. This method does not make those businesses unnecessary for everyone. It lets one owner do the few steps a chainsaw and a jig can do, and keep what those steps would have cost. That is where the rungs above the wood come from.

chapters.title: What the ladder does not say
chapters.promise: The generous figures, and the ones against me.
narration: Three cautions, because a ladder like this is easy to oversell. First, my mill figure is generous to the mill: the simulator's own packing of this log keeps 45 percent, and I used 60. Second, my sawing rate may be high. A survey of portable sawmill owners in 2010 found them charging $0.20 to $0.30 a board foot. Prices have risen since, but the sawn path may cost less than I said. Third, the top two rungs are not cash. The 2,400 dollars counts only if you would otherwise have bought the frame, and the financed rung is nominal payments, spread over 30 years.

chapters.title: Thousands of dollars of structure
chapters.promise: The difference is what you do with it.
narration: So a twenty-dollar pine is not a twenty-dollar pine. On the stump it brings about 24 dollars. Burned, 113. Sawn, 398. Split, 584. Built into a shell, it replaces 2,400 dollars of framing, and 5,461 of payments on a loan. The tree is the same on every rung. What moves it up the ladder is how much of it you keep, and how many of the steps between the tree and the wall you are willing to take yourself.

the model, and the wiring on the floor was routed to reach it.

chapters.title: Glass Studio Loft
chapters.promise: Four frequency, glazed, on a deck: the expensive, beautiful end.
narration: Raise the frequency and the shell gets rounder and much more
complicated: two hundred and fifty struts instead of a hundred and
sixty five. Every panel here is glass, which is why you can see the
furniture through the wall, and why the shader is putting a highlight
on the panels facing the sun. It stands on a wood deck rather than a
slab.

chapters.title: Split-Log Homestead
chapters.promise: Hubless, framed from split logs, cedar shakes over the top.
narration: This is the design this whole project argues for. Two frequency,
hubless doubled framing, quarter wedges split straight from logs.
There is not one hub connector in the building. Every triangle brings
its own three members and bolts to its neighbours, and the cedar
shakes you can see are a cladding layer sitting over the sheathing,
not a texture painted on it.

chapters.title: Whole Trunk Lodge - 20 ft
chapters.promise: Whole trunks, sized so the longest member is just under twenty feet.
narration: Now use the tree whole. The radius is set so the longest member lands
just under twenty feet, which is what two people can actually move.
Sixty five round trunks, canvas stretched between them, gravel
underneath. It is the largest floor in the catalogue by a wide
margin and it is framed from the fewest pieces of anything here.

chapters.title: Grow Dome
chapters.promise: Aluminium and polycarbonate: the greenhouse configuration.
narration: The same three frequency skeleton as the workshop, framed in
aluminium and glazed in twinwall polycarbonate, with grow racks and
water storage inside. The geometry did not change at all. Only the
material list did, and the price came down by nearly half.

chapters.title: Hex Cell Pavilion
chapters.promise: A hexagonal cell frame in structural steel.
narration: Not everything here is triangulated the same way. The hex cell style
groups the geometry into hexagonal tiles on a steel frame, and the
panels are composite hexagons with a seam bead around each one. It is
heavier and dearer than anything timber, and it looks like nothing
else on the site.

chapters.title: Continuous Steel Arc Hangar
chapters.promise: Curved ribs running over the shell instead of straight struts.
narration: The hangar swaps short straight struts for twelve continuous steel
arcs and three rings, with fabrication and site power equipment
inside it. Two frequency, eight metre radius, open between the ribs.
This is what the same geometry looks like when a steel shop builds it
instead of a carpenter.

chapters.title: Rebar Garden Dome
chapters.promise: A dense meridian and ring lattice, bent from rebar.
narration: Rebar is the cheapest structural steel there is, and it bends, so the
tool draws it as twenty two meridians and seven rings rather than
sticks between hubs. Seven thousand dollars, which is the cheapest
building in the catalogue, and it is the one closest to what people
actually put up in a back yard on a weekend.

chapters.title: Concrete Monocoque Form
chapters.promise: The frame as formwork for a poured shell.
narration: Here the frame is not the building, it is the formwork. Rebar and
shuttering panels carry a poured concrete shell, with shoring jacks,
scaffold, a mixer and a bender on the floor. The dome is doing the
thing concrete is best at, standing in pure compression, and it is by
some distance the heaviest thing here.

chapters.title: Woodland Hex Mirror
chapters.promise: Hexagonal mirror tiles that reflect the site back at you.
narration: The mirror designs exist because the renderer can do it. Those tiles
are reflecting a sky and a tree line the shader computes per pixel,
which is why the dome looks different from every angle as the camera
moves. Structurally it is the same three frequency shell as the
workshop.

chapters.title: Woodland Square Mirror
chapters.promise: The same trick at four frequency, on square tiles.
narration: Four frequency on a steel frame, square mirror tiles instead of
hexagons. More panels, each smaller, so the reflection breaks up
finer. Between the two mirror designs you can see exactly what
frequency does to a faceted surface: it stops looking like a machine
and starts looking like a curve.

chapters.title: Treehouse Canopy Dome
chapters.promise: An elevated dome on a supported timber platform.
narration: The smallest one, and the only one that is not on the ground. A two
frequency hex tile dome on a timber platform with a central trunk,
six posts, braces and a ladder, all of which the tool builds because
the foundation menu has a treehouse platform in it. Six hundred
square feet, up in the canopy.

chapters.title: One dome, step by step
chapters.promise: The tool's own construction order, played end to end.
narration: The mesh is not assembled in a random order. The builder emits it the
way a trailer home is manufactured: site prep, then the slab, then
the floor layout, the frame from the base ring upward, the hubs, the
doorway, the sheathing bottom to top, the cladding, then rough
electrical, rough plumbing, partitions, equipment, and finally the
monitoring system.
The ring on the floor is where the record says the crew is standing
for the step on screen, and the hours are the tool's own estimate for
the work done so far.

chapters.title: The labour model, phase by phase
chapters.promise: Three hundred and forty eight work steps, grouped.
narration: Those steps add up, and grouping them says something useful about
where a dome's time actually goes. The frame, which is the part
everybody pictures when they think about building a dome, is not the
expensive phase in hours.
This is a model, not a stopwatch, and I want to be clear about that:
it is an estimate attached to each work step. But it is the same
estimate applied to every design, so comparing two of them is fair
even where the absolute number is soft.
equations: Timber Workshop: 348 work steps, in build order:
two people, eight hour days: 6.1 days
97 hours is the tool's estimate, not a stopwatch -- but it is the same estimate for every design, so the comparisons between them hold even where the absolute number does not

chapters.title: Frequency
chapters.promise: One radius, four subdivisions, all four built.
narration: Now the menus, one at a time, and this is the first of them. Same
radius, same material, same foundation: only the number of times each
face is divided changes.
One frequency is twenty five struts in one length. Four frequency is
two hundred and fifty in six lengths. Frequency buys you a smoother
shell and charges you in part variety, which is the thing that
actually slows a build down.

chapters.title: The four dials, and why they are countable
chapters.promise: Radius, strut width, recess and pad size move in fixed steps.
narration: The tool also has sliders, and sliders look like they have infinite
settings. They do not: each one moves in a fixed step, and those
steps are written in the menu code, so they can be counted exactly
like the drop-downs can.
And not one of them changes the part count. Doubling the radius gives
you four times the floor off the same list of operations, which is
the whole economic argument for this shape.

Foundation size       1 to 1.6  step 0.05    13 settings   x radius
446,823 settings from four dials, and not one of them changes the part count: frequency alone decides how many pieces there are

chapters.title: Six ways to join the same sticks
chapters.promise: Hub and strut, hubless, hex cell, arcs, lattice, formwork.
narration: The frame style menu changes how the members meet, and it changes the
building far more than the material does. Hub and strut is the
classic. Hubless doubled gives every triangle its own three members.
Hex cell groups them into hexagons. The arc and lattice styles throw
out straight struts entirely and run continuous ribs over the shell.
Formwork treats the frame as shuttering for something poured.

chapters.title: The six, counted -- including where the tool argues with itself
chapters.promise: And one disagreement inside the tool, said out loud.
narration: Here they are as numbers, off the same shell. The interesting one is
at the bottom, and it is not flattering.
Two of these styles report hub connectors in the bill of materials
that their own assembly never fits. The picture and the price
disagree. The picture is the one to believe, because it is the
assembly, so treat those two totals as high by their hub line.
I would rather this film state that than quietly average it away.

Rebar Lattice          bills $596 for 61 hub connectors its own assembly never fits
