chapters.title: A thing we found out the hard way
chapters.promise: No panel of this dome fits a four-foot sheet. Not in any rotation.
narration: One finding, because it changed how the thing gets made.

We assumed the core would be cut triangle by triangle out of ordinary four-by-eight sheet. It cannot be. A triangle cannot get narrower than its own shortest altitude no matter how you turn it, and both of this dome's triangles are wider than forty-eight inches.
So the core is sheeted across the frame and the joints are taped, which is how a boat is built anyway. We would rather find that here, in a model, than halfway through a production run.

chapters.title: The top of the dome is a socket
chapters.promise: Power and water come up the middle and out through the apex.
narration: Now the part the whole system hangs off.

Power, water and drain arrive in the middle of the pad. They come up through the floor into a column that carries the shower, the sink, the drain and the outlets at working height. And then they keep going -- up past the ceiling, through a sleeve at the apex, and out.
So the top of this dome is not a roof. It is a socket. A gasketed cap bolts down over it: meant to stay shut for years, meant to come off in ten minutes.
Which means every service in the building is already on the outside of the weathertight surface before anybody has decided what to plug in.

chapters.title: Everything else snaps onto the outside
chapters.promise: Fan, water heater, cooling, shower. None of them cut a new hole.
narration: Under that cap, a line runs down the outside of the shell to a panel hanging off the rim.

The panel sits outside the footprint -- it does not eat any of your two hundred and seventy-seven square feet -- and it reaches back in through one gasketed port. Modules snap into it. An exhaust fan. A tankless water heater. A cooling unit. A shower.

The point is what does not happen. Adding a service to this building never cuts a new hole in a surface that was keeping the rain out. The hole already exists, it is at the top, and it has a cap on it.

chapters.title: The core moves to the next dome
chapters.promise: You buy the plumbing once. The shell is the thing that grows.
narration: And because the services are a column rather than a system built into the walls, they come out.

Unbolt it, cap the lines, crate it. It goes into the next dome. Outgrow this one, build a bigger frame, lift the core across, and the part you paid a plumber and an electrician for does not get bought twice.
That is what we mean by modular, and we mean it literally. Not 'our product has options'. The physical object comes out and goes into the next one.

chapters.title: What buying it once is worth
chapters.promise: A fifth of the dome's materials, and it walks to the next build.
narration: Put a number on it.
The core -- the column, the manifold, the drain, the sub-panel, the light, the fan and the cooling unit -- is about a fifth of everything material in the dome.
Moving it costs a couple of hundred dollars. Buying a second one costs what the first one cost. So every move is that difference, spent on a bigger shell instead of on the same plumbing again.

that is 30% of everything material in the dome.

chapters.title: It gets warmer every winter
chapters.promise: Lift the shell. Add a layer. Put the shell back.
narration: The cavity ships empty, and that is on purpose.

Because the shell comes off, insulation is not a thing you decide once at the factory. Lift it, lay in a quilted layer, put it back. Six hundred dollars, an afternoon, and the R-value of the building goes up. Do it again next season.
People push back on this, so: put on seven t-shirts and tell me how cold you are. It is the same argument, and the fabric is a waste stream.
A finished house does not get warmer every winter. This one does, for as long as somebody owns it and feels like it.

chapters.title: This only works as a system
chapters.promise: The landowner rents ground. You own the house. Nobody owns both.
narration: Step back, because none of this makes sense as a product on its own.

A landowner builds pads and rents them. That is passive income with no building to maintain -- nobody can wreck a house they are renting, because the house is not the landowner's. They own the ground and the hookups, and that is all.
Which is exactly what lets a dome be sold for what a dome costs, instead of what a dome plus a foundation plus a piece of land costs. Nobody is buying all three at the same time.

And the joining hardware is made to fit this dome and the next two sizes up. So when the time comes for a bigger one, the hardware goes up with you, and so does the utility core. It is a house that gets better instead of a house you finish paying for.

chapters.title: The ground is not ours and it is not yours
chapters.promise: The landowner builds the pad. It stays when the dome leaves.
narration: Here is the half of tiny-house pricing that everybody adds together and should not.

A dome needs somewhere to stand: a deck on blocks, a moisture barrier, a port for the services, a tank, some storage under the floor. That is the landowner's build. It happens once, it stays in the ground, and the next dome lands on the same port.
We design to hook onto it. We do not sell it, and we do not put it in the price of the dome -- because if we did, you would be buying a deck every time you moved.

chapters.title: The platform, built one course at a time
chapters.promise: Piers, beams, joists, boards. A hundred and sixteen of them.
narration: Before any of that lands anywhere, somebody builds the thing it lands on -- and this is the part people imagine is expensive.

It is not. It is a list of boards. Gravel goes down and gets compacted. Precast piers sit on it. Doubled two-by-six beams go across the piers, joists across the beams at sixteen inches, and deck boards across the joists. Two coats of sealer and it is done. A hundred and sixteen boards, about three thousand dollars, and two people can do it in a weekend.

And here is the part that surprised us when we costed it properly. A concrete slab is *cheaper* than this deck. Concrete is cheap by the yard and this is only a few yards; framing lumber is not cheap by the foot any more. Pouring a ring and framing the middle is more expensive than either.

So we are not going to tell you wood is the cheap option, because it is not. Wood is the option that comes apart. Unbolt the piers and the ground goes back to being ground -- and that is the whole reason a pad is a reasonable thing to try instead of a foundation you are stuck with.

narration: Three things we are going to say against our own pitch, because a proposal that only shows its good numbers is not a proposal.

The cavity ships empty. Six hundred dollars and an afternoon buys a layer, and you can keep doing that for years -- but on day one this is a weathertight shell, not a winter house, and somebody has to do that work.
The frame wastes wood. Eighty percent more stock than a dome that shares its struts. We think the joint is worth it; the arithmetic does not care what we think.

And you may have noticed that sits awkwardly next to chapter three, where splitting a log took twice as much of the tree as milling it. Both are true, and they are about different things -- one is how much of a trunk you keep, the other is how many sticks the dome needs. chapters.title: Two things that multiply
chapters.promise: A dome has 41% less skin. The paint takes 15% off what is left.
narration: Here is where the shape starts paying you back.

A dome of this floor area has about forty-one percent less outside surface than a box with the same floor. Less skin to lose heat through in winter and less to gain it through in summer. That is free and it is already true.

Now paint the weather face with one of the barium sulphate radiative coatings. Those reflect almost all of the sun and radiate heat straight out through the atmospheric window, which means a surface under a clear sky can sit *below* air temperature. On this shell that takes another fifteen percent off the cooling load.

And those two multiply rather than add, because the second one works on what the first one left. Against a painted box of the same floor, this dome needs about half. Which is why the whole design cooling load of a two hundred and seventy-seven square foot house comes out under four thousand BTU an hour.

chapters.title: The buildings a homestead wants second
chapters.promise: A gym. A study. A guest room. A workshop. A garage.
narration: Last thing, and it is the one most people actually want first.

Not everybody needs a house. Most people who would build one of these already have somewhere to live, and what they are short of is a second building. A gym that is not the spare bedroom. A study with a door that shuts. Somewhere for guests that is not your sofa. A workshop. A garage with one wide opening across three base bays.
Every one of those is the same hundred and twenty members, the same pad, the same core and the same hardware. The difference is which panels are in the bays.

And because it is panels, the building can change its mind. A nursery becomes a study becomes a guest room. The gym becomes the guest house when your parents visit. That is not a marketing line -- it is what happens when the wall is something that lifts out.

That is the manufacturing argument, and it is the whole reason any of this is affordable.

chapters.title: A dome is a head, and it wears hats
chapters.promise: One waterproof layer, on the outside. Everything under it stays dry.
narration: I stood lookout in the Arctic Circle.

Forward and aft lookout means you are outside the skin of the ship, in the weather, for hours. You do not stay warm by wearing one very good thing. You wear a lot of ordinary things, and then you put one waterproof shell over the lot. Ours was a pumpkin suit, and it was the only waterproof layer any of us had on.
That is this building. A dome is a head. Bare, it is a head in the cold. Put a knit hat on it, then another over that -- and the second one has to be a size up, because the first one is in the way.
Then one waterproof cap over everything. The layers underneath are not waterproof and they must not be. They are warm because they are dry.
Put a second waterproof layer underneath them and you have built a bag that collects your own sweat. On a building that is called a moisture trap, and it rots the thing from the inside.

chapters.title: A mast through the column, and a floor that comes later

A mast runs through the utility column: steel core where the strength is, timber cladding everywhere else. Structure and services share one hole in the building.

chapters.title: Three things at once
chapters.promise: Quilters, pad hosts, dome owners. Each one needs the other two.
narration: This is not a campaign to sell domes.

A dome's insulation is a quilted layer of recycled clothing -- about a hundred and thirty t-shirts a layer. It is the only building insulation we know of that a person can make at a kitchen table. So we want a register of people who will sew them, paid and listed, not a charity drive.

A pad host has land and does not want to be a landlord. You maintain a deck and a service connection -- not a roof, not a boiler, not somebody's kitchen. The building is theirs and it leaves when they do.

A dome with nobody to quilt for it is a cold dome. A dome with nowhere to stand is a kit in a garage. A pad with no dome on it is a deck. That is why it is one campaign.

A utility core is the one part of this dome that is identical in every dome we make -- every size, every fit-out, every shape -- because the interface it plugs into never changes. So it is the first thing worth learning to build, and the first thing worth building a jig for.
Fourteen steps, five stages, about seven hours once you have done a few. Your first will take closer to seventeen, and anybody who tells you otherwise has not built one.

Load centre at chest height on the dry face, inlet at the base. Feeder to the main lugs, strain relief at both ends, and every lug torqued to the figure printed inside the panel door -- with a torque screwdriver, not by feel. A loose terminal is how a panel burns, and it is the failure nobody sees coming.

Four breakers. Outlet ring, lighting, the window unit, and one spare that exists so the first module somebody snaps on does not need this door opened again. Label them in writing, on the door, now -- not from memory in a year.

chapters.title: Close it, prove the cap, stand it up
chapters.promise: 2 steps, 50 minutes.
narration: Close it, prove the cap, stand it up.

Sleeve on the chase, cap on the sleeve, six catches set so the gasket compresses evenly all the way round. Then open and close it five times on the bench. If it is stiff down here it is impossible at the top of a dome in the rain, and that cap is the one thing between the building and the weather.

Cover on captive fasteners so there is no bag of screws to lose. Then two people stand it up and it goes onto the pad's service port as one object -- and every joint you made in the last thirteen steps is still reachable with that cover off.

chapters.promise: Twenty-three lines. None of them exotic.
narration: And the shopping list, which is the least exciting slide here and the one people actually screenshot.

Twenty-three lines, and nothing on it is exotic. PEX and crimp rings, ABS and cement, a load centre and four breakers, four sections of insulated chase, and a cap. Every one of these is a thing you can buy this afternoon from somewhere that is already near you.
Parts come to about fourteen hundred dollars. Labour at shop rate is two hundred more once you are practised. That is the object that turns a frame and a platform into a building with services in it.

chapters.title: One core, every dome
chapters.promise: Build it once. It moves to the next dome when you outgrow this one.
narration: Last thing, and it is the reason this film is separate from the others.

This object is not consumed by the dome it goes into. It unbolts from four joints and a lift, and it goes into the next one. When somebody outgrows a stem cell and builds the size up, the core they built on a bench in a weekend goes with them.
Which means the seven hours you just watched is not seven hours per dome. It is seven hours, once, for as long as you keep building.

lessons.brand: THE STEM CELL DOME / THE SEAM
lessons.title: The seam does four jobs

chapters.title: The channel is already there
chapters.promise: 55 seams, 309 feet of void.
narration: Two sawn faces meeting at an angle cannot close flush.
So every one of this dome's 55 seams carries a void running its whole length. 309 feet of it, threaded through the structure, touching every panel, arriving at the apex and at the base ring.
You are going to fill it with something. This film is about what.

chapters.title: What is actually in there
chapters.promise: A key, and room around it.
narration: Open the frame and you can see the shape of the problem.

The key fills the angle the two faces leave. It does not fill the channel -- there is a run of usable section above it and below it, the whole length of every seam, and it is the only continuous void in the building that reaches both the weather and the ground.

chapters.title: Rain in at the ridge
chapters.promise: 185 gallons an inch.
narration: First job: guttering.

A slot along the outer cap takes water where it already runs. The seam is the low line between two panels, which is where a roof sends water anyway. Under the slot is a gutter with suction inlets, and under that a drain to the tank.
One inch of rain on this roof is 185 gallons. The building's guttering is inside its structure rather than bolted onto its edge.

chapters.title: The air barrier
chapters.promise: 4 pascals, and a leak stops being a leak.
narration: Second job, and it is the one that changes how you think about leaks.

Run the fan so the inside sits about 4 pascals above outside, and the net flow at every gap is outward. A gap in an inward-leaking building admits weather. The same gap in an outward-flowing one does not, because the air is going the wrong way for anything to ride in on.
It is 18 cubic feet a minute over 309 feet of seam -- a bathroom extractor. And it only works while it runs, which is why it is a second line behind the cap rather than a replacement for it.

chapters.title: Drying the wood
chapters.promise: Air along the faces, or through the silica.
narration: Third job.
A perforated liner washes air down both sawn faces of every member. That is the surface most at risk in a timber frame and the hardest to reach, and it now has moving air on it permanently.
When the weather is too wet for moving air to dry anything, a three-way gate routes the same flow through a silica cartridge instead. The cartridge pulls out of a hatch and goes in an oven.

chapters.title: Condensing on purpose
chapters.promise: 76 gallons a year, and here is what that is worth.
narration: Fourth job, and this is the one the film has to be honest about.

Thermoelectric plates on the cold side of the channel, dropping moisture out of the air as liquid straight into the gutter the rain already uses. The appeal is obvious: the plate sits exactly where the moisture is highest and the drain is right there.

Now the number. 651 watts of plates make 76 gallons in a year. That is 0.4 inches of rain. At 5.0 kilowatt hours a litre it is several times worse than a compressor, and a compressor is already not how anybody sensible makes water on a roof.
So they are a dehumidifier that happens to yield liquid. They are not a water supply. The water supply is the roof.

chapters.title: What it costs
chapters.promise: $7,665 of module on a dome that lists at $12,036.
narration: And the price, because a system that is half the cost of the building it is fitted to has to argue for itself.

The module is $7,665 across the whole dome. The cap, the liner, the gutter and the drain are per foot of seam and grow with the building; the gates, the cartridges and the plates are per seam and grow more slowly.
If you fit one part of it, fit the gutter. Water off the roof is the best return here, it needs no power, and it is the only piece that pays for itself in a season.

lessons.title: A house you can take apart

chapters.title: A house you can take apart
chapters.promise: 19.4 feet across. 277 square feet.
narration: This is a house you can take apart.
Nineteen feet across, two hundred and seventy-seven square feet, and every piece of it fits in a pickup.

chapters.title: The frame is already on your land
chapters.promise: Two trees. A hundred and twenty wedges. No hubs.
narration: The frame is already standing on your land.
Two trees, split into a hundred and twenty wedges. No hubs, no jig, and three saw settings for the whole building.

chapters.title: A dome is a head, and it wears hats
chapters.promise: One waterproof layer, and it is the outside one.
narration: I stood lookout in the Arctic Circle, outside the skin of the ship.
You do not stay warm in one very good thing. You wear a lot of ordinary layers, and you put one waterproof shell over the lot.
A dome is a head. It wears hats, and only the cap is waterproof.

chapters.title: It gets warmer every winter
chapters.promise: Each layer buys the next cap a size up.
narration: Every quilted layer you add makes the next cap a size bigger, so there is no limit.
A rigid shell fills up and stops. This one does not.

chapters.title: The insulation is a thousand t-shirts
chapters.promise: Sewn by somebody, tagged with their name.
narration: The insulation is recycled clothing, quilted at a kitchen table.
A fully dressed dome wears nearly a thousand t-shirts, and every layer is tagged with the name of whoever sewed it.

chapters.title: Twelve thousand, and here is the invoice
chapters.promise: $10,030 to build. $2,006 is ours.
narration: Twelve thousand dollars.
Ten to build, and two thousand is our profit -- twenty per cent, marked up on cost. The whole invoice is on the page.
The ground it stands on is quoted separately and we do not mark it up.

chapters.title: And it can be better later
chapters.promise: The hull, the mast, the floor, the rig.
narration: Nothing here is finished, on purpose.
A laminated hull, a steel mast, a floor bought later, and a rig that hangs the whole building between two trees. Buy them when you want them.

chapters.title: It needs three kinds of people
chapters.promise: Quilters. Pad hosts. Dome owners.
narration: This only works if three different people turn up.
Somebody who sews. Somebody with land who does not want to be a landlord. And somebody who wants a building.
A dome with nobody to quilt for it is a cold dome.

chapters.title: Every number is a model you can run
chapters.promise: Including the ones that argue against us.
narration: Every figure you just saw came out of a model you can run yourself -- including the three that argue against us.
Back it, and tell us which price is wrong.

chapters.title: One log
chapters.promise: Every member starts here.
narration: Every member of this dome starts as one of 8 wedges, ripped from a log with a chainsaw, straight through its heart.

chapters.title: One dome
chapters.promise: The last triangles go up.
narration: 120 of those members make the frame, and 2 crown triangles are still to go up.

chapters.title: One log
chapters.promise: A whole house frame, before it is cut.
narration: This is a house frame before it is cut. One log, ripped with a chainsaw straight through its heart into 8 wedges. Every stick in the dome behind it is one of those wedges. By the end of this film you will know what each one does, and what the gap between two of them can carry.

chapters.title: Point in, round face out
chapters.promise: Nothing is squared.
narration: Each wedge is a 45 degree slice of the log. In the frame the round outer face looks out at the weather and the point faces the centre of the dome. Nothing is squared, so the only wood that leaves the log is the width of the saw.

chapters.title: Two lengths, flat panels
chapters.promise: Built on the ground, one triangle at a time.
narration: There are 120 members in two lengths: 60 cut to 70.2 inches and 60 to 62.7. Three of them make a triangle, and each triangle is built flat on the ground as its own panel. 40 panels make the dome.

chapters.title: No hubs
chapters.promise: The sticks hold each other.
narration: Inside a panel the three members do not meet at a point. Each one butts into the side of the next, all turning the same way, like a pinwheel. That is why this dome has no hubs. The corners hold because the sticks lean on each other, not because a steel star is holding them.

chapters.title: Every edge is two sticks
chapters.promise: And between them, a seam.
narration: Where two panels meet, each one brings its own member, so every inside edge is two sticks side by side. That is 55 seams, and 110 of the 120 members. The last 10 sit on the rim. Everything interesting from here on happens inside those seams.

chapters.title: The V
chapters.promise: Two sawn faces cannot close flat.
narration: Look at the two members end on. Their sawn faces touch at the ridge on the outside and open toward the inside, at the sector angle less the fold between the two panels. This dome has only two folds: 18.0 degrees at 25 seams and 22.5 at 30. So every V is 27.0 or 22.5 degrees, and 6 inches deep: the radius of the 12 inch log.

chapters.title: The key
chapters.promise: Solid, a spline. Hollow, a pipe.
narration: The key fills the V, and it is what 8 bolts a seam pull the two panels against. Make it solid and it is just a spline. Make it hollow and it is a pipe running the length of every seam: 309 feet of it, touching every panel, reaching the crown and the ground.

chapters.title: How much room
chapters.promise: That is the whole budget.
narration: Inside a key with 3 millimetre walls there are 5.3 square inches in the tighter seam and 6.5 in the wider one. The largest round thing that passes through is 1.69 inches, or 1.97. Everything that follows has to fit in that.

chapters.title: The sizes we assumed
chapters.promise: Nominal where there is a standard; estimates where there is not.
narration: Before anything goes in, here are the sizes this film counts on. Pipe and tubing sizes are nominal, from their standards. Cable sizes are estimates, because every brand differs. And the rule for how full a channel may be is borrowed from conduit: 40 percent of the area, so things can still be pulled through.
equations: 14/2 NM-B cable, 15 A circuit: 0.400 in x 0.20  (estimate)
12 V pair to the Peltier plates, 14 AWG: 0.300 in  (estimate)
condensate drain, 1/4 in ID vinyl: 0.375 in  (nominal)

chapters.title: Water and wire fit
chapters.promise: Room to spare.
narration: A half-inch PEX water line, a fifteen-amp circuit, the twelve-volt pair to the cooling plates and the condensate drain. All four fit in either seam, and together they fill 11 percent of the tighter one, against the 40 allowed. There is room left over, and that room matters next.

chapters.title: Round ducts do not
chapters.promise: The number that does not help.
narration: Now the number that does not help. The smallest ordinary air duct is three inches round, and the key's largest opening is 1.97 inches at best. A three-inch duct does not fit. A four-inch one is nowhere close. If the plan was round ducts through the seams, the plan does not work as drawn.

chapters.title: The channel is the duct
chapters.promise: It does not need a duct in it.
narration: But the channel does not need a duct in it, because it already is one. With the water, wire and drain inside, one seam still moves 13 cubic feet a minute at a quiet 400 feet a minute. The whole dome needs 18 for fresh air. 2 seams carry the building.

chapters.title: Peltier plates and the three-way gate
chapters.promise: Drying the air where the wood is.
narration: That air runs past a thermoelectric plate, a Peltier: cold on the channel side, throwing its heat into the room below. Water drops out on the cold plate and runs to the drain. A three-way gate on each seam sends the air along the wood faces to dry them, through a silica cartridge when the weather is too wet, or shuts the air path off from the water path entirely.

chapters.title: What the plates are worth
chapters.promise: A dehumidifier, not a water supply.
narration: And honestly: 651 watts of plates, run 6 hours a day, make 76 gallons a year. That is 0.4 inches of rain on this roof. The plates are a dehumidifier that happens to make water. They are not a water supply. The roof is the water supply.

chapters.title: If you want a duct: the key becomes a spacer
chapters.promise: Every panel moves out.
narration: If you do want a round duct, the key stops being a filler and becomes a spacer. Push every panel out along its own face and every seam opens. A three-inch duct needs the panels moved out 7.0 inches. A four-inch duct with everything else beside it needs 16.4, and the seams open to 6.4 and 5.1 inches at the ridge, each needing a cap.

chapters.title: What the spacer costs
chapters.promise: A bigger dome, all round.
narration: And a spacer is not free. Moving every panel out makes the whole dome bigger: 6 percent for the three-inch duct, 14 percent for the four. More wood, more skin, a bigger pad, to carry air the plain channel was already carrying.

chapters.title: Or start with a bigger log
chapters.promise: The room grows with the square of the radius.
narration: The other lever is the log. The room in the channel grows with the square of the log's radius: a 10 inch log gives 3.5 square inches, a 12 inch log gives 5.3 square inches, a 15 inch log gives 8.8 square inches, a 18 inch log gives 13.1 square inches. Even the 18 inch log opens only 2.65 inches round: still not a three-inch duct.
equations: 10 in log: 3.5 sq in, 1.37 in round
12 in log: 5.3 sq in, 1.69 in round
15 in log: 8.8 sq in, 2.17 in round
18 in log: 13.1 sq in, 2.65 in round

chapters.title: Printing the key in halves
chapters.promise: Each member carries its own half.
narration: Here is how the key gets made. Split it down the middle and each member carries its own half, printed and screwed to its sawn face before the panel is built. When two panels meet, the halves close into one channel. The whole dome is 110 half-keys in just 2 profiles, printed 8 pieces to a stick on a 250 millimetre printer.

chapters.title: What printing costs
chapters.promise: Print the seams that carry something.
narration: Printing every seam is 121 kilograms of plastic, about 2,425 dollars and 1,768 printer hours: 74 days of one printer running flat out. So print only the seams that carry something, 2.2 kilograms and 32 hours each, and cut solid keys from the offcuts for the rest.

chapters.title: Where the channels meet
chapters.promise: The frame has no hubs. The services do.
narration: The frame has no hubs, but the services need them. The channels meet at 6 five-way and 10 six-way points, and 10 more on the rim, where they drop to the pad. As built, the V's close to a point there, so each junction is a printed rosette box on the inside of the vertex, where a pipe turns and a wire is spliced, somewhere you can reach. With the four-inch spacer the vertex opens into a hole about 11 inches across, and the hub becomes a printed node the channels plug into.

chapters.title: Two rules
chapters.promise: A hidden leak is the failure this exists to prevent.
narration: Two rules. Keep pressure joints out of the seams: run the PEX continuous, and make every fitting in a rosette you can open. A hidden leak inside a wooden seam is the one failure this whole system exists to prevent. And whether a cable may run in this chase is your inspector's call, not this film's.

chapters.title: What the fitted seam costs
chapters.promise: Before a single printed key.
narration: Fitted out as gutter, vent and dehumidifier, the seam module across the whole dome is 7,665 dollars, before a single printed key. If you fit one part of it, fit the gutter.

chapters.title: The wedge dome
chapters.promise: One log at a time.
narration: One log, 8 rip cuts, 120 sticks, 55 seams, and a channel in every one of them. Water and wire for free, air if you let the channel be the duct, and a round duct only if you pay for it in size. That is the wedge dome.

lessons.title: Linseed Oil for a Dome: Uses, Limits and Method

chapters.title: Linseed oil for a dome
chapters.promise: Where it earns a place in the build.
narration: The Lost Handyman video offers 20 linseed oil tricks. Here we bring the useful ones into the wedge dome workshop. Start with the exposed interior wood, shelves, trim and hand tools. Then look at the seams, windows and weather skin, where a finish must work with the rest of the assembly. The source is a set of claims, not a comparison test. We will show the work, the quantities and the limits before calling anything a saving.
equations: SOURCE: The Lost Handyman / transcript record
Applications adapted to the solver's wedge dome
No measured service-life or cost comparison

chapters.title: Set up the rag station first
chapters.promise: Oxidation makes heat.
narration: Before opening the oil, prepare for the used cloths. Linseed oil reacts with oxygen as it cures and gives off heat. A pile of oily cloths can trap that heat and ignite without a spark. Keep them out of pockets, sawdust and ordinary bins. Follow the label and local fire-service guidance: fully cover used rags with water and an oil-breaking detergent in a tight-lidded metal container, stored away from the building and combustibles. Arrange proper disposal. A wet rag can become hazardous again if it dries in a heap.
equations: Never accumulate oily rags in a heap
Water + detergent + tight metal lid; local disposal

chapters.title: Read the exact can
chapters.promise: Raw, boiled and polymerized are not interchangeable.
narration: Raw linseed oil generally cures slowly. Many hardware-store boiled oils contain drying additives; some products use heat-polymerized oil instead. Read the ingredient information, safety sheet and intended uses. Do not boil oil yourself. The source's raw-only rule for food contact is too broad: some polymerized finishes are specifically sold for kitchen wood. Choose the exact product for that use and follow its cure instructions. A name like natural, boiled or Danish does not identify a complete formulation.
equations: Product label + safety sheet + intended use
Kitchen contact: verify the exact formulation

chapters.title: Prepare the member
chapters.promise: Finish sound wood; preserve clean joint surfaces.
narration: Inspect the wedges before finishing. Reject decay and address splits or loose joints through the actual repair design. Oil cannot restore lost load capacity. Let the timber reach the moisture condition required by the finish and the building design; check with an appropriate wood meter. Remove dirt and unsuitable old coatings, smooth splinters and clear the dust. Test an offcut for color and cure. Mark and mask the places that must bond to adhesive, tape, sealant or gaskets. Finish accessible approved faces while the members are easy to reach.
equations: Moisture target: selected finish and assembly
Keep glue, tape and sealant lands uncontaminated

chapters.title: Two product labels, two schedules
chapters.promise: Manufacturer claims, not DomeSim measurements.
narration: Here are declared examples from Tried and True. Its Danish Oil lists at least 5 minutes before rubbing dry and at least 8 hours of curing. Its Original oil-and-wax finish lists at least 60 minutes before rubbing dry and at least 24 hours of curing. These are different products for interior work. They demonstrate why the original video's generic timing cannot be applied to every can. Minimum intervals do not guarantee full readiness in cold, damp conditions.
equations: CLAIMED / Tried & True Danish: 5 min; 8 h minimum
Use the current label for the product actually bought

chapters.title: Apply thinly, then wipe dry
chapters.promise: The sample should not carry puddles.
narration: On the prepared sample, rub on a very thin coat using the applicator the manufacturer specifies. Work in a manageable area and wet it evenly. After that product's penetration interval, rub away the excess until the surface is dry to the touch. Provide the specified ventilation and cure conditions, then assess the surface before another coat. Do not bury a sticky layer under more oil. Check end grain for extra uptake but prevent drips into joints. Do not enclose uncured finishes inside panels or occupied air passages. Handle every cloth through the rag station.
equations: Thin application -> label interval -> wipe dry
Cure with suitable temperature and ventilation
End grain: inspect uptake; remove excess

chapters.title: Keep the seam doing its jobs
chapters.promise: Finish decisions follow the assembly.
narration: This is the actual wedge seam specimen and its service channel. Oil on an exposed interior face is different from oil on a sealing land. Adhesives and tapes need compatible, prepared substrates. Keep the printed key, gasket lands, drainage route and electrical services clean. Before coating wood beside a gasket or sealant, check both manufacturers' compatibility instructions and test the complete joint. Do not treat an oil coat as the air seal, rain seal or a remedy for condensation. Inspect the finished seam before closing the panel.
equations: Approved exposed face != bonding or sealing land
WEST SYSTEM: bonding surfaces free of oil and wax

chapters.title: The outside needs a weather system
chapters.promise: Rain shedding is an assembly job.
narration: The source describes linseed oil as outdoor protection and waterproofing. A dome roof still needs a specified weather skin, flashed openings, drained joints and a drying path. Plain oil does not establish those functions or prove resistance to ultraviolet light, decay or insects. Damp linseed-rich finishes can also support mildew. Use an exterior system rated for the substrate and exposure when the wood is outdoors. A compatible pigmented finish may be appropriate, but adding pigment at home does not establish weathering performance. Keep timber off persistent wet surfaces and repair leaks at their source.
equations: No roof, rot, insect or UV rating inferred
Water control: skin + flashing + drains + drying
Exterior product and exposure determine upkeep

chapters.title: Declare the planning assumptions
chapters.promise: These are estimates to replace with an offcut trial.
narration: For a worked allowance, assume 2 flat sawn faces per member and 2 coats. Use an estimated coverage of 350 square feet per US gallon per coat, plus 15 percent extra volume for handling. For active application work, assume 2 minutes per member per coat. These are illustrative inputs, not measurements. The face allowance is an area calculation, not an instruction to oil every joint. Measure the actual selected surfaces and the consumption on representative offcuts before purchasing.
equations: ESTIMATE: 350 sq ft / US gal / coat
ESTIMATE: 2 min / member / coat; active work only

chapters.title: Measure wood, not floor area
chapters.promise: Use the dome model's actual stock schedule.
narration: The reference solver gives 120 members and 664.3 feet of total member stock. Each flat radial face is 6.0 inches deep. Multiply total stock length by that depth in feet and the declared face count: the planning envelope is 664 square feet. This includes the stock allowance already in the model. It excludes curved backs, end cuts, panels, floors and trim. Subtract masked or hidden surfaces and add only the other surfaces you actually intend to finish.
equations: Not shell area; subtract uncoated lands

chapters.title: The oil allowance
chapters.promise: A calculation is only as good as the coverage input.
narration: At our estimated coverage, the declared coats consume 3.80 US gallons for that planning envelope. The handling allowance brings it to 4.37 gallons. This is a scenario, not a shopping prescription or a cost saving. Roughness, end grain, masking and the actual finish change consumption. Measure how much you dispense for a known sample area through the complete coat schedule. Scale that result to the approved finish surfaces. Account for cloth uptake and leftover material as part of the job.
equations: Illustrative allowance; replace with sample results

chapters.title: The number that argues against it
chapters.promise: Low material cost does not remove labour.
narration: The Danish Oil label advertises coverage up to 1000 square feet per gallon. That is a manufacturer claim, not a rough-sawn wedge measurement. Even without a price comparison, hand application has a real time cost. Our estimated 2 minutes per member per coat, multiplied by 120 members and 2 coats, is 8.0 hours of active work. That excludes preparation, access equipment, inspection and waiting for cure. A cheap can can still make an expensive finishing job.
equations: CLAIMED: label coverage UP TO 1000 sq ft / US gal
No measured lifespan or savings advantage

chapters.title: Look after the builder's tools
chapters.promise: Sound handles first; moving parts need their own lubricant.
narration: The handle trick transfers well to the dome workshop when the handle is sound. Inspect the hammer, mallet and jig handles for cracks, splinters and loose fittings before finishing. Prepare bare wood, apply the selected finish thinly, wipe it dry and let it cure before gripping it. Oil does not repair a broken handle or tighten a structural joint reliably. A compatible drying-oil film can be considered on clean nonmoving steel for storage. Keep it out of bearings, hinges, chainsaw chains, brakes, electrical contacts and fastener threads. Those need their specified products.
equations: Sound wood -> thin finish -> full usability check
Storage film is not moving-part lubrication

chapters.title: Putty belongs to a specified window
chapters.promise: A sash demonstration is not a dome skylight design.
narration: Linseed-based putty has a real place in traditional sash glazing. Use a formulated glazing compound and follow its sash preparation, bedding, retention and painting instructions. This demonstration includes mechanical retainers: putty alone must not carry the glass. The DAP glazing sheet excludes plastic panes and insulating glass units with organic seals, and requires retainers to hold the glass. For sloped or overhead dome glazing, use a complete system explicitly specified for that location; a sash putty example does not establish suitability. Do not transfer the video's homemade chalk-and-oil recipe to the dome's weather seams.
equations: Glazing putty is not a structural adhesive

chapters.title: Finish the parts people touch
chapters.promise: Match the finish to use and future repairs.
narration: Interior shelves, trim and sound furniture are the most straightforward uses. Test for ambering and for compatibility with any old coating. A labelled linseed-and-wax blend can give a low-sheen surface, but wax complicates later bonding or recoating. Use a floor-rated system for floors; assess wear, cure and slip instead of assuming a furniture oil fits. Kitchen surfaces need a product explicitly suitable for that contact. Use a prepared blend instead of heating an unknown oil formulation. Follow product directions for thinning; the source supplies no universal safe mix.
equations: Floor and food use: exact product suitability
Wax affects later coats; no heated DIY mixture

chapters.title: Inspect, clean, then renew
chapters.promise: Improved color is not restored strength.
narration: Make a finish record: product, batch, preparation, application date and where it was used. Keep a sample with the building notes. Inspect exposed surfaces for wear, tack, mildew and water marks; renew only after finding the cause and following the finish instructions. Gray wood can darken beautifully under oil, but that does not reverse decay. Loose toolbox joints still need repair. The transcript's leather, gunstock and masonry tricks add no validated building function here. In particular, give no foundation waterproofing or freeze-thaw credit to an oil wipe.
equations: Record -> inspect -> repair cause -> compatible renewal
No annual promise for every exposure

chapters.title: A useful finish in the right places
chapters.promise: Plan the surfaces, joints, work and cleanup together.
narration: Use linseed oil where a maintainable wood finish suits the job: accessible interior faces, selected trim and sound tool handles. Keep sealing and bonding lands compatible, give the roof its own weather system, and choose glazing for the actual opening. Base quantities on measured surfaces and a representative sample. Allow for hand labour and cure time. Finish the day by accounting for every oily cloth and arranging its disposal. The worthwhile old skill is careful application, backed by a clear understanding of what the finish can and cannot do for the dome.
equations: Test the finish and the complete joint

chapters.title: One channel, many jobs
chapters.promise: Which way should the seam breathe?
narration: Every one of this dome's 55 seams has a channel inside it. Air can go in through it, out through it, round in a loop, through a desiccant or past one, over a cold plate or a warm one. That is a lot of choices. This film works out which one to make, and when, from one number.

chapters.title: Inner skin, outer skin
chapters.promise: The line from the centre outward has a name.
narration: First, the word you were looking for. The line that runs from the centre of the dome straight outward is the radial direction. Through a wall it is the wall's thickness. In a seam it runs from the V's open mouth on the room side up to the ridge on the weather side. So the channel has two skins: an outer one that touches outside, and an inner one that touches the room. Put a Peltier plate on each and you can set the temperature of both.

chapters.title: A plate is a heat pump
chapters.promise: And it runs both ways.
narration: A Peltier plate is not a cooler. It is a pump that moves heat from one face to the other, and reversing the current reverses the direction. So the rule for both plates is simple: throw the heat to the side you want warmer. In winter, into the room. In summer, outside. The first film, The Wedge Dome Explained, showed the plate throwing its heat into the room. That is right in winter and wrong in summer.
equations: winter: cold face in the channel, heat to the room
summer: cold face in the channel, heat to the outside skin

chapters.title: Compare dew points, not humidity
chapters.promise: The one rule that ends the confusion.
narration: Now the rule the whole system runs on. Never compare relative humidity. Compare dew points. Outside air at minus 5 degrees and 60 percent sounds damp. Its dew point is minus 11.6. Inside at 21 degrees and 45 percent, the dew point is 8.6. Per kilogram, the damp-sounding air carries 1.6 grams of water; the room's carries 6.9. Bring it in, and it dries the dome.
equations: out minus 5 C 60% -> dew -11.6 C, 1.6 g/kg

chapters.title: Will it condense?
chapters.promise: Dew point against surface temperature.
narration: The second question: will this air leave water on that surface? It will whenever the air's dew point is above the surface's temperature. So a condensing plate must be colder than the dew point. And every piece of wood must be warmer than it, with room to spare. This film keeps wood 3 degrees above the dew point of the air that touches it.
equations: wood: T > dew point + 3 K (assumed margin)

chapters.title: Fifteen to twenty degrees colder
chapters.promise: The question you asked, with numbers.
narration: You asked: if the wood sits at the dew point and the metal channel is fifteen to twenty degrees below it, will the water go to the metal? Take a room at 21 degrees and 55 percent. Its dew point is 11.6. The middle of your range, 17.5 degrees under that, is minus 5.9. The plate freezes. Frost stops the water running and chokes the fins. So hold the plate 6 degrees under the dew point and never below 1: here, 5.6 degrees.

chapters.title: Plate first, wood second
chapters.promise: A colder surface elsewhere does not protect the wood.
narration: And the real answer: a colder surface somewhere else does not protect wood that is already at the dew point. Wood touching raw room air still gets wet. What protects it is the order. Send the air over the plate first. It leaves with a dew point of 7.6, so wood at 11.6 is now 4.0 degrees clear. One more rule: the cold metal must never touch the wood, or it chills the wood to its own temperature.
equations: raw air: wood at 11.6 C = dew point -> wet
after the plate: dew point 7.6 C (plate + 2 K, assumed)

chapters.title: Seven modes
chapters.promise: Two of them never touch the room.
narration: That gives the channel its modes. Take outside air in. Push inside air out. Condense inside air on a cold skin before it leaves. Loop the seam's own air through the desiccant. Purge a wet seam with outside air and send it straight back out. Supply dried air and hold the room at a slight positive pressure. Or shut the exposed intakes in the rain. The loop and the purge never touch the living space.
equations: CONDENSE: inside -> cold seam -> drain -> outside
DRY_SUPPLY: dehumidified air in, slight positive pressure

chapters.title: The weathers we assumed
chapters.promise: Estimates, not measurements.
narration: To test the controller, here are the weathers from your table, plus one more. These are typical conditions, our estimates, not measurements from a site. Each one gets inside and outside temperatures and humidities, and the wet ones get a wood moisture reading at or over 19 percent, where lumber stops counting as dry.
equations: Cold + dry outside: out minus 5 C 60%, in 21 C 45%
Cold outside + humid inside: out minus 5 C 80%, in 21 C 68%
Cold outside, harvesting water: out minus 2 C 80%, in 21 C 68%
Mild + dry outside: out 16 C 40%, in 21 C 45%
Hot + dry outside: out 33 C 18%, in 21 C 50%
Hot + humid outside: out 32 C 70%, in 21 C 50%
Hot + humid, cooling on: out 35 C 60%, in 24 C 50%
Rain: out 14 C 97%, in 21 C 45%, rain
After rain, dry outside: out 18 C 45%, in 21 C 45%, wood 21%
Sun on a wet skin: out 24 C 55%, in 21 C 45%, wood 20%
Muggy outside, wet frame: out 36 C 60%, in 24 C 55%, wood 20%

chapters.title: What the controller chose
chapters.promise: All of them match your table.
narration: And here is what the code chose, working only from dew points. Cold and dry: take it in. Hot and humid: dried supply only. Rain: shut. After rain, with dry air outside: purge the seam. Muggy outside with a wet frame: close the loop. All 11 weathers get the answer your table gives, and the film's own test fails if one ever does not.
equations: Cold + dry outside: dew minus 12 out / 9 in -> INTAKE
Cold outside + humid inside: dew minus 8 out / 15 in -> EXHAUST
Cold outside, harvesting water: dew minus 5 out / 15 in -> CONDENSE
Mild + dry outside: dew 2 out / 9 in -> INTAKE
Hot + dry outside: dew 6 out / 10 in -> INTAKE
Hot + humid outside: dew 26 out / 10 in -> DRY_SUPPLY
Hot + humid, cooling on: dew 26 out / 13 in -> DRY_SUPPLY
After rain, dry outside: dew 6 out / 9 in -> PURGE
Sun on a wet skin: dew 14 out / 9 in -> PURGE
Muggy outside, wet frame: dew 27 out / 14 in -> FRAME_LOOP

chapters.title: The loop and the purge
chapters.promise: Drying the structure is not ventilating the house.
narration: The two modes worth the extra plumbing are these. The frame loop takes the seam's air, dries it in the desiccant and sends it back: nothing thrown outside, nothing muggy pulled in. The purge takes dry outside air through a wet seam and straight back out. That needs two outside ports per circuit, and it means drying the frame is a separate job from ventilating the house.

chapters.title: The dome's levels, from the solver
chapters.promise: Four rings, five bands of seams.
narration: Now where each job goes. The solver's dome stands on five heights: 10 corners at the rim, 5 and 5 in a belt that zigzags between two heights, 5 round the crown, and the apex. The seams between them fall into five bands: 20 in the lower band, 10 in the belt, 15 in the upper band, 5 round the crown pentagon, and 5 to the apex.
equations: lower band, rim to belt: 20 seams, 113 ft, 57 deg
the zigzag belt: 10 seams, 53 ft, 8 deg
upper band, belt to pentagon: 15 seams, 87 ft, 37 deg
the pentagon ring: 5 seams, 30 ft, 0 deg
the cap, to the apex: 5 seams, 27 ft, 16 deg

chapters.title: The ring that cannot drain
chapters.promise: Air at the top, water never.
narration: The slopes decide the jobs. The lower band's seams rise at 57 degrees, and water runs down them fast. The belt zigzags at only 8 degrees, but that zigzag has 5 low points, and each one is a natural drain. The pentagon ring round the crown is dead level. Water there stands in the wood. So that ring carries air, never water.

chapters.title: Condense low, drain at the rim
chapters.promise: Your first-ring idea is right.
narration: Your idea of putting the plates on the first ring is right, and here is why. Condensate falls. A plate at the rim drops its water straight into a drain at one of the 10 rim corners, with no seam to travel through. The rain belongs outside, in a gutter at the rim. It should not come in through a seam higher up. Every foot of seam that carries liquid water is a foot of wood waiting for a leak.
equations: rain: outside gutter at the rim

chapters.title: Warm air rises
chapters.promise: In low, out high, and the fan still does the work.
narration: Air has its own preference. Warm inside air wants to leave at the top, so take air in at the rim and let it out at the pentagon ring and the apex. But the pull is small. With the inside ten degrees warmer, the height of this dome makes 1.2 pascals. The barrier fan holds 4. The stack helps; it does not replace the fan.
equations: stack = rho g h dT / T = 1.18 Pa at 10 K

chapters.title: Why the desiccant stays out of the seams
chapters.promise: The number that ends the rainbow.
narration: Now the cartridge. Could you pack the beads into the seams themselves, round a ring, or over the top like a rainbow, a path of 32 feet? Push one seam's share of air, 13 cubic feet a minute, through one packed seam and the beads resist with 65,848 pascals. A small in-line fan manages about 250. At that, a packed seam passes 0.29 cubic feet a minute. The rainbow is longer still.

chapters.title: And it cannot be dried where it sits
chapters.promise: The temperature that rules out the walls.
narration: There is a second reason. A molecular sieve gives its water back only when it is hot: about 200 degrees. Even silica gel wants 120. The printed key softens at 80, and this film never sends air hotter than 60 through a seam. A desiccant in the seams could never be regenerated in place.

chapters.title: Two drawers and a gate
chapters.promise: One drying while the other is regenerated.
narration: So the desiccant lives in drawers, at the rim, where the channels come down. One drawer 30 centimetres square and 5 deep holds 2.9 kilograms of beads, and passes the whole dome's 18 cubic feet a minute at 20 pascals. Use two: one working, one being dried. The gate that picks between drawer and bypass should fall back to the bypass when the power goes, so air never stops.
equations: beads = 2.92 kg, holds 0.58 kg of water

chapters.title: What the desiccant will not do
chapters.promise: It does not dry a soaked frame.
narration: And the number that does not help. A frame that gets wet, over 19 percent, has 54 kilograms of water to lose to get back to 12. That is 93 drawer fills, and 56 kilowatt hours to regenerate them. The desiccant is for the weather when no air is dry enough. Drying a wet frame is the purge's job, on the next dry day.

chapters.title: The stove's heat, never its air
chapters.promise: A sealed exchanger, and nothing else.
narration: The stove can help, but only through a wall of steel. A sealed exchanger on the flue warms clean air, and that air can dry the frame or regenerate a drawer. The smoke side never meets it. Keep the seam air under 60 degrees. Give the stove its own outside combustion air. And never let the stove push or pull the seam air, or a back draught puts smoke in the walls.
equations: exchanger: flue gas | steel | clean air
combustion air: its own outside duct

chapters.title: The layout
chapters.promise: Every level with one job.
narration: So here is the layout. At the rim: 10 ports, the condensing plates, the drains and the two drawers. The lower band carries air up and water down. The belt's 5 low points drain it. The pentagon ring is the exhaust manifold: air only. The cap vents at the apex. Sensors inside, outside and in the seam read temperature and humidity, the wood's moisture, and the rain.
equations: lower band: air up, water down
belt: drains at the low points
sensors: T, RH in / out / seam, wood %, rain

chapters.title: A correction: the cap never opens
chapters.promise: Chapters 15 and 21 put a hole in the roof.
narration: First, a correction. Earlier in this film, the stack chapter let the exhaust out at the pentagon ring and the apex, and the layout said the cap vents at the apex. That is wrong. A vent at the apex is a hole in the cap, at the place the weather hits hardest, with the frame right under it. The cap is one watertight layer, and it is never opened. Here is how the dome breathes anyway.
equations: was: exhaust out at the apex
now: no opening in the cap above the rim

chapters.title: In at the crown, under the cap
chapters.promise: The stalest air is at the top.
narration: Warm air rises, and the warmest air in the room is also the wettest and the stalest: breath and steam, carried up. In a dome it collects at the crown. So a grille there, inside the shell and under the cap, takes the room's air into the seam channels, inside their printed keys. Holes through the cap above the rim: 0.
equations: intake: a grille at the crown, inside the shell

chapters.title: Down the seams, out facing the ground
chapters.promise: Every falling seam is a path.
narration: From the crown the air goes down. 50 of the dome's 55 seams fall all the way from the apex to the rim without climbing; the 5 level seams of the pentagon ring stay off the path. It leaves at the rim, through ports under the cap's brim that face the ground. Rain falls; an opening that faces down takes in only water that would have to climb. The dome needs 17.6 cubic feet a minute, and the five cap seams carry 4.2 times that at a quiet speed.

chapters.title: In winter the air falls by itself
chapters.promise: A loop that turns itself.
narration: Here is why down is the right way. In winter the room's warm air rises to the crown. In the channel the exhaust gives its heat to the cold shell, gets heavier than the room's air, and falls. A warm column rising and a cool one falling make a loop that turns itself. At -5 degrees outside it pulls with 1.5 pascals and carries 100 percent of the need with no fan. In cool weather, 77 percent. In summer sun it runs backwards, and the fan does it all against 3 pascals, where a small fan pushes 250.
equations: hard winter: 2.13 Pa, 100% of the need
summer sun: -1.66 Pa, 0% of the need

chapters.title: The water leaves by the same door
chapters.promise: Air and condensate, the same way down.
narration: When the channel is colder than the room air's dew point, the exhaust drops water inside the key: 0.24 litres a day at -5 degrees outside, 1.9 at -15. That water runs downhill, which is the way the air is already going, and out of the same ports. Sent up, it would run back against the air and pool. Sent down, nothing pools, and the wet air never touches the wood: it runs inside the key.
equations: out with the air, at the rim

chapters.title: Two ways, both doors at the bottom
chapters.promise: Fresh in low, stale out high.
narration: The dome breathes both ways. Fresh air comes in through its own ports at the rim, facing the ground, and into the room low, past the drawers and plates. Stale air leaves from the crown, down the seams, and out at the rim. The room itself is the loop's rising leg. Run the two flows equal, and the room is neither pressed nor pulled, so no air is forced through the frame either way.

chapters.title: Where it stops working
chapters.promise: Ice, snow, screens and summer.
narration: And where it stops. With the channel halfway between inside and outside, the outlets reach freezing below -21 degrees outside, and ice can close them: heat the outlet stubs, or run the exhaust through the rim drawers on those nights. A port under a snowdrift does nothing, so keep the ports above the snow line. Screen every one. And in summer the fan carries the whole need.
equations: outlets freeze below -21 C (channel halfway, assumed)
ports above the snow line, screened

chapters.title: Seventy on the box
chapters.promise: Ten modules at the rim, run day and night.
narration: Now the plates themselves. You bought one thermoelectric module, a TEC1-12706, for 20 dollars, and want 10 round the rim, one at each port, running day and night on the sun. The listing says 70 watts. Worked from the listing's own maxima, the most it can move is 50, and only with no temperature difference across it. Mounted here, hot face on a finned sink outside at 30 degrees, cold face in a room at 26 and 60 percent, it settles at 14.8 degrees, draws 4.6 amps, and moves 28 watts of heat for 65 watts of electricity, its fans included.
equations: listed 70 W; physics 50.0 W at dT = 0
mounted, 12 V: cold face 14.8 C, 4.62 A

chapters.title: A correction: less water per watt
chapters.promise: Two earlier films assumed a yield.
narration: A correction. The Seam Does Four Jobs and The Wedge Dome Explained counted 6 plates at 60 watts, making 0.35 litres of water per kilowatt hour. That yield was an assumption, and it was wrong. Solved from the module, the cold face is 2.9 degrees under the room's dew point, and only 32 percent of the heat it takes is water. The yield is 0.20 litres per kilowatt hour: a litre costs 5.0 kilowatt hours, not 2.9.

chapters.title: Slower is better, until it stops condensing
chapters.promise: Voltage against water.
narration: Run a Peltier gently and it gets far more efficient: at 3 volts it moves 3.05 watts of heat per watt, at 12 only 0.51. But at 6 volts the cold face stops at 18.4 degrees, above the dew point, and the water stops. The most water per kilowatt hour comes at 9 volts. And the controller asks for the plate 6 degrees under the dew point, 11.6. At full drive the module stops 3.1 short, so chasing that setpoint just runs it flat out. Cap the drive at 9 volts instead.
equations: 3 V: 10 W, COP 3.05, plate 22.0 C, ten make 0.0 L/day
6 V: 19 W, COP 1.40, plate 18.4 C, ten make 0.0 L/day
9 V: 25 W, COP 0.81, plate 16.0 C, ten make 2.1 L/day
12 V: 28 W, COP 0.51, plate 14.8 C, ten make 3.1 L/day

chapters.title: A day of ten
chapters.promise: Heat and water out, against what the room takes on.
narration: Ten at 12 volts, all day, on a humid day: 281 watts of heat out of the room, and 3.1 litres of water a day. Two people, their cooking and washing, and the fresh air put in 9.1 litres. The ring takes out about 35 percent. It helps; it does not keep up. And the hot faces must be outside: they throw 836 watts. Mounted the other way round, the ring is a 651 watt heater that drips.
equations: ten: 281 W of heat, 3.1 L/day of water
room takes on 9.1 L/day, 190 W (sun not counted)

chapters.title: Feeding it on the sun
chapters.promise: Twenty-four hours a day, priced.
narration: Running all day and all night, ten stations draw 651 watts: 15.6 kilowatt hours a day, 10.4 of them off a bank at night. From 4.6 peak sun hours, that takes about 4,508 watts of panels, and a 28.9 kilowatt hour bank to cover the night and one dark day. That is 16,347 dollars, for 200 dollars of modules. A small compressor dehumidifier takes out the same water for 1.7 kilowatt hours a day.

chapters.title: What to do instead
chapters.promise: Daylight surplus, a cap on the drive, a compressor.
narration: So keep the plates for the job only they can do: drying a seam that will not dry itself in warm, still, humid weeks. Run them on daylight surplus, 6 hours a day: 3.9 kilowatt hours the array was making anyway, and 0.79 litres a day, with no extra battery. Cap the drive at 9 volts. And if the room itself needs drying or cooling for weeks, buy the compressor: the smallest window air conditioner moves 3.2 watts of heat per watt; the ring moves 0.43.
equations: window AC 3.2 W per W; the ring 0.43

chapters.title: Dew point decides
chapters.promise: Send air toward the wood only when it is drier.
narration: One rule runs all of it. Send air toward the structure only when its dew point is lower than the moisture you are trying to remove, unless you are sending wetter air to a cold metal surface built to collect and drain the water. The same seams, winter and summer, rain and sun.

lessons.title: The Panel Method: A Three-Frequency Dome, Framed on a Jig

chapters.title: Two ways to frame a dome
chapters.promise: Same hill, two methods.
narration: On this hill stand two domes framed two different ways. One is the wedge dome: 120 members split from logs with a chainsaw, carrying their angles in their own shape. The other is a three-frequency dome of framed panels: 105 triangles, each one its own small frame of sawn sticks, built flat on a jig, skinned in the shop, and screwed to its neighbours on site. It is how most small timber domes built from bought plans are made, and it is worth knowing properly.

chapters.title: A popular build, tried and true
chapters.promise: Shown for comparison.
narration: The three-frequency five-eighths dome built from framed panels is one of the most popular small domes people build. It is tried and true: a great many of them are standing. That is why it is here, beside the wedge dome, for comparison. Every length, angle and count in this film is solved by this project's own code, at our own size, and every picture is drawn by our own software.
equations: a popular build, tried and true
geometry, figures and drawings: this project

chapters.title: Three frequency
chapters.promise: Three strut lengths, two kinds of point.
narration: Take the icosahedron's twenty faces and cut each into nine smaller triangles, three to an edge, then push every new point out onto the sphere. That is a three-frequency dome, and it has only three strut lengths. At our size, 16 feet across the base, A is 34.0 inches, B is 39.4 and C is 40.2. Twelve points have five neighbours and every other point has six. The triangles round the fives make pentagons; the rest make hexagons.

chapters.title: Five eighths
chapters.promise: Cut below the middle.
narration: This sphere has no level ring of points at its middle, so the usual cut goes lower, to the points nearest five-eighths of the way down. What is kept is 105 triangles: 30 in pentagons and 75 in hexagons. Its height is 0.594 of its width, a little under the five-eighths of its name. That wall below the middle is the point of the cut: it stands up nearly straight, so the floor near the edge is floor you can stand on.

chapters.title: A base that zig-zags
chapters.promise: Some sections taper; some do not.
narration: The bottom of the cut is 15 edges, and it does not lie on one level. Its corners alternate between two heights, 40 millimetres apart, about 1.56 inches. So 10 of the base sections must be tapered, low at one end and high at the other, and 5 sit level. Build the base ring first, set it on the deck, check its diagonals, and fasten it down. Everything above it goes together easier when this first ring is right.

chapters.title: Two panels, over and over
chapters.promise: A pentagon triangle and a hexagon triangle.
narration: Every panel in the dome is one of two triangles. The pentagon panel has a 39.4 inch base and two 34.0 inch sides, and there are 30 of them. The hexagon panel has the same base and two 40.2 inch sides, and there are 75. These outlines are the outside faces of the panels. Nothing may stick out past them, and nothing may fall short of them.

chapters.title: Finish, then rip in half
chapters.promise: A cut through the centre makes two copies.
narration: The sticks are sawn lumber. Finish the boards first, while they are whole: the face you rip will be hidden in the joint. Then tilt the table saw blade to the bevel and rip each board down its middle. A cut through the centre of a rectangle leaves two pieces that are copies of each other, turned end for end. It is the same symmetry that makes a split log give identical wedges. Turn the offcut over and send it back through for a hair more, and the two halves come out exactly alike.

chapters.title: Draw the jig with two arcs
chapters.promise: Three lengths make one triangle.
narration: The jig is a sheet of plywood with the panel drawn on it full size. Snap a straight line for the base and mark its two ends. A thin stick with a nail at each end is a trammel. Set it to one side length and swing an arc from one end; set it to the other side and swing from the other end. Where the arcs cross is the third corner. Measure all three sides again, then join the points. For the hexagon panel the apex lands 35.1 inches above the base.
equations: two arcs from the base ends

chapters.title: Rails, and the line
chapters.promise: The jig holds any stick of the right section.
narration: Lay a stick along each side, flat face down and bevel out, with its outer edge splitting the line. Clamp it, butt a rail against its inside edge, and screw the rail down. Do all three sides. Now any stick pushed against a rail lands exactly on its line. The jig does not care what size the sticks are, so long as every stick is the same size and the bevel is right.

chapters.title: Sticks that turn like a pinwheel
chapters.promise: Equal sides, different sticks.
narration: The three sticks do not meet at a point. Each runs to one corner and butts into the inside face of the next, so from above the corners turn like a pinwheel. That is why the two equal sides of a panel still take different sticks. In a hexagon panel the two C sticks are 38.47 and 38.51 inches along their outer edges, with tail cuts 31.4 and 29.3 degrees off square. Cut one end, lay the stick in, mark where the next stick crosses it, and cut that end with the miter and the bevel set together. Clamp a stop block and repeat, and check the fit every few sticks.

chapters.title: One bevel cannot be exact
chapters.promise: The number that does not flatter the method.
narration: Here is the number that does not flatter this method. The panels do not all turn by the same angle where they meet, so the exact bevel runs from 5.7 degrees to 7.2. A shop rips every stick at one setting, 6.5 degrees, so the worst joint is 0.8 degrees off. That is too small to see and not too small to leak. Lay a bead of sealant or a gasket between the frames as they go together; that is what takes up the difference.

chapters.title: Skin it in sections
chapters.promise: One sheet per pentagon or hexagon.
narration: Before raising, screw panels into whole pentagons and hexagons on the shop floor and cover each group with one sheet. At this cut 6 pentagons and 10 hexagons come out whole, and 15 panels are skinned one at a time. Pull the film tight across the group and staple it on the bevelled edges, where the next section hides the staples. A torn section is then one section to replace, not the whole dome.

chapters.title: A window is a panel with hinges
chapters.promise: A spare frame on two hinges.
narration: For each window, build one extra frame. Leave the skin off that panel in the dome, cover the spare frame, and hinge it along its top edge. A small gas strut of the kind kitchen cabinets use holds it open. Weather-strip the face it closes on so rain running down the dome cannot creep under it, and tape the hinge seam once the dome is up.

chapters.title: Raise it loose, then tighten
chapters.promise: Flexible until the last panel.
narration: Assemble from the base up, with a helper and plenty of clamps. Put only a few screws in each joint until the last panel closes the dome: until then the shell flexes, and that flex is what lets the last panels in. Lay a bead of sealant or a gasket between frames as they meet. Then tape the open seams between sections from the bottom up, each strip lapping over the one below, so water always runs onto tape and never under it. Do not raise a loose shell in a wind.

chapters.title: A floor the shape of the base
chapters.promise: Joists to the corners, girders on the five-fold.
narration: This dome stands on a radial deck that copies its base: 15 joists from the centre, one to each base corner, and a rim board along each base edge, each end cut 12 degrees off square. Under the joists, a ring of 5 girders follows the dome's own five-fold symmetry, with a post under each girder joint. Mark the centre, lay the girders out on the ground to place the posts, set the post heights to a level line, then roll in the joists.

chapters.title: Hold it down
chapters.promise: Light for its size; wind lifts.
narration: A dome is light for its size, and wind lifts. On a deck like this one, angle brackets tie every base section to the frame below. On gravel or earth, steel stakes driven at a slant and strapped to the base sections do the same job. Anchor it before the skin is finished, not after the first storm.
equations: gravel or earth: slanted stakes + straps

chapters.title: A zome without a bevel
chapters.promise: One stick, one miter, per row.
narration: The same panel thinking frames a zome. On the bench is a one-to-5 model of a nine-sided zome, 36 panels in 4 rows of 9. Each panel is four identical sticks in a pinwheel, square through their depth, with a miter at each end and the two ends parallel. Nothing is bevelled at all: one stick and one miter for every panel in a row.

chapters.title: The gap that is allowed
chapters.promise: Square edges leave a V outside.
narration: Square-edged panels butted on their inside edges leave a V-shaped gap on the outside. In a two-by-four on edge ours opens from 1.2 to 1.7 inches. On a small zome, screw the inside edges together and let the roof bridge the gap. On a big one, a wedge block bevelled to half the fold fills it and gives the joint more to bear on. Fasten loosely at first: the panels hinge, and the angle sets itself as the inside edges line up. The hub problem of a zome is gone.

chapters.title: What each method asks of you
chapters.promise: Choose by what you have.
narration: Side by side: the wedge dome is 19.4 feet across, with 120 members of two lengths cut from logs with a chainsaw. The panel dome is 16 feet across, with 105 panels and 315 sticks of 6 kinds, sawn from bought boards on a table saw and a miter saw, and 10 tapered base sections. The panel dome is the better-trodden road; many people have built one. The wedge dome asks for trees, and gives back fewer, bigger pieces. Choose by what you have.

chapters.title: Two good roads
chapters.promise: Choose by what you have.
narration: Every number in this film came from this project's own solver, and the same numbers are in the book. The panel dome is a road a great many builders have already walked, and it works. The wedge dome is the other road, starting from trees instead of boards. Both end in a dome. Choose by what you have.

lessons.title: The Shop the Campaign Buys: A 10 x 5 Plasma Table and Its Router

chapters.title: The shop the campaign buys
chapters.promise: Two machine lines, one frame.
narration: Part of what backing this project pays for is a shop. Not a building: two machines. A plasma table that cuts a whole sheet of steel into the panels of a dome, and a router that cuts the jigs and the wooden panels. This film is what those two machines are, what they make, and what they cost when you build them rather than buy them. Here is the first thing the table makes: one 120 by 60 inch sheet of plate, 40 panels.

chapters.title: One sheet, forty panels
chapters.promise: The torch follows the nest.
narration: Steel plate comes in sheets ten feet by five, and the table's bed is exactly that size. The torch walks every panel's outline in turn: about 181 feet of cut, roughly 24 minutes of torch time. What comes off the table is the whole shell of a dome, every triangle already the right size, already the right angle at every corner. Nothing is measured with a tape. The machine does the measuring.

chapters.title: How the panels fit
chapters.promise: Strips of triangles, up and down.
narration: The panels are laid out in 8 strips, each one triangles pointing alternately up and down, the way they tile with nothing between them but the cutting gap. Every panel is slid along until it sits exactly a quarter inch from its neighbour, and then the whole layout is checked part by part. 78 percent of the sheet ends up inside a part. The panels come from the solved dome, so if the geometry changes, the nest changes too.

chapters.title: Almost fits
chapters.promise: A little off each point.
narration: You can squeeze a slightly bigger shell out of the same sheet by trimming each panel's point and welding a small cap over every vertex. Here the best trim is 0.30 inches off each point, with 16 caps, and it makes the shell 1.4 percent bigger. That is real, and it is small: the strips are already full. Most of the time, cut the panels whole.

chapters.title: Welded up
chapters.promise: Forty panels, one shell.
narration: Welded together, the forty panels make a steel shell 5.2 feet across and 2.6 feet tall. That is 55 seams and 82 feet of weld, about 2.1 hours at a steady hand. In three-millimetre plate the panels weigh 188 pounds; in two-millimetre, 126. Every seam is a butt weld, ground flush where it shows.

chapters.title: What one sheet becomes
chapters.promise: A tub, a stove, a fire bowl, a seat.
narration: Turned over on three short legs, the shell is a bowl holding 237 gallons: a tub. In heavier plate, with a hinged panel for a door and a flue at the top, it is the body of a wood stove. Smaller jobs are a fire bowl, a planter, a seat. A hemisphere does not care which way up it is used, and these are the right first projects while you learn the machine.

chapters.title: What it is not
chapters.promise: One sheet does not make a shelter.
narration: Here is the number that does not help the pitch. At 2.6 feet tall, a one-sheet shell holds nobody standing up. It is not a storm shelter, and it is not a room. To shelter a person you need a bigger dome, cut from several sheets, and that is the next step.

chapters.title: A dome in plate
chapters.promise: Size the dome to the sheet.
narration: The same table cuts the triangles of a building. A three-frequency dome has two panel shapes, and how many sheets it takes depends on whether two strips of its biggest panels fit on a five-foot sheet. At 13 feet across they do: 9 sheets, 69 percent of the steel in parts, about 1,005 pounds in two-millimetre plate. One foot bigger, at 14 feet, they do not, and it takes 16 sheets. Size the dome to the sheet, or cut the big panels in two and weld them.

chapters.title: The table, by the plans' own rules
chapters.promise: Credit: Homemade Madness.
narration: The table is the Homemade Madness DIY CNC plasma design, and the credit for it is theirs. Their plans are drawn for a two-by-one-metre sheet and give two rules for building it bigger: the frame is two hundred and fifty millimetres longer and wider than the sheet, and the gantry tube is two hundred and fifty-three longer than the cut width. For a ten-by-five-foot sheet that makes a frame 3,298 by 1,774 millimetres. Ours is half again as long as theirs, so we add one change: a leg pair at the middle, so no rail span goes unsupported.

chapters.title: Long rails, joined
chapters.promise: Alignment is everything.
narration: No single rail is three metres long at this price, so each side takes three, joined end to end: 10 rails in all, which is 5 of the two-rail kits already bought. Both long sides are driven, so both need rack: 7 half-metre lengths a side, four on the gantry and a spare, 19 in all. Every joint is cut on the tooth and aligned with a spare piece held across it. A joint set by eye makes a machine that cuts a curve.

chapters.title: The number that has to be right
chapters.promise: Steps per millimetre.
narration: A fifteen-tooth pinion at module one and a half has a 22.5 millimetre pitch diameter, so one turn of the motor moves the axis 70.69 millimetres. With eight microsteps on a two-hundred-step motor, that is 22.64 steps per millimetre. That number goes into the controller before anything is cut. The plans prefer a thirteen-tooth pinion for torque, and say to use what you can find and set the ratio in software.

chapters.title: Motors that fit the pinion
chapters.promise: The bore decides the shaft.
narration: The pinions have a ten-millimetre bore, so the motors must have a ten-millimetre shaft. A NEMA 23 of three newton-metres has one, and fits with no sleeve; a bigger NEMA 34's shaft would not. Two of them on the long axis push a gantry of about 40 kilograms at 6.7 metres per second squared on half their torque, far more than a plasma ever asks for, because a plasma torch pushes on nothing.
