equations: two motors: 6.7 m/s^2 at half torque

chapters.title: Pilot arc and a floating head
chapters.promise: Keep the noise out of the wiring.
narration: The torch rides a floating head that touches the plate to find its height before every cut. Pick a plasma with a pilot-arc start: a high-frequency start puts electrical noise into the control wiring. A torch height controller is left out on purpose. The plans' breakout board cannot run one, and touching off the plate again partway through a long cut does the job for nothing.

chapters.title: What it costs, and what kind of number each is
chapters.promise: Paid, quoted, estimated.
narration: Built, the plasma table comes to $4,151, and the bill keeps three kinds of price apart. $1,157 is what we actually paid for rack, pinions and rails. $1,654 is current retail listings for the motors, drivers, power supply, Mach3, the plasma cutter and the frame steel. $1,339 is still estimates, labelled as estimates until they are quoted: the slats, the water pan, the plate, the ballscrew and the wiring.

chapters.title: The router head
chapters.promise: Same frame, different tool.
narration: For $990 more, the same frame becomes a router. The rails, rack, motors and controls stay. The floating head becomes a rigid ballscrew axis with a water-cooled spindle, the slats lift out, and a flat spoilboard goes in. The gantry tube sags 0.03 millimetres under a router's side load, less than the cutter's own wobble. This is the machine that cuts the jigs, the templates and the wooden panels the rest of the method needs.

chapters.title: Budgeted, and built
chapters.promise: The honest version of the line item.
narration: The campaign budgets $11,800 to buy a plasma table and $14,500 for a router: $26,300 together. Built on one frame, both machines come to $5,141. That difference is real, and so is what it does not include: a bought machine comes with support, a warranty and a phone number. A built one takes weeks of evenings, and its first troubleshooter is its owner. We print both numbers because the choice is real.

chapters.title: What the backing builds
chapters.promise: A shop that makes shops.
narration: That is what this part of the backing buys: a table that turns a sheet of steel into a dome's panels, a router that turns a sheet of plywood into the jigs that build the wooden ones, and the first things they make. Every number in this film comes from the same code as the book. The table's design is Homemade Madness's; the steel and the sawdust will be ours.

lessons.title: The Cell Wall: A Dome Skin in Layers

chapters.title: The cell wall
chapters.promise: A skin that does work.
narration: Most walls do one job: they stand between you and the weather. This one is built like the wall of a living cell, a stack of layers, each made as one piece, each with its own channels built into it, carrying water, air, heat, vacuum and signal. Every layer can run on its own, run backwards, or hand what it carries to the layer beside it. Here they are, cut open, all of them running at once.
equations: wall 261 mm; drawn 4x thicker to be seen

chapters.title: Why build this way
chapters.promise: Paid for once, used for decades.
narration: Why build like this? Because a channel, once it is in the wall, can be used again and again for different jobs. The network that glues the house together while you build it carries rain to a tank while you live in it, floods the sheathing when a wildfire comes, and finds the leak when something fails. This design lists 31 uses for 14 networks: 3 while you build, 14 while you live in it, 8 to protect it, and 6 to look after it. Every use after the first costs a valve and a few lines of code, not a new wall.
equations: 2.2 uses per network (counted from the design's list)

chapters.title: Two kinds of number
chapters.promise: Measured off the dome, or typed in with a reason.
narration: First, the two kinds of number in this film. Measured: the triangles, seams, areas and lengths, read off the solver's dome. Nobody typed those. Declared: the groove's size, the hoses, the foam, the pressures, the weather, the fire. A person typed those in, 69 of them, each with a unit, a kind and a reason. Each one is marked where it is used, and if one changes, every figure after it moves.
equations: MEASURED, off the solver's own dome:
gaskets 182 m, seams 94 m, rim 18.3 m
DECLARED, typed in by a person: 69, a reason each
groove 0.75 x 0.75 in; hoses 10 and 25 mm bore (assumed)
clamp 1 kPa, central vac 25 kPa, gust 40 m/s (assumed)
every figure after this reads the table

chapters.title: A groove in every round face
chapters.promise: The C-channel, and what it costs the member.
narration: It starts with one cut. Down the middle of every member's round face, the fat, curved side of the wedge, rout a groove three quarters of an inch wide and three quarters deep. That middle line is exactly where the sheathing bears, because each wedge sits square to its own panel. A hose goes in the groove. The groove takes 4.0 percent of the wood out of the member, and 4.8 percent of its bending strength. That is the structural price of everything that follows.
equations: wedge section 14.1 sq in (12 in log)

chapters.title: Forty gaskets
chapters.promise: A hose that reaches one triangle and nothing else.
narration: Every triangle has its own three members, so the three grooves round one triangle make a closed loop. The hose laid in them does two jobs. It is a gasket, sealing the board to the frame. And it is a channel that reaches that one triangle and nothing else. The dome has 40 of them, 4.5 to 4.9 metres each, 182 metres in all. Because each one closes on itself, one triangle can be filled, emptied, warmed or tested without touching its neighbours.

chapters.title: Three ports in every gasket
chapters.promise: Inside the seam, over it, or capped.
narration: Now drill each gasket where it passes the middle of a side: three through-holes a triangle, 120 in all. Each port has three choices. A jumper down through the V, the inside seam, to the gasket next door. A jumper over the ridge, the outside seam. Or a cap, and that triangle keeps to itself. The 10 ports along the bottom edge go to a manifold round the rim, which is where the tank, the pump and the outside world connect.
equations: a port: inside jumper, outside jumper, or cap

chapters.title: A network of locals only
chapters.promise: Beside the global channel, never part of it.
narration: Jumper every port and the gaskets become a network of their own: locals joined only to locals, running beside the global channel in the key but never part of it. 40 gaskets and 55 jumpers make 16 independent loops, so anything in it can always go round. Take away any one jumper and every triangle can still be reached: there is no single point of failure. From the nearest rim port, the farthest triangle is 4 jumpers away.
equations: farthest from a rim port: 4 hops; corner to corner: 10

chapters.title: The global channel
chapters.promise: Along the seams, everything is connected.
narration: Between the triangles run the seams, and in every seam is the channel the earlier films built, the key. That one is global. It runs from triangle to triangle all over the dome: 55 seams, 94 metres, 309 feet, down to the rim, where all of it can be reached from one place. Local and global: a gasket that touches one cell, and a network that touches every cell.

chapters.title: What fits in a seam
chapters.promise: Not every layer gets a one-inch run.
narration: Can every layer have its own run along every seam? Not at full size. The tightest seam's key has 5.3 square inches inside, and the rule the channel film used fills 40 percent of that. A one-inch hose fits 2 times. A three-eighths hose fits 10 times: room for all 9 networked layers, with 1 to spare. So the seams carry the small runs, and the big flows, air and flood water, ride the rings.

chapters.title: Bands, like a greenhouse
chapters.promise: Channels that run round the dome.
narration: There is a third kind. A greenhouse holds its plastic down with channels that run round the house, level. A dome can have those too: a ring at every height where its corners stand, 16.6, 15.8 and 9.8 metres round, and the rim at 18.3. A ring reaches every triangle at its height, so it serves one band of the dome at a time: the bottom, the belt, the crown.

chapters.title: Every triangle an address
chapters.promise: One pair of wires, like a car's.
narration: Give every triangle a small board on the room side: a few sensors, a few valves, and one pair of wires along the seams to all of them. That is how a car's body works, one bus with every part addressed. Forty triangles need 6 bits of address. Along every seam the bus is 94 metres. At 500 kilobits a second a bus is good for about 100: it fits, with 6 metres spare, which is too close. At 125 kilobits it is good for 500. Run it slow. Nothing in a wall needs to be fast.

chapters.title: Every layer is one piece
chapters.promise: Fabric, semi-flexible or hard, channels built in.
narration: Each layer is made as one piece, the way a quilt or a sheet of twin-wall plastic is, with its channels built in rather than added afterwards. Heat runs in a capillary mat, fine tubes woven into fabric. Room air runs in a textile duct, sewn into cells and perforated. Water runs in twin-wall sheet, the fluted plastic greenhouses are glazed with. Vacuum runs in a spacer fabric whose pile holds the gap open. The bladders are drop-stitch, two skins tied by thousands of threads, as inflatable paddleboards are. 7 layers are fabric, 3 semi-flexible and 3 hard. Outside the frame the whole skin is 78 millimetres thick, inside it 30.
equations: frame: frame and foam, 152 mm, hard (geometry)
skin: 78 mm outside the frame, 30 mm inside

chapters.title: A quilt of forty shirts
chapters.promise: Each patch one cell, sewn together.
narration: The fabric layers are made like a T-shirt quilt: forty triangular patches, one for every triangle of the frame, each one a cell of its own, sewn together along the seams. The stitching is where the channels run, so one patch can be filled, drained or warmed while the rest stay as they are. A quilt folds flat for carrying. It stacks on the layer below it. And it can be added years later, or taken off and cleaned, without touching the frame.

chapters.title: The stack, as first drawn
chapters.promise: Every layer outside the wood.
narration: Now the stack, the way you first drew it, from the wood outward. Water nearest the wood, catching rain and flooding in a fire. Then the air intake, the filter, the vacuum network, the Faraday cage, the smoke channel, the bladders, heating and cooling, the hard cover, the one watertight cap, and plants on top. Every one of those can work. Not all of them work on the outside of the wood.
equations: wood > water > air in > filter > vacuum > cage > fog
bladders > heat/cool > OSB > cap > plants > sky

chapters.title: The insulation splits the stack
chapters.promise: Heat inside the foam, water outside it.
narration: Fill the frame with foam and it becomes the insulation, and insulation splits a wall in two. On a 15 below night, with the room at 21, the room side of the foam sits near 20 degrees and the weather side near minus 15. A heating layer outside the foam sends 97 percent of its heat to the sky. Inside it, 98 percent reaches the room. So heat, cooling, room air and fog move inside the frame. Water, filter, vacuum, cage and bladders stay out, and anything wet out there drains before it freezes.
equations: room side 20.2 C; core 3.1 C; weather side -14.5 C
heat outside the foam: 3% to the room
heat inside the foam: 98% to the room

chapters.title: The wall in section
chapters.promise: Every layer over one seam, drawn thick.
narration: Here it is in section, over one seam, drawn several times thicker than it is so every layer can be seen. In the frame, two members and the key between them, a gasket in each member's groove, and the jumper that joins them through the V. Glued to the frame, the board. Above it the weather side: water, filter, vacuum, cage, the one watertight cap, bladders and plants. Below the frame, an inner skin and the room side: signal, fog, air and heat. Every layer shows its channels where the cut passes through them.
equations: weather: OSB, water, filter, vacuum, cage, cap, bladders, plants
room: bus, fog, air in, heat/cool

chapters.title: All of it, at once
chapters.promise: Every layer running, none in another's way.
narration: Now the whole wall, cut open, with everything running at once. Warm water climbs one side of the room-side mat and comes down the other. Fresh air rises through the duct. Signals run down to the controller at the rim. In the core, foam. Outside the board, rain water falls through the flutes toward the tank, filtered air rises through the pleats, vacuum draws toward the rim ring, and water drips through the plants' felt. Each layer does its own job, in its own channels, and not one of them is in another's way.
equations: heat: up one side, down the other
air: up the duct; signal: down to the rim
water: down the flutes; filtered air: up the pleats

chapters.title: Glue from the inside
chapters.promise: And a vacuum to clamp it while it cures.
narration: Now the build, and the first thing the gaskets are for. Lay a triangle of board on its frame and push glue through the gasket's hose. Flooding the whole groove would take 42 litres for the dome, 140 cartridges. A perforated hose that pushes out a bead takes 5.5 litres, 19 cartridges. While it cures, pull a vacuum on the cavity. At one kilopascal the air presses the biggest panel down with 148 kilograms of force. Boat builders call it vacuum bagging. Every triangle glued to its frame from the inside, with no nails.

chapters.title: Foam after the cover
chapters.promise: Three lifts, and the panel becomes a sandwich.
narration: Then the foam, after the cover is on. Each triangle's cavity holds 156 litres. The whole dome takes 6.25 cubic metres, 2,648 board feet, 5 two-part kits, about 3,750 dollars. Pour it in 3 lifts, 52 litres a triangle at a time, with the clamp still on, so the foam's push cannot lift the cover. Glued on the outside and foamed within, each triangle becomes a sandwich panel, and the wall becomes R-36.
equations: cavity 156 L a triangle; 6.25 m3 = 2,648 bd ft

chapters.title: One-way doors
chapters.promise: Foam and glue spend the core's channels.
narration: Against all that: foam and glue are one-way doors. The glue fills the gaskets it went through, and the foam fills the cavity, so the core's own channels are spent the day they are used. Here is what that costs. A hollow core could soak its whole frame to fibre saturation in a fire, with 124 litres, 27 percent of the tank. A foamed one cannot be reached. Decide which layers are permanent before you build, and keep the ones you will want to change where they can come off.
equations: only while the core is hollow

chapters.title: Rain to the tank
chapters.promise: And drained before it freezes.
narration: The water layer lies on the board, nearest the wood. A dome standing on 27.5 square metres catches 40 inches of rain a year: 6,276 gallons off the cap, about 17 a day. The rim channel takes it to the tank, and the 120 gallon tank fills 52 times a year. Below freezing the layer drains: on a 15 below night it sits at minus 15 degrees, and water left in it would split it.

chapters.title: The whole shell is the filter
chapters.promise: Air in, slower than a breeze.
narration: Air in. Draw outside air in under the cap at the rim, through a filter layer that covers the whole shell, and hand it to the room-side air layer at the rim. The house needs 17.6 cubic feet a minute. Spread over 51 square metres of filter, it moves 0.16 millimetres a second: 15,401 times slower than a furnace filter. A filter that slow catches nearly everything and almost never clogs. Does it also pick up the heat leaking out? About 4 watts of the 274 the wall loses. The cap is too close to the cold.

chapters.title: Venting the skin
chapters.promise: Dry air through the flutes.
narration: Venting is the quiet job the network does every week. After a storm, or after the sheathing has been flooded on purpose, dry air pushed through the water layer's flutes carries the wet away and out at the rim. A film of half a millimetre over the side that got wet is 13 kilograms of water. A small fan moving 100 cubic feet a minute, on a 20 degree day at 50 percent, takes 1.4 kilograms an hour: dry in about 9 hours. With only the house's own fresh air it would take 53. The same moving air, under the cap in summer, carries the sun's heat off before it reaches the board.

chapters.title: The services' numbers
chapters.promise: Typed in, before they are used.
narration: Before the services, the numbers they lean on. How warm a wall is run, and how fast it trades heat with a room. The design night. The heat a fire throws and the heat water takes to boil away. How long embers fall. The mesh, the doorway and the radio band. What a floor and its contents weigh. How steep soil will hold. All typed in, all marked as what they are.
equations: warm wall 10 K over the room; h = 8 W/m2K (estimate)
water takes 2.26 MJ/kg to boil off (standard)
embers 30 min; a 0.5 mm film; a 100 cfm fan (assumed)
mesh 6.35 mm, door 0.9 m, Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz
floor and contents 120 kg/m2; bladders 20 cm deep (assumed)
soil holds to 30 deg; wet 120 kg/m2, felt 30 (estimates)
each one marked where it is used

chapters.title: A wall a degree and a half warm
chapters.promise: The whole wall is the radiator.
narration: Heating. On the room side, a layer of warm water makes the whole wall a radiator. A wall 10 degrees warmer than the room gives 4.1 kilowatts. The foamed dome loses only 634 watts on a 15 below night: 274 through the wall and 360 in fresh air. So the wall needs to be just 1.6 degrees warmer than the room, cooler than your skin. Warm walls, not warm air: the most comfortable heat there is.
equations: wall needs 1.55 K over the room

chapters.title: A cool wall, above the dew point
chapters.promise: And where the cold comes from.
narration: Cooling is the same layer run the other way, with one limit: a wall colder than the room's dew point gets wet. On a humid day, 26 degrees and 60 percent, the dew point is 17.6. Keep the wood's 3 degree margin and the coolest the wall may be is 20.6. Even so, the whole wall takes 2.2 kilowatts out of the room, against the Peltier ring's 281 watts. The cold can come from the water layer outside at night, giving heat to the sky, about 2.0 kilowatts, kept in the tank for the afternoon.

chapters.title: A vacuum is a load
chapters.promise: It holds; it does not insulate.
narration: A vacuum across a sheet is a load. The clamp's one kilopascal puts 1.45 kilonewtons on the biggest triangle. A 40 metre a second gust sucks on the same panel with 1.39, so the clamp holds the skin down, by 4 percent. A central vacuum's 25 kilopascals across that sheet would be 3.7 tonnes: that strength lives in hoses only. A layer completely under vacuum, the kind that insulates, would carry 15 tonnes on one panel. The clamp leaves the air 99 percent as dense: it holds, it does not insulate.
equations: central vac on a sheet: 36 kN = 3.7 t
air left at 1 kPa: 99% as dense

chapters.title: Three vacuums at once
chapters.promise: Each strength only where it is safe.
narration: So, different vacuums at once, at different levels. The rim ring is a central vacuum: 25 kilopascals, enough to lift water 2.5 metres, sealed in hoses, with an inlet at every rim corner. A regulator feeds the water layer at 5, which lifts rain 0.5 metres into a raised tank. Another feeds the clamp at 1. One pump, three levels, each strength only where it is safe.
equations: rim ring, in hoses: 25 kPa, lifts water 2.55 m
water draw: 5 kPa, lifts water 0.51 m
sheet clamp: 1 kPa, lifts water 0.10 m

chapters.title: How a wildfire takes a house
chapters.promise: Embers, radiant heat, and flame.
narration: Now the case this network was built for. A wildfire takes a house three ways. Embers, carried far ahead of the flames, find a vent or a gap and start the fire from inside; that is how most houses are lost. Radiant heat, which Australia's building standard measures in kilowatts on every square metre: a house rated BAL-29 is built to take 29 at the fire's edge. And flame contact. Above 40 kilowatts a square metre is the flame zone, where no skin is enough and only a cleared perimeter helps.

chapters.title: Close every door
chapters.promise: Nothing for an ember to find.
narration: So first, the house shuts. All 10 intakes at the rim close. The filter layer stops drawing outside air, and the room runs on its own air for the hour that matters. The cap has no openings to begin with: the breathing film showed why the cap is never cut, and in a fire this is the reason. An ember landing on this skin finds nothing to climb into.
equations: filter layer: off; room on its own air

chapters.title: Flood the sheathing, metered
chapters.promise: Water where the heat is, as fast as it boils off.
narration: Then the water layer floods the sheathing on the side facing the fire, and here is the multiplier. At a sprinkler's rate, wetting the whole dome takes 55 gallons a minute and empties the tank in 2.2 minutes. But the heat arriving on the fire's side, 741 kilowatts at BAL-29, only boils away 4.5 gallons a minute. Metered to the heat by the sensor in every cell, the same 120 gallon tank lasts 27 minutes: 12 times longer, 89 percent of the half hour embers keep falling. That flow runs through the local-net's jumpers at 0.4 metres a second, on a 111 watt pump.
equations: tank: 27 min vs 2.2 at sprinkler rate

chapters.title: Aim the water
chapters.promise: A nervous system, not a sprinkler.
narration: What the network changes is where the water goes. A sensor in every cell knows which triangle is hot. One triangle takes 1.4 gallons a minute at the sprinkler's rate, and on one triangle at a time the same tank lasts 87 minutes. Water where the embers are landing, nowhere else. That is the difference between a sprinkler and a nervous system.

chapters.title: After the front
chapters.promise: Check, vent, dry.
narration: When the front has passed, the network turns from defence to recovery. The sensor in every cell reports which triangles got hot. The local-net pressure-tests the cells for damage, halving the search each time: 6 tests find one bad triangle in forty. And the venting run dries the flooded side in about 9 hours. The house defended itself with its own skin, and then it checks itself over.
equations: sensors: every cell's heat and moisture

chapters.title: A cage is its biggest hole
chapters.promise: Bond every seam, or it is not a cage.
narration: Bond a mesh into one layer and the dome is a Faraday cage: lightning goes round the people inside, and radio is cut down. But a cage is only as good as its biggest hole. Quarter-inch mesh stops everything below 23.6 gigahertz, and cuts Wi-Fi by about 20 decibels. An unbonded seam is a slot 1.8 metres long that lets in everything above 82 megahertz. An open door lets in everything above 167. So bond all 55 seams, 309 feet of it, and give the door a conductive gasket.
equations: unbonded seam 1.83 m: leaks above 82 MHz
open door 0.9 m: leaks above 167 MHz

chapters.title: Fog, not pepper
chapters.promise: And backwards, a smoke exhaust.
narration: Security. You asked about pepper spray. A device that sprays a person by itself is a trap, and in many places a trap that hurts an intruder is illegal, even in your own home. It would also gas your family, your dog and the firefighters. Fog does the job instead: a security fog unit fills the dome's 54 cubic metres in about 5 seconds, and nobody can see to take anything. Run the same channel backwards in a fire and it is a smoke exhaust: smoke out of the crown, down the seams, and out at the rim.

chapters.title: If the water comes up
chapters.promise: Bladders float it. A sealed floor floats it dry.
narration: And if the water comes up. The house, frame, cover, floor and everything in it, is about 4.6 tonnes, so it floats once it pushes aside 4.6 cubic metres of water. Bladders round the lower half of the dome, 25.5 square metres inflated 20 centimetres deep, hold 5.1: enough, with 11 percent to spare, from one cylinder of carbon dioxide. But they only lift it when the water is 1.3 metres up the wall, and by then the floor is under water. Seal the floor and the foot of the wall instead and it is a hull: it floats in 17 centimetres, dry inside. Either way it needs guide posts, as amphibious houses have, or it floats away.
equations: bladders lift at 1.29 m of water: floor flooded
sealed floor: floats at 17 cm, dry

chapters.title: Every layer runs both ways
chapters.promise: A pipe with valves at both ends.
narration: Most of these layers run both ways. Air in, or air out. Warm water, or cold. Fog out, or smoke in. Vacuum to clamp, or pressure to test for leaks. Rain in to the tank, or the tank's water back out as a flood. A layer is a pipe with valves at both ends, and the valves decide the direction, not the layer.

chapters.title: Plug one layer into another
chapters.promise: A short list of allowed routes.
narration: And a layer can be plugged into another. The filter hands its air to the room's air layer. Rain runs to the tank, and the tank feeds the flood, the plants and the warm or cool wall. The vacuum pulls the water layer toward the tank, and holds the core while its glue cures. A cylinder fills the bladders. 9 routes in all, and the controller refuses anything not on the list.

chapters.title: Situations, not settings
chapters.promise: And the interlocks that keep them apart.
narration: So the house runs in situations, not settings. A winter night: the wall warm, air in through the filter, the water layer drained, the clamp on. A humid afternoon: the wall cool, the plants watered. The summer night after it: water out under the sky, filling the tank with cold. A storm: rain to the tank. Embers: the flood, the smoke drawn out, no outside air. Someone breaking in: fog. Rising water: the bladders. And the interlocks that keep them from fighting.
equations: a winter night: wall warm, air in, filtered, water drained, clamp
a humid summer afternoon: wall cool, air in, filtered, plants watered
the summer night after it: water under the sky, air in, filtered
a rainstorm: rain to tank, clamp, air in, filtered
embers on the wind: FLOOD, smoke out
the water coming up: BLADDERS, water drained
building the wall: glue in, clamp
interlocks: no fog with air; no clamp by a flood or the bladders; nothing wet below 0 C

chapters.title: And more
chapters.promise: A leak found in six tests; smoke smelled in seconds.
narration: And more, from the same network. Find a leaking triangle by pressurising half the cells, then half of those: 6 tests find one in forty. Draw air from every gasket to one smoke detector, as big buildings do with sampling pipes: from the farthest triangle a sample takes 10 seconds, inside the 120 the standard allows. Treat bare timber with borate from inside: 10 litres for the frame. Kill insects in a layer with carbon dioxide: 0.45 kilograms. Melt snow off the crown with 1.8 kilowatts. Or run the water layer as a solar collector in summer: up to 7.2 kilowatts off half the dome.
equations: smoke sample: 9.7 m at 1 m/s = 10 s
CO2 at 60% in one layer: 0.45 kg
snowmelt, crown: 1.83 kW; all of it 15.3 kW

chapters.title: The chia-pet
chapters.promise: Plants on the outside, fed from within.
narration: And the outside can be alive. Over the cap, a root barrier, and over that, plants, watered and fed from inside through the living layer, with the food dissolved in the water, which growers call fertigation. But a dome is steep. Only 12 percent of it, the 5 crown triangles at 19 degrees, is flat enough to hold soil. The rest takes felt pockets. Wet, all of it weighs 2.1 tonnes, 2.4 times the frame, and drinks 153 litres a summer day. It can be done. It is a structural decision, not a decoration.
equations: wet total 2,081 kg = 2.4 x frame (869 kg)

chapters.title: The multiplier
chapters.promise: Counted, not claimed.
narration: Count it. 31 uses from 14 networks: 2.2 for every network built. The water layer alone does 7 jobs: rain to the tank, solar heat, night cooling, snowmelt, borate, drying, and the fire flood. Then the stacked uses: filtered air handed to the room's air layer, the tank feeding the wall and the plants, the vacuum holding the glue. A wall that does one thing is paid for once and used once. This one is paid for once and used every day, in every season, for as long as it stands.

chapters.title: The price of an address
chapters.promise: Valves and joints.
narration: Now the price of all those addresses. 9 networked layers over forty triangles, with the bladders only on the lower half, is 340 cells. A valve in and a valve out on every cell is 680 valves, and joining every cell and every seam run at both ends is 1,600 joints, every one of them a place to leak. Address by band instead, a pair of valves per band per layer at the rim, and it is 82. Address by triangle only where it pays: the water in a fire, the sensors, the bus. Everything else by band.

chapters.title: Start with three
chapters.promise: The skin is an organ.
narration: So where to start? Three layers earn their place on day one. Glue and foam through the core while you build, because the gaskets are already there. The bus and its sensors, because a wall that reports its own moisture is a wall that does not rot unseen. And the water layer, because the rain is free and the fire will come. The rest can be added later, if the ports, the rings and the seam runs go in now. The skin of this dome is not a wall. It is an organ.

lessons.title: The Sky Web: Building a Dome in the Air

chapters.title: Built in the air
chapters.promise: Forty triangles, hung from a web.
narration: Most domes are built from the ground up, a ring at a time, with scaffolding inside. This one is built in the air. A web of cable strung between four living trees, and every triangle of the dome hauled up by a battery winch, swung into its place, and left hanging there on three cords. Then joined, gathered to one point at the top, skinned, and perhaps never let down. The ground, the foundation and the gasket can wait. Here is how, with every load worked out, and the numbers that argue back.

chapters.title: What is weighed, what is assumed
chapters.promise: Two tables, before the numbers.
narration: First, what this rests on, in two tables. What the owner weighed and owns: struts of 15 to 22 kilograms, and a 1,500 pound, twelve volt winch. And what a person assumed, each with a reason: where the trees stand, how high the ropes are tied, how far they sag, what rope, wood and cloth will take. 53 figures. Every load in this film uses the heaviest strut. Change any line, and every number after it changes.
equations: WEIGHED OR OWNED, by the owner:
12 V winch 1,500 lb; planned x4 to x8
solver's own estimate: 869 kg of frame (7.2 kg a strut)
DECLARED, typed in by a person: 53, a reason each
trees 9 m square, ties at 8 m; next trees 8 m out
sag 10% of the span; rope worked at 1/5
trunk 45 cm; green pine 35 MPa, E 7 GPa (estimates)
skin: cotton 340 g/m2 + silicone 150 g/m2 a layer (estimate)
Ropes are drawn 5x thicker, to be seen.

chapters.title: Two corrections
chapters.promise: The winch, and what a strut weighs.
narration: The first cut of this film got two things wrong. It showed a hand winch. The winch is electric: twelve volts, off a battery, rated 1,500 pounds, 6.7 kilonewtons. And it weighed the frame with the solver's estimate, 7.2 kilograms a strut. The owner's struts, weighed, are 15 to 22: 2.1 to 3.0 times as heavy. So a triangle is 45 to 66 kilograms, and the frame 1,800 to 2,640. Every load from here on is the heavier one.

chapters.title: Four trees, a square
chapters.promise: The X runs corner to corner.
narration: Four trees round the pad, near enough a square, 9 metres a side. The ropes run corner to corner, so each one spans the diagonal: 12.7 metres, about 42 feet. They are tied 8 metres up, 26 feet, on tree-saver straps, never wrapped bare round the bark. Real trees are never a perfect square. The arithmetic only needs the longest diagonal, and the height of the lowest tie.

chapters.title: Two ropes make an X
chapters.promise: And how hard they pull.
narration: Two wire ropes, crossing in the middle, carrying 2,640 kilograms of frame. A rope with weight on it pulls sideways on its ends, and the flatter it hangs, the harder it pulls. Sagging ten percent, 1.3 metres, with each triangle's cords on the rope nearest it, the worse rope pulls 27 kilonewtons: five-eighths wire rope, worked at a fifth of its strength. Pull it flatter, to five percent, and it doubles, to 51, and wants 3/4 in rope. With real struts, a deep sag is not a choice. It is the design.
equations: H = M / s: the beam moment at midspan over the sag

chapters.title: Guy to the next tree
chapters.promise: Unguyed, a flat web breaks its trees.
narration: And the trees take all of it, eight metres up, as a lever. A 45 centimetre pine, green, breaks in bending at about 35 megapascals. Unguyed, the ten percent web works its trunk to a margin of 1.5, where a living tree should keep three; the five percent web, to 0.77, which is past breaking. So every anchor tree is guyed, and the guy goes where the owner put it: to the base of the next tree out, 8 metres behind. No ground anchors to buy or dig. The guy pulls 36 kilonewtons, 5/8 in rope, on a trunk at its strongest point, its roots.
equations: M = 25.4 kN x 8 m = 204 kN m
guy at 45 deg to the next tree's base: 36.0 kN

chapters.title: A tree is a better post
chapters.promise: Why cut it down to hold something up?
narration: Guyed at the tie, the anchor tree stops being a lever. It becomes a post, squeezed from above by 33 kilonewtons, held at the top by its guy, and fixed in the ground by its own roots. Cut that tree, mill it, haul it to a store and back, and you get a six by six post. Eight metres tall, that post buckles at about 90 kilonewtons. The living trunk it came from, at about 4.4 meganewtons, is 49 times stiffer, and it carries this web with 134 times to spare. The tree was already the better post.

chapters.title: A spiral over the footprint
chapters.promise: So a thrown cord always finds a strand.
narration: Then the spiral, woven out from the crossing and seized to the X wherever it crosses. It covers the dome's footprint, a circle 5.9 metres across, but above it. The turns are 50 centimetres apart, so a cord thrown up from anywhere under it always lands across a strand. That is 5.9 turns, 55 metres of line, and 24 seizings. The X carries the weight. The spiral gives the pigtails somewhere to land.

chapters.title: A twelve-volt winch
chapters.promise: Forty lifts on a fifth of one battery.
narration: The winch is a twelve volt one, bolted to the first tree and run off a battery. Its line runs up the trunk to a block at the tie, along under the rope to a pulley at the crossing, and down to a hook. The heaviest triangle, 66 kilograms, pulls 0.65 kilonewtons against a winch rated 6.7: 10 times over. Lifting it 6.1 metres costs about 3 watt hours, so all forty take 126, about 21 percent of what one hundred amp hour battery should give.
equations: pull 66 kg x g = 0.647 kN; winch x10.3
energy = m g h / 0.35 = 3.1 Wh a lift

chapters.title: A harness that hangs it flat
chapters.promise: Three legs, one eye, over the balance point.
narration: A triangle comes up in a harness: three legs, one to each corner, meeting in an eye 1 metre above the point the triangle balances on. Hook the eye and it rises flat. The dome has 2 shapes of triangle, so there are 2 harnesses. The one with two short sides needs legs of 1.35 and 1.42 metres; the equal one, three of 1.45. Make them once, label them, and use them forty times.

chapters.title: Up, flat
chapters.promise: Under two minutes a triangle.
narration: Up it goes, flat, under the crossing. The hook tops out 6.1 metres up, 20 feet. A small twelve volt winch brings in about 4 metres a minute at this load, so a triangle takes 1.5 minutes to raise, and all forty about an hour of winding. Flat matters: a triangle that tips on the way up catches the line, the X, and anyone underneath.

chapters.title: Swing it out
chapters.promise: From the centre to where it belongs.
narration: At the top it hangs from the centre, and its place is somewhere else. A tag line from the ground swings it out from under the crossing, and as it goes it is turned, from flat to the angle it will sit at in the finished dome. The hook stays on. Nothing lets go until the pigtails are on.
equations: end: its own place, its own angle

chapters.title: Three pigtails over the web
chapters.promise: Then it slips the harness.
narration: Every triangle carries three pigtails, a cord tied at each corner. Thrown up over the spiral and tied back, they hold it where it is. Then it slips the harness, and the hook goes back for the next. The pigtails are 1.3 to 4.5 metres long: 120 of them, 363 metres of cord. Each holds 216 newtons, on a cord that breaks at 9 kilonewtons: 42 times over.
equations: pigtail = web height - corner + 0.5 m tie

chapters.title: Rim first, crown last
chapters.promise: Keep the middle clear for the hook.
narration: The order matters. The hook comes down at the centre, so the middle has to stay clear until the end: hang the rim first, then the band above it, and the crown last. And the crown is where the hook runs out. With a metre of harness above them, 5 crown triangles would need the hook higher than it can climb. They are hung low, the pigtails go on, and they are hauled the last 44 centimetres on their own cords.
equations: order: by distance from the centre, outermost first
5 crown triangles short by up to 44 cm

chapters.title: Forty, floating
chapters.promise: None of them touching.
narration: And there it is. Forty triangles, each in its place, each on its own three cords, none of them touching. The rim hangs 3.0 metres up, 10 feet, the crown at 5.9. Walk underneath and look up through it. Every seam is still open, every edge is reachable, and nothing is holding anything else up.

chapters.title: Join them later
chapters.promise: The gap closes on the cords.
narration: Joining is later, and it is easy from here. Each triangle swings a little on its cords, so its neighbour can be drawn up to it and the seam closed, a pair at a time, with nothing to lift. When the last seam closes, forty separate triangles are one dome, still hanging where they were.
equations: each triangle: its own three cords
joined: one dome, the same cords

chapters.title: Lashed, not screwed
chapters.promise: Cord, strut to strut, under a hard shell.
narration: And the seams need not be screwed. A dome works mostly in compression: its triangles lean on each other. A joint only has to stop them sliding apart, and cord can do that. Lash each of the 55 seams in 3 places, 8 turns round both struts, and it takes 165 lashings and about 1,101 metres of cord. Cord stretches and creeps, so lashings want re-tightening, and they suit best a dome whose shell, fibreglass, say, takes the pulling. Under a hard shell, the lashings only hold the shape.
equations: 8 turns x 0.77 m + tie = 6.7 m each

chapters.title: Every cord to the apex
chapters.promise: Through the air, not along the struts.
narration: Then the pigtails come off the web and are gathered to the top, so the whole dome hangs from one point, and the shell can go over the cords. How they run matters. Laid along the struts, a cord pressed on a curved surface lifts nothing where it lies: what it pulls up at its corner it pushes back down along its length, and the whole weight ends up on the cap. Run straight through the air inside, from each joint to one free ring just under the cap, every joint is lifted by its own cord. 20 cords and the apex, and one line out through the cap. The rim cords lean in at 40 degrees and squeeze the rim with 1.3 kilonewtons, which a dome takes happily. 5 joints sit too close to the ring for a cord, and hang from the apex on their struts.
equations: joints 26: 20 cords + apex; 5 hang on struts
cord T = w / sin(angle); rim 40 deg
apex line carries 7.7 kN; hardest cord squeezes 3.7 kN

chapters.title: Cords across the room
chapters.promise: The price of one point.
narration: And here is what that costs. Through the air means through the room. A cord from the rim to the ring under the cap passes, halfway to the wall, only 1.2 metres above a floor laid at the rim. Fine while it is a frame hanging in the trees. In a home, those cords are lowered away once the dome is set where it will stay, or it is hung by its rim instead.
equations: halfway out: 1.23 m above the floor

chapters.title: One winch, the whole dome
chapters.promise: Today's winch lifts a quarter of it.
narration: With every cord at one point, one winch can lift the whole dome, up and down, evenly. But this is the whole weight: the frame and a skin, 2,695 kilograms, 26.4 kilonewtons. Today's winch lifts 25 percent of it. The planned one, 4 times bigger, lifts it with almost nothing to spare. 8 times bigger lifts it twice over, and that is the one to buy. Hang the winch itself at the crossing: pulled from a tree, the line turns at the pulley and loads the X with 37 kilonewtons, not 26. And now every kilogram is at the crossing, so the ropes pull 34: still 5/8 in, with the guys at 47.
equations: block, winch at a tree: W x 1.41 = 37.4 kN
X, all at the crossing: 33.7 kN, 5/8 in

chapters.title: It hangs level, if you sort the struts
chapters.promise: A dome's weight is on its axis.
narration: This is what a dome can do that a house cannot. Its weight sits on its own axis, so hung from one point it hangs level by itself. A house, with its kitchen at one end and its loads everywhere, would hang at whatever angle its contents chose. But your struts are not all the same. Placed at random, struts of 15 to 22 kilograms tip it about 1 degree, and one time in twenty more than 2: 22 centimetres across the rim. Every heavy strut on one side, 14. So weigh them, and spread the heavy ones round the dome. Sorted, it hangs dead level.
equations: tilt = atan(offset / 1.04 m below the ring)

chapters.title: A silicone skin
chapters.promise: Cotton, soaked in silicone dissolved in naphtha.
narration: The covering. Sailcloth would do, at about 25 dollars a square metre. The owner's way is cheaper: dissolve one hundred percent silicone in naphtha, soak cotton in it, and let the naphtha evaporate. The silicone stays in the fibres, a waterproof, chemically quiet skin. Two layers over 51 square metres of dome, with laps, take about 55 tubes of silicone, 65 litres of naphtha and 112 square metres of cotton: about 1,486 dollars, against 2,809 in sailcloth, and 55 kilograms. Silicone sticks to silicone, so layers stack into one skin; almost nothing else will stick to it later. Naphtha is very flammable: soak outdoors, far from any flame.

chapters.title: A taut web is a stiff web
chapters.promise: Trees move. Give the rope a spring.
narration: Trees move in the wind, and they move apart. A rope sagging ten percent goes straight once its trees lean apart 34 centimetres; at five percent, after only 8.5. After that the rope stretches, and every further centimetre adds about 4 kilonewtons. So the deep sag earns its keep twice, and the X still gets a heavy spring at every end, to let it give.

chapters.title: Wind on a hung dome
chapters.promise: Heavy and round, it barely swings.
narration: Skinned, the dome catches wind. Side on it shows 13.8 square metres. A 90 kilometre an hour gust pushes it with about 2.6 kilonewtons; it weighs 26, so it swings 6 degrees. A 144 kilometre an hour storm, 6.6 kilonewtons, 14 degrees. Its weight is what keeps it still, and its round shape sheds the wind the same from every side. Tie it down to the trees on three sides before a storm all the same.
equations: F = 1/2 rho v^2 Cd A, A = pi R^2 / 2 = 13.8 m2

chapters.title: Building with the trees
chapters.promise: Posts, shade and drainage, already standing.
narration: Step back and look at what the trees are doing. They are the posts, stronger than anything sawn from them. Their crowns shade the dome in summer. Their roots draw water out of the ground round it, a mature pine perhaps 150 litres on a summer day, 600 for the four. Nothing touches the soil, so there is no foundation, no damp rising, and air moves under and round it. And the guys tie to the next trees out, so the anchors are trees too: a network of trees, doing a foundation's work. Why cut a tree to make a post, when it is already the post?

chapters.title: A second web, if the trees allow
chapters.promise: Experimental, and planned before the trees are chosen.
narration: Higher still is possible, and it is experimental. It depends on the trees, and it has to be planned before they are chosen; the owner's are not set up for it. Strung at 12 metres, the same pull is half again the lever: unguyed, the trunks would be worked to a margin of 1.0, at the edge of breaking, and the guys pull 46 kilonewtons. Here is how it would go, if the trees allowed it.
equations: unguyed margin 1.03; guy 45.9 kN at 56 deg

chapters.title: The first web is in the way
chapters.promise: It has to come out.
narration: The first web is in the way. Hung from the second, the crown rises to 9.9 metres, and the first web crosses at 6.7: the dome would pass 3.2 metres up through it. So the dome is handed over first, on long cords from the second web, a corner at a time. Then the first web comes out: the spiral unwound from its outer end, and each rope of the X untied at one tree and pulled through from the other.

chapters.title: A corner at a time
chapters.promise: Thirty-two pulls, and a bigger winch.
narration: Then up, a corner at a time: the block moves over one corner, the winch raises that side 50 centimetres, its cords are re-tied, and on to the next, each step a tilt of 4.8 degrees. 4 metres up is 8 rounds of four, 32 pulls. The heaviest corner is 726 kilograms, 7.1 kilonewtons: more than today's winch, well within the 4 times one.
equations: rise 4.0 m / 0.5 m = 8 rounds x 4 = 32 pulls

chapters.title: Leave it hanging
chapters.promise: The shell, yes. A floor full of life, on bigger rope.
narration: So, leave it up? The shell, frame and skin, 2,695 kilograms, hangs from this X on 5/8 in rope at 34 kilonewtons, the trees guyed. Add a floor and what a household puts on it, by the cell wall's own figure 3.3 tonnes, and it is 6.0 tonnes, pulling 75 kilonewtons: 1 in rope, and every guy and tree checked again. It can be done. It is a structure an engineer and an arborist should sign, and it is priced here, not rated.

chapters.title: What the trees ask in return
chapters.promise: Lightning, growth, deadwood, rot.
narration: The trees give a lot, and they ask some things back. They are the tallest things on the hill, and now they carry steel rope to the dome: bond the ropes and ground them, or lightning will use them. Trunks grow, so tree-saver straps are loosened every year, never left to girdle the bark. Dead branches fall, so the crowns are cleaned before anything hangs under them. And rot hides, so an arborist looks at all eight trees every season, and after every big storm.
equations: bond and ground the wire rope

chapters.title: Never under the load
chapters.promise: Sixty-six kilograms at nearly forty kilometres an hour.
narration: And the rule that matters most. Nobody stands under a triangle on its way up. Dropped from the top of the hoist, 6.1 metres, a 66 kilogram triangle lands at 39 kilometres an hour, with 4.0 kilojoules. Mark a ring under the hook and keep it empty. Wear a helmet. Climb on a proper climbing system, tied in twice, or hire an arborist for the ties. The web is only as safe as the worst knot in it.
equations: v = sqrt(2 g h) = 11.0 m/s = 39 km/h

chapters.title: The ground can wait
chapters.promise: Built with the trees.
narration: Two ropes for the X, 55 metres of spiral, four guys to four more trees, 363 metres of pigtails, one battery winch and, one day, a bigger one at the top. Forty triangles hung, joined and lifted without a scaffold, a crane or a foundation, by a network of living trees that were already doing the job. The ground can wait. Maybe it can wait for good.

lessons.title: Every Piece, Numbered: Filling the Triangles and Framing the Floor

chapters.title: Every piece, numbered
chapters.promise: A triangle and a floor, cut by the numbers.
narration: Two things are built from wood in this film. One of the dome's forty triangles, filled with wedges split from a log. And the floor the whole dome stands on, framed from five twenty-foot half trunks. Every piece of both has a number. Every number has a length, an angle, and a way of cutting it, worked out by one calculator and shown on the saw before anyone picks up a blade.

chapters.title: What is solved, what is assumed
chapters.promise: Two tables before any number.
narration: First, what this rests on. The shapes are solved: the dome from its 72 inch strut, the triangles from the dome, every piece from its triangle and the log it is split from. What cannot be solved is written down, each line with its reason. 34 figures for the triangles: saw kerfs, the sizes things are sold in, prices. And 33 for the floor, from the forty pounds a square foot a floor must carry, to how strong ungraded wood is taken to be. Change any line, and every number after it changes.
equations: SOLVED, from the strut length and the log:
dome 22.57 ft across from a 72 in strut
two triangle shapes; every piece from its triangle and log
saw kerfs, sheet and board sizes, densities, prices
floor load 40 + 10 lb/ft2; wood 875 psi (a guess)
soil 1,500 lb/ft2 under every pier pad

chapters.title: Two triangles, forty panels
chapters.promise: Only two shapes.
narration: A dome whose longest stick is 72 inches is 22.6 feet across, and its forty triangles come in only two shapes. 30 have a long base of 83.7 inches and two short sides of 74.0. 10 have three long sides. Fill one of each well, and you have filled them all.

chapters.title: The stock budget has assumptions
chapters.promise: State the example before using it.
narration: Before estimating a wooden face, state the example. The planning reference takes the long chord as 72 inches, not the finished stick. Its log is 12 inches across, split 8 ways, with 60 feet of uniform usable trunk. The frame allowance is one 72 inch blank per member. For the opening estimate, we assume the frame occupies half the outer chord width inward from each edge. The actual tray opening is solved separately. Pair coverage, kerf, taper, defects and sealing still need a measured layout.
equations: nominal long chord 72 in; NOT the tool's maximum finished member
uniform log 12 in, 8 splits, usable trunk 60 ft
frame blank 72 in; frame inset ASSUMED 2.296 in
pair pitch (2-p)w assumes continuous coverage; p is projected overlap
kerf / taper / defects / end cuts / seals / packing loss NOT included

chapters.title: Three different timber totals
chapters.promise: A drawing, a cut, and the blank it came from.
narration: Every panel owns its three members: 120 members for 65 shared geometric edges. In the nominal-chord example their edge lengths total 678.35 feet. The live solver's physical cut-stock total is 664.31, because the joints stop at faces. But buying a blank for every member reserves 720 feet of wedge stock. These are three different ledgers. A shorter finished member leaves an offcut; it does not make the original blank shorter. Reuse that offcut only when the cutting plan gives it a job.

chapters.title: Pair span is not face coverage
chapters.promise: An overlap range, with its condition attached.
narration: The outer chord of an eighth of this log is 4.592 inches. Under the stated half-width inset, the clear area estimate is 427.63 square feet. If a pair continuously covers two chord widths, it uses the least timber in this model. If two wedges cover only one width, the timber doubles. That is an assumed face-pitch range, not proof that sliding a bowtie closes the face. The alternating-point infill pictured here is solved by the tool. Two points both inward are another seating problem. An opposed-point section experiment has another orientation again. Sliding changes void and contact, not the wood already in the pair.
equations: infill wedge ft = 2 x clear sq ft x 12 / continuous pair pitch
bowtie span / void fraction do NOT prove coverage, strength or R-value

chapters.title: Count raw trunk before finished timber
chapters.promise: Reserve the frame first, then add infill.
narration: A uniform usable trunk of 60 feet gives 10 six-foot rounds and 80 wedges in the ideal model. Reserve 90 feet of raw trunk for the framing blanks, then add the infill wedge footage divided by the splits. The conditional range is 229.7 to 369.4 feet of usable trunk: 4 to 7 whole reference-tree equivalents. These are uniform-diameter equivalents, not guaranteed standing trees. A real pine tapers, cuts consume wood, and short triangle courses need a packing plan.
equations: ideal tree yield = 60 x 8 = 480 wedge ft

chapters.title: The frame is a tray
chapters.promise: Forty-five degree walls.
narration: Each frame member is a wedge, an eighth of a 12 inch log, lying on one sawn face with its point toward the opening. Its other sawn face rises at forty-five degrees, so the opening is a tray, narrow at the flat side and widening up the slope, 4.24 inches deep. Every piece that fills it rests on that slope. Next door, the panels fold away at 18.0 and 22.5 degrees, and a covering has to meet those too.
equations: walls: 45 deg (an eighth of a log)

chapters.title: Seventeen wedges
chapters.promise: Stripes, flip-flopped.
narration: Fill it with wedges split from a 12 inch log, in stripes along the long base, flip-flopped: one point up, the next point down, so they nest. It takes 17, from 75.6 inches long down to 5.9. Each one ends where it meets a forty-five degree wall, so every end is a compound cut, and no two pieces are the same length.

chapters.title: A number on every piece
chapters.promise: Chalked on as it is cut.
narration: Every piece gets a number, chalked on as it is cut, and the number carries everything: which stick it comes from, its length along each edge, and both end cuts. Take piece 5. Along its point it runs 58.38 inches. Its other two long corners run 50.56 and 43.08. Three lengths, because its ends lean.

chapters.title: Cut one, on the mitre saw
chapters.promise: Sawn face down, bark corner to the fence.
narration: Here is its first cut. The stick lies on its sawn face, the bark corner against the fence, the keeper to the left of the blade. Swing the mitre 34.4 degrees, tilt the blade 45, and take just enough to clear the raw end. What falls away is a tapered sliver, 8.15 inches at its longest and 0.50 at its shortest. The calculator found that setting by trying every face down, both ends toward the fence, and keeping the one a single-bevel saw can make.
equations: mitre 34.4 deg, bevel 45.0 deg (blade tilted left)

chapters.title: Cut two, and an offcut to keep
chapters.promise: Measure from the first cut.
narration: Then end for end, the point against the fence, and measure from the first cut: 58.38 inches along the point, and the other two corners. Join the marks and the blade follows the line, at the same 34.4 and 45. This offcut is 20.77 inches long. That is a piece in its own right, so it goes back on the pile for a shorter run.

chapters.title: Too steep for the saw
chapters.promise: A sheet's edges, bevelled by hand.
narration: Not every cut fits a mitre saw. Cover the panel instead, with a sheet of strand board cut in 2 halves, and each edge has to lean to meet the next panel's covering, half the fold at its seam: 9.0, 11.2 and 11.2 degrees. Those cuts run the length of a sheet, so they are snapped with a chalk line and made with a circular saw, its blade tilted.

chapters.title: Ten ways to fill one triangle
chapters.promise: Every one with its cut list.
narration: The same triangle, ten ways. Wedges in stripes, 17 pieces. Wedges in a chevron, 18. Sixteenth slices, points alternating, 60. Wedges in rings, 15. Milled boards, 9. Fence pickets as vent louvers, 13. Log rounds, 139. Or covered over: a sheet in 2 halves, 3 strips of metal, 1 piece of film. Every one comes with its cut list, and the calculator will put any of them on the saw.
equations: Wedges (1/8 log), stripes parallel to one edge: 17
Wedges (1/8 log), chevron to the centre line: 18
1/16 slices, stripes parallel to one edge: 60
Milled 1x6 boards, stripes parallel to one edge: 9

chapters.title: Rounds, and the gaps cut to fit
chapters.promise: Copy a round over the gap, trace, cut.
narration: Log rounds are the odd one out: slices across a whole trunk, 1.5 inches thick, in a honeycomb 3 layers deep. 18 go in whole, 38 are cut where they meet the wall, and the 83 gaps left over are filled the way a carpenter would: lay another round over the gap, trace the gap onto it from below, and cut to the line. 139 pieces in all.

chapters.title: Turn it over
chapters.promise: The inside face.
narration: Turn the panel over and look at it from the inside, the face the room will see. The flip-flop shows: every other wedge has its point down, and the frame's points run round the edge. The calculator shows every pattern from underneath too, so you can see how the pieces meet before cutting any of them.
equations: flat side: points of the frame and of every other wedge

chapters.title: Five trunks, one pentagon
chapters.promise: Round back out, flat face in.
narration: Now the floor. The dome stands on a platform, and the owner already has its edge: five half trunks, twenty feet long. Stood on edge, round back out, flat face in, and joined at the corners, they make a pentagon whose backs measure the full 20 feet. The biggest circle inside the flat faces is 13.26 feet in radius. The dome needs 11.78: its sphere, plus 6 inches for its frame at the foot. It fits, with 1.48 feet to spare.

chapters.title: Every corner, one cut
chapters.promise: Thirty-six degrees, plumb, by chainsaw.
narration: Each corner is a mitre, and every one is the same: 36 degrees off square. Along the round back a trunk is the full 20 feet. Along its top, where the flat face starts, the cuts take 4.36 inches off each end, so it is 231.28 inches. No mitre saw takes a log that size: mark the line across the top, plumb it down both sides with a level, and cut to it with the chainsaw.

chapters.title: The star divides the stock
chapters.promise: Golden-ratio lengths, before the saw.
narration: The floor's regular pentagon has a diagonal 1.618034 times its side. A diagonal crosses two others and splits into long, short and long. One long plus one short is exactly a perimeter side in the centreline drawing. That gives complementary stock, but not zero saw waste. The actual pieces stop at other members' faces and the saw consumes a kerf. Also distinguish the corner's 108 degree included angle from a symmetrical 36 degree mitre, a nominal 18 degree perimeter side-face butt, and a 54 degree diagonal-to-side butt. Those are plan angles for different joints, not bevel settings through a wedge.
equations: plan cuts: mitre 36, side butt 18, diagonal butt 54 deg

chapters.title: A star across it
chapters.promise: Strong, and not enough.
narration: Inside goes a five-point star, corner to corner, in half trunks again. Each line crosses two others, so each is cut in three: 15 pieces of 148.3 and 91.7 inches, mitred where they meet. A star braces a pentagon across every corner. But on its own it leaves the floor in big triangles. The widest gap a deck board would have to cross is 119 inches, and a two by six deck may cross 24. The star alone fails.
equations: diagonal = 1.618034 x side, cut in three

chapters.title: Joists between the points
chapters.promise: Every gap inside a deck board's reach.
narration: So every space between the points is filled with joists, 2x8 on edge, 24 inches apart, each cut to meet the star or the frame where it lands. 55 of them. Now the widest gap is 22.5 inches, inside the 24 a deck board may cross.

chapters.title: A joist on the saw
chapters.promise: Too tall on edge, so it lies flat.
narration: A joist meets a star line at an angle, so its end is cut off square. Stood on edge, a two by eight is 7.25 inches tall, beyond the saw's 6 inch reach. So it lies flat, and the angle moves from the mitre to the bevel: mitre zero, bevel 18 degrees. Its other end, 54.0° off square, is past the blade's 46 degree tilt, and is marked and cut by hand.

chapters.title: Where the weight goes
chapters.promise: Every pound, to a pier.
narration: Every square foot of floor has to go somewhere. Forty pounds for living, ten for the floor itself, over 688 square feet: 34,417 pounds. Each patch goes to the member nearest it. Joists hand theirs to what they hang on; the star and the frame hand everything to the piers; and the piers carry 34,417 pounds, every pound accounted for. Every span is checked for bending and for sag. Where one fails, a pier goes under it: 8 of them, and now the hardest span works at 94 percent of what it can carry.

chapters.title: 43 piers, each sized
chapters.promise: A pad for every load.
narration: 43 stump piers, rounds of log on tamped gravel. Each pad is sized from its own load, at 1,500 pounds a square foot of soil. Most need only the smallest pad, 16 inches square. The heaviest carries 2,902 pounds, and needs 18.

chapters.title: Seven ways to frame the floor
chapters.promise: Same trunks, same joists.
narration: The star is one way. The calculator builds seven, from the same trunks and joists, and checks each the same way. The star with joists. The star alone, which fails its deck. A wheel, five spokes with rings of joists. A sunburst of ten. A fan, its joists square to the walls. Beams across with joists between, the way a deck is usually framed. And nested rings, the idea this began with.
equations: Fan: 5 spokes + joists square to the walls: 56 pieces, 26 piers

chapters.title: The most to spare, the heaviest pier
chapters.promise: Spokes bring their load to one point.
narration: They do not pass equally. Beams with joists works its hardest span at only 68 percent. Only the nested rings have more to spare, 59 percent, and they take 130 piers to get it. The fan is the other end: five spokes meet at one centre pier, and that pier carries 7,551 pounds, on a pad 28 inches square. The wheel's carries 5,090. Bring the spokes to one point, and you bring the load there too.

chapters.title: Or lay it on gravel
chapters.promise: Where the nested rings belong.
narration: On a levelled gravel bed nothing spans. Every member bears along its length, and the piers go away. That is where the nested rings belong: 25 rings, each one's back pressed against the flat face of the ring outside it, every corner the same 36 degree cut, the gaps packed with gravel or cob. About 342 dollars of gravel, and nothing else to buy. But it eats logs: 34 of them, against 5 for the star with joists.

chapters.title: Trunks, quarters or lumber
chapters.promise: Swap what the star is made of.
narration: Swap what the star is made of, and the floor changes round it. Half trunks: 43 piers and 7 logs. Whole logs: the same piers, but 12 logs. Quarter trunks, weaker: 48 piers. Six by sixes: 48 piers, and about 3,352 dollars, because they are bought. Four by fours: 58 piers, 23 of them propping spans a four by four cannot carry.
equations: Half trunk on edge: 43 piers, 7 logs, $2,598

chapters.title: The dome on its floor
chapters.promise: Five corners left over.
narration: And the dome goes on it, its foot inside the flat faces, 1.48 feet to spare at the narrowest, with the pentagon's five corners left over outside it.

chapters.title: What these numbers are not
chapters.promise: Checked and priced, not rated.
narration: A word about these numbers. The floor loads are a dwelling's. But the wood's strength, 875 pounds per square inch, is a guess: these logs are not graded, and the guess is a careful one, stricter than a lumber span table. The prices are estimates. Change any of it in the calculator and every pier and span is worked again. Before people live on it, an engineer signs it. Here it is checked and priced, not rated.
equations: an engineer signs a floor people live on

chapters.title: Cut by the numbers
chapters.promise: In the launcher: Triangle Infill.
narration: 17 wedges and their offcuts. Five trunks and a star. 75 members and 43 piers, every one numbered, every cut shown before it is made. The calculator that worked all of this out is in the launcher, called Triangle Infill, and it will do the same for whatever is stacked by your saw.

lessons.title: The 40 Hour Cabin, Styled Twelve Ways

chapters.title: The cabin, bare
chapters.promise: The book's dome, in the Creator.
narration: This is the forty-hour cabin's dome, built in the Dome Creator at its own size: two-frequency, 19.4 feet across, 120 struts and 40 panels. Bare -- plywood panels, cedar shakes and a gravel pad -- the Creator prices it at 3,947 dollars. Now the same frame, dressed twelve ways.
equations: 120 struts, 40 panels, 550 sq ft of shell

chapters.title: Timber Workshop
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Timber Workshop.
narration: The Timber Workshop's finish on the cabin's frame: plywood, standing on concrete slab. 5,323 dollars, 1,564 pounds, and about 47 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Glass Studio Loft
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Glass Studio Loft.
narration: The Glass Studio Loft's finish on the cabin's frame: glass window, standing on wood deck. 8,266 dollars, 2,509 pounds, and about 59 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Split-Log Homestead
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Split-Log Homestead.
narration: The Split-Log Homestead's finish on the cabin's frame: plywood under cedar shakes, standing on gravel pad. 3,947 dollars, 2,577 pounds, and about 50 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Whole Trunk Lodge - 20 ft
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Whole Trunk Lodge - 20 ft.
narration: The Whole Trunk Lodge - 20 ft's finish on the cabin's frame: canvas, standing on gravel pad. 1,802 dollars, 877 pounds, and about 47 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Grow Dome
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Grow Dome.
narration: The Grow Dome's finish on the cabin's frame: polycarb twinwall, standing on grass pad. 2,546 dollars, 1,012 pounds, and about 47 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Hex Cell Pavilion
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Hex Cell Pavilion.
narration: The Hex Cell Pavilion's finish on the cabin's frame: hex composite, standing on concrete slab. 7,060 dollars, 1,777 pounds, and about 47 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Continuous Steel Arc Hangar
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Continuous Steel Arc Hangar.
narration: The Continuous Steel Arc Hangar's finish on the cabin's frame: open, standing on concrete slab. 4,404 dollars, 820 pounds, and about 31 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Rebar Garden Dome
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Rebar Garden Dome.
narration: The Rebar Garden Dome's finish on the cabin's frame: open, standing on grass pad. 1,116 dollars, 820 pounds, and about 31 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Concrete Monocoque Form
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Concrete Monocoque Form.
narration: The Concrete Monocoque Form's finish on the cabin's frame: concrete form panel under poured concrete shell, standing on concrete slab. 11,606 dollars, 16,359 pounds, and about 50 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Woodland Hex Mirror
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Woodland Hex Mirror.
narration: The Woodland Hex Mirror's finish on the cabin's frame: hex mirror, standing on grass pad. 11,842 dollars, 2,284 pounds, and about 47 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Woodland Square Mirror
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Woodland Square Mirror.
narration: The Woodland Square Mirror's finish on the cabin's frame: square mirror, standing on grass pad. 11,076 dollars, 2,284 pounds, and about 47 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

chapters.title: Treehouse Canopy Dome
chapters.promise: The cabin, dressed as the Treehouse Canopy Dome.
narration: The Treehouse Canopy Dome's finish on the cabin's frame: hex composite, standing on treehouse platform. 11,219 dollars, 1,777 pounds, and about 47 hours of work by the Creator's estimate.

lessons.title: Beyond the Dome: Building With Wedges

chapters.title: Beyond the dome
chapters.promise: The same wedges, other buildings.
narration: The dome on this hill is framed from 120 wedges split from logs with one chainsaw. This film is about everything else those wedges can build. A zome, framed from the same pile. Square posts, made from wedges on demand. A roof whose pitch is already in the log. An octagon, a set of joints, and a seam that carries water. And it starts where every wedge does: with a log.

chapters.title: Why wedges
chapters.promise: The log does the geometry.
narration: A log split through its centre, halved, halved again and halved once more, gives 8 wedges of exactly 45.0 degrees, and nobody measures an angle. The saw takes only its kerf: 89 percent of a 12 inch log is kept as members. And because every flat face runs through the heart, wedges move least as they dry: pine shrinks 7.4 percent around its rings and 4.8 across them, and a radial face sits square across the rings.

chapters.title: The wedge, measured
chapters.promise: Two faces, a back, two angles.
narration: Know the stick you have. An eighth of the reference log has two flat faces meeting at the pith at 45.0 degrees. Trim its curved back flat and the back is 4.59 inches wide, 5.54 inches from the point, with corners of 67.5 degrees. Those angles never change with the size of the log. Only the split changes them.

chapters.title: Square on demand
chapters.promise: Two wedges, slant to slant.
narration: Now take two. Turn one end for end and lay it against the other, slant to slant. What you hold looks like a two by four pushed sideways, with corners of 67.5 and 112.5 degrees. Plane it square to its long face and the board inside it is the radius times the cosine of the point angle, by the radius times the sine. For an eighth, those are the same number. The pair planes to a square, 3.87 inches on a side. It costs wood: it keeps 53 percent of the log, against 89 for the wedges as they are. So you square only what needs it. Square, on demand.
equations: planed board = R cos(theta) x R sin(theta)

chapters.title: Back to back
chapters.promise: Quarters make a post.
narration: Put two wedges together on their backs instead. Quarters, back to back, are already a square, 5.62 inches on a side, with nothing to plane: the heaviest square the method makes, and the one for posts. Two eighths back to back make a diamond, a poor board but the right shape for a ridge, a rail that sheds water both ways, or a spline.

chapters.title: Split finer, get boards
chapters.promise: Thinner wedges pair flatter.
narration: The thinner the wedge, the closer a pair is to a board, because a pair keeps the cosine of its point angle when it is planed. But every split is another saw cut. On the reference log the two balance at 16 ways: pairs plane to boards 4.81 by 1.92 inches and keep 65 percent of the log. Quarter the butt for posts, split the middle 8 ways for frames, and take the top 16 ways for boards.

chapters.title: Shims from the same log
chapters.promise: Halve once more.
narration: Where a wedge has to meet the square world for a short way, shim it there and leave it a wedge everywhere else. Lying on its back, an eighth's face stands at 67.5 degrees. A plumb face needs 22.5 more, which is half the point, which is exactly a wedge from a log split 16 ways. The shims come from the same log. Halve one more time.

chapters.title: The skew is a roof pitch
chapters.promise: 5.0 in twelve, from the log.
narration: Keep the skew where the building already slopes. A pair of eighths laid flat has faces at 22.5 degrees, a rise of 5.0 in twelve: an ordinary roof. Use pairs as rafters and the sheathing seats flat with no bevel cut. Twelfths give 3.2 in twelve, a low shed roof; quarters 12 in twelve, a steep one. Choose the split for the roof you want.

chapters.title: The octagon is in the log
chapters.promise: 45.0 degrees, 8 times.
narration: An eighth's point is the angle at the centre of an octagon. Eight wedge joists meet at the middle of a round deck with no angle measured, and the corners round the rim are the 135 degrees an octagon needs. Gazebos, round decks, yurt floors and tables are the log, put back together flat.

chapters.title: Joints wedges make easy
chapters.promise: Lap, bird's mouth, key.
narration: Wedge lumber has flat faces at known angles, and each is the start of a joint. Two pairs laid slant to slant and offset make a scarf, a long member from short wedges. A wedge's point, set down over a square plate, is a bird's mouth already cut. A butterfly key let in across a glued pair stitches it. None of them needs a square face to start from: the joint line is the reference.
equations: slant lap, bird's mouth, butterfly key

chapters.title: The pinwheel
chapters.promise: Nothing meets at the corner.
narration: The dome's joint, and the zome's. Where sticks meet at a corner, none of them runs into it. Each reaches the corner ahead of it, and its tail butts the side of the stick behind, round the corner like the blades of a pinwheel. Nothing meets at a point, so nothing has to be cut to a compound angle there. Here it frames one zome panel, flat on its jig.
equations: each stick: head at the corner, tail on the stick behind

chapters.title: The seam is a channel
chapters.promise: The V is the duct.
narration: Square lumber laid side by side closes up. Wedges on their backs open a V, the full length of the member, of exactly the wedge's point, 45.0 degrees. Capped, it is a gutter that cannot overflow sideways, a cable run you can open, a way to breathe a wall. Big services go in the building's core; the seams take water, wire and air.
equations: V = 45.0 deg, every seam the same

chapters.title: Against the mill
chapters.promise: The number that argues back.
narration: Here is the method measured against a sawmill, on the reference log. Split, the log keeps 89 percent. With the backs trimmed, 80. Split 16 ways and paired into boards, 65. The project's sawmill simulator, packing two by fours, keeps 57. And eighths paired and planed square keep only 53, less than the mill. That is the number that argues back, and it is why the title says on demand.

chapters.title: A zome from the same pile
chapters.promise: 36 panels, 4 rows.
narration: Now a whole building that is not a dome. A zome: 36 rhombus panels in 4 rows twisting round a point, 13.8 feet across and 8.7 feet tall, every panel side 35.4 inches. It is the same zome the Complete Edition works through, framed here from the dome's own wedges: eighths of a 12 inch log.

chapters.title: Wedges, back out
chapters.promise: The seams close by themselves.
narration: Every panel is four wedge sticks in a pinwheel, framed flat, with the wedge's back on the outside and its point toward the room. A wedge's sides lean 22.5 degrees away from square, so where two panels fold together their backs close tight along the outside seam, and the inside opens into a V of 17.2 to 30.8 degrees: the wedge's point less the fold. Every fold of this zome, up to 27.8 degrees, is less than an eighth's point, so nothing collides and nothing needs a block. The weather side is closed. The inside is a channel.

chapters.title: One bevel for every cut
chapters.promise: Only the mitre changes.
narration: And this is the part a builder will like. Solve every stick's two end cuts in three dimensions, and every end of every stick in the zome takes the same bevel: 22.5 degrees, half the wedge's point. Set it once. Only the mitre changes, once per row: 57.9 / 27.3 / 1.0 / 15.6 degrees, and the two stick types in a row are mirror images. 144 sticks, 8 types.

chapters.title: A panel on the jig
chapters.promise: Built flat, at waist height.
narration: Each row has its own jig: stops screwed to a sheet at the row's rhombus, full size. Row three's sharp corner is 89.0 degrees, nearly square; the crown's is 32.1. Lay four sticks in, back down, glue and screw each butt in the thick part, and the panel comes off true. Nine times a row, four rows.

chapters.title: The other way: square sticks
chapters.promise: Wedge blocks in the gaps.
narration: There is a second way, the one the Complete Edition describes: square sticks, two wedges paired and planed 3.87 inches square. Square-edged panels meet on their inside edges and open a V outside, which a wedge block fills. A block's point is three hundred and sixty degrees divided by its split, so each fold wants a log split that many ways: 25 / 19 / 15 / 13. It works, and it takes 18 log sections against 9.

chapters.title: What it takes
chapters.promise: 9 sections of log.
narration: Framed the wedge way, the zome's 144 sticks come 2 from each wedge of the dome's own 72 inch sections: 72 wedges, 9 sections of log. The dome on this hill takes 15. And every one of the zome's 63 inside seams is a channel before anybody runs a wire.

chapters.title: Meeting the square world
chapters.promise: Posts, shims and a sill.
narration: A zome's rim zigzags: 18 corners, 9 of them 20.8 inches above the rest. Stand a post under each high corner, quarters back to back, 5.62 inches square. Set a sill ring under the low ones. Where a door frame or a square wall meets a wedge, shim it there. The wedge stays a wedge; only the joints learn to be square.

chapters.title: Buildings that suit wedges
chapters.promise: Triangles, slopes, octagons.
narration: Some buildings want boards. The ones made of triangles, slopes, octagons and posts want wedges. A shed with pair rafters at the log's own pitch. An A-frame. A gazebo on an octagon of wedge joists. A zome. The pattern is the same in every one: square the pieces that meet the level world, and leave everything triangulated, sloped or radial as wedges.

chapters.title: Built by veterans
chapters.promise: A system, a crew, a village.
narration: This method was written by a veteran. On one night in January 2024, 32,882 veterans had no home of their own, 13,851 of them unsheltered, by HUD's count. A building that is a system, maintained on a schedule, with parts you swap in the field and a crew that builds together, fits the way a lot of veterans already work. It is designed to sit beside HUD-VASH, SSVF, VA Grant and Per Diem, and to be built and kept by veterans.

chapters.title: Safety at the log
chapters.promise: Never alone.
narration: All of it starts with a chainsaw in a log, the most dangerous part of the work. Never alone at the log. Full protective gear. The log cradled for the first cut. A chain filed for ripping.
