Every split made with the saw, never with an axe or a maul. And none of these buildings is rated by this film: an engineer checks anything that carries people, snow or wind before anyone lives in it.
equations: two people at the log, every session
an engineer before anyone lives in it

chapters.title: Split everything. Square on demand.
chapters.promise: The zome is in the toolkit.
narration: Split everything, and square only what needs it. The book is called Square on Demand, and the zome you have just watched go up is a tool you can walk round: every stick, every cut, every jig, from the same software that solves the dome.

chapters.title: The staple house
chapters.promise: What a dome should be.
narration: When people ask me what this dome is, I don't say shelter. I say it's a McDouble. Cheap, fast, reliable, consistent, known everywhere. Not the five-course meal. The staple the whole menu stands on.

chapters.title: What a staple is
chapters.promise: Always there, always the same.
narration: A staple isn't the best thing on the menu. It's the thing that's always there, always the same, priced so nobody thinks twice, and known so well nobody reads the ingredients to trust it. Its job is that everybody who walks in walks out fed.

chapters.title: A first home, not a last one
chapters.promise: The eighteen-year-old.
narration: An eighteen-year-old doesn't need his first home to be a five-course meal. He needs one that's honest and filling and gets him through, so he can save for the rest. Without that staple, most people never get into the housing market at all.

chapters.title: The papercuts
chapters.promise: Counted, from the builders' own survey.
narration: Here's what I mean by papercuts. By the home builders' own survey, a new house sells for $665,299. 10 lines of that are things like building permit fees, impact fee, water and sewer fees, financing, overhead, marketing, commission and profit. Together, $178,746.

chapters.title: None of it is the house
chapters.promise: A share, not a number.
narration: That's 27 percent of the price, and not one line of it is a board, a nail or an hour of work on the house itself. Each one has a reason. None of them is the house. That's 15 of these domes.

chapters.title: Fifteen sets of hands
chapters.promise: Every stud's road to the wall.
narration: Under all that, the building itself is 32 separately priced trades, and every stud in its frame has passed through 15 sets of hands between the tree and the wall. Every one of them took a margin. A thousand small cuts, and they belong to somebody who isn't you.

chapters.title: The biggest papercut
chapters.promise: Paid by the month.
narration: And then the loan. Borrow $100,000 at 6.5 percent for 30 years and the interest alone is $127,544. More than you borrowed. That's 10.6 of these domes, paid a month at a time, so it never looks like a cut.

chapters.title: The staple's bill
chapters.promise: One sheet, one seller.
narration: Now the staple. The stem cell's whole bill is 9 lines from one seller, and it adds to $12,036. The margin's on it, $2,006, 20 percent, where you can see it and argue with it. A staple's allowed to make money. It's not allowed to hide where the money goes.

chapters.title: Side by side
chapters.promise: One scale, both bills.
narration: Put the two bills side by side at the same scale. On the left, only the papercuts. On the right, the staple's whole bill, frame, shell, services, labour, overhead and margin. Every line of it is shorter than the tallest papercut.

chapters.title: Not like for like
chapters.promise: What this does not say.
narration: That's not like for like, and I won't pretend it is. The survey house is many times the floor and comes with $91,057 of land. The dome is 277 square feet on a pad. A family that needs four bedrooms needs the bigger house. What I'm comparing is the shape of the bills: how many hands, how many lines that aren't the building.

chapters.title: A baseline
chapters.promise: What a staple does to a market.
narration: Here's the hope. When a dry, serviced, movable building costs $12,036, a $23,993 manufactured home of the same floor has to say what the other $11,957 buys, and a $60,107 site-built one has to say it again. Some of it buys real things. Some of it is papercuts. A staple on the menu is how you find out which. That's a hope, not a measurement. Not enough of these exist yet to move anything.

chapters.title: A family event
chapters.promise: Known, and added to for life.
narration: A house bought the usual way is a transaction with a long row of people you never meet. This one's a family event. Felling, splitting, a jig on the grass, forty panels, a weekend of lifting. The kids learn the triangle. Every part's on one list and every cut's in one book, and you add to it a panel at a time for a lifetime, instead of paying for it a month at a time.

chapters.title: The first rung
chapters.promise: The staple underneath.
narration: A staple doesn't end the menu. It's what makes the menu possible. Everything else in the book is optional: the panels, the fit-outs, the bigger frames. The staple underneath isn't. Build the first rung like a staple, and a lot more people get to climb.

lessons.title: The House That Was a Tree

chapters.title: This was a tree
chapters.promise: Now it's a house.
narration: This was a tree. Now it's a house. And it cost less than a used car: $12,036.

chapters.title: The cheapest part
chapters.promise: Stay for the end.
narration: Stay to the end, because the strangest number in it is the trees. They were the cheapest part.

chapters.title: The papercuts
chapters.promise: Not one board.
narration: A new house sells for $665,299. $178,746 of that is fees and margins. Not one board. Not one hour on the house.

chapters.title: The biggest cut
chapters.promise: Paid by the month.
narration: Borrow $100,000 and you pay back $227,544. The interest alone would build more than 10 of these.

chapters.title: Fifteen hands
chapters.promise: Every one took a cut.
narration: Every stud in that house went through 15 sets of hands. Every one of them took a cut.

chapters.title: So I cut them out
chapters.promise: One saw.
narration: So I cut them out. One chainsaw. One log. Eight wedges, and nobody measures an angle.

chapters.title: Two lengths
chapters.promise: One jig, forty panels.
narration: 120 members in two lengths. One jig. Forty flat panels, built on the grass and lifted into a dome.

chapters.title: Even the floor
chapters.promise: The golden ratio.
narration: Even the floor is free geometry. Cut a twenty foot log at 148.3 inches and what's left is 91.7: the golden ratio. Five logs make a pentagon.

chapters.title: The whole bill
chapters.promise: On one sheet.
narration: The whole bill is 9 lines, from one seller. $12,036, with the margin printed on it.

chapters.title: The trees
chapters.promise: As promised.
narration: And the trees? The frame and every wall closed in wood: 4 to 7 pines.

chapters.title: Not yet
chapters.promise: What it isn't.
narration: Is it engineered yet? No. That's the first thing the money buys. Everything else is open: every number you just heard is computed in code anyone can check.

chapters.title: Who it's for
chapters.promise: Follow the build.
narration: It isn't for everyone. It's for the eighteen-year-old, the veteran, the mother who's done paying for someone else's papercuts. Follow the build.

chapters.title: Closing the triangle
chapters.promise: The same wedges, again.
narration: The frame is done: three wedges round every one of these 40 triangles. Now close the middles, with the same wedges.
equations: one triangle: 72 in base, 63.67 in sides

chapters.title: One wedge
chapters.promise: Its face and its depth.
narration: Here is one wedge, end on, three times life size. Its face is 4.59 inches wide. From the face to the point it is 5.54 inches deep. Deeper than it is wide.

chapters.title: A pair, points in
chapters.promise: Solid.
narration: Now a pair. Turn the second one over so the points face each other, and lay the slants together. That's a solid block, and it reaches one depth down the triangle: 5.54 inches. Its faces bear on the next pair's, and the slants are what shows.

chapters.title: Slide it to a bowtie
chapters.promise: Twice the reach, half the wood.
narration: Slide one along the other's slant. The pair reaches further down, and opens in the middle. At the end only the points touch: a bowtie. It reaches 11.1 inches, and it's half air.

chapters.title: Filled nested
chapters.promise: Top corner down.
narration: Fill a triangle from its top corner down, nested. Each pair is as long as the triangle is wide where it lies. 9 pairs close it: 18 wedges, 51 feet.

chapters.title: Filled bowtie
chapters.promise: Fewer pairs.
narration: The same triangle with bowtie pairs. Each one reaches twice as far, so 5 pairs close it: 10 wedges, 31 feet.

chapters.title: Side by side
chapters.promise: The same opening.
narration: Side by side: the same opening, 51 feet of wedge nested, 31 as bowties.

chapters.title: The whole dome, nested
chapters.promise: Every triangle, closed.
narration: Now every triangle. Nested pairs, laid from each top corner down, every wedge cut to the walls and planed flush with the frame. 800 pieces, 2,646 feet.
equations: the Triangle Infill tool's dome: 22.6 ft across

chapters.title: Slide them all
chapters.promise: Nested, half, bowtie.
narration: Slide every pair at once. Nested, 800 pieces. Half slid, 580. Bowtie, 420, and 1,371 feet.

chapters.title: Dial it in each triangle
chapters.promise: Solid at the corners.
narration: Or dial it inside every triangle: nested at the top corner and along the base, where the frame carries its load, opening to bowties through the middle. 540 pieces, 1,866 feet.

chapters.title: Cut flush
chapters.promise: No stubs, no gaps.
narration: Close in. Every pair ends on the opening's wall in the frame's own compound cut, and both faces are planed flush with the frame. Planing takes 17% off a nested pair, 5% off a half slid one, and 1% off a bowtie.

chapters.title: The book's count
chapters.promise: The reference dome.
narration: The book counts its reference dome, seventy two inch chords, laid the same way. Nested: 760 wedges, 2,166 feet. Bowtie: 420 wedges, 1,292 feet.

chapters.title: In trees
chapters.promise: Frame and all.
narration: With the frame, the whole dome is 2,012 to 2,886 feet of wedge: 4.2 to 6.0 sixty foot pines of a foot across.

chapters.title: Two layouts, two counts
chapters.promise: Which face shows.
narration: The first count divided the open area by the wedge's face width. That fits a different layout: faces out, points in, each wedge covering its own face. With the points facing each other down the triangle, the reach sets the pitch. Laid pair by pair that way, nested is 2,166 feet against the first count's 2,235, and bowtie 1,292 against 1,117. Both are ideal counts, before kerf and offcuts.

chapters.title: Rings
chapters.promise: The frame, repeated inward.
narration: That is one family. The Triangle Infill tool knows others, and the dome wears every one. Rings: the frame repeated inward, ring by ring. Flip-flop: every other piece turned upside down, 600 pieces. Same hand: every piece lies like the frame, 270 pieces. Shimmed: full pieces flipped onto the slope, 720 pieces. Standing: slices standing on their points, 1,020 pieces. Comb: slices all standing on their points, 510 pieces.

chapters.title: Parallel
chapters.promise: Along one edge.
narration: Parallel: runs along one edge, stepping across, every run ending in a compound cut on the walls. Flip-flop: every other piece turned upside down, 720 pieces. Same hand: every piece lies like the frame, 380 pieces. Shimmed: full pieces flipped onto the slope, 710 pieces. Standing: slices standing on their points, 1,220 pieces. Comb: slices all standing on their points, 630 pieces.

chapters.title: Across
chapters.promise: Square to an edge.
narration: Across: runs square to one edge, stepping along it. Short pieces, many of them. Flip-flop: every other piece turned upside down, 920 pieces. Same hand: every piece lies like the frame, 520 pieces. Shimmed: full pieces flipped onto the slope, 920 pieces. Standing: slices standing on their points, 1,720 pieces. Comb: slices all standing on their points, 880 pieces.

chapters.title: Chevron
chapters.promise: Two sides, one centre line.
narration: Chevron: runs along the two sides, meeting on the centre line. Flip-flop: every other piece turned upside down, 740 pieces. Same hand: every piece lies like the frame, 400 pieces. Shimmed: full pieces flipped onto the slope, 740 pieces. Standing: slices standing on their points, 1,300 pieces. Comb: slices all standing on their points, 660 pieces.

chapters.title: Louvers
chapters.promise: Covered, but open to air.
narration: Louvers: slats tilted and lapped. Covered from above, open to the air: a dome that breathes. 590 pieces, 1,892 feet.

chapters.title: Or cover it
chapters.promise: Over the frame, not in it.
narration: Or leave the frame open and cover it, laid over the outside and bevelled to meet the next panel across each seam. 16 ways. First, parallel. Flip-flop: every other piece turned upside down, 750 pieces. Same hand: every piece lies like the frame, 460 pieces. Shimmed: full pieces flipped onto the slope, 750 pieces. Standing: slices standing on their points, 1,420 pieces. Comb: slices all standing on their points, 710 pieces.

chapters.title: Covered, across
chapters.promise: Square to an edge, over the frame.
narration: Covered across. Flip-flop: every other piece turned upside down, 1,000 pieces. Same hand: every piece lies like the frame, 600 pieces. Shimmed: full pieces flipped onto the slope, 1,000 pieces. Standing: slices standing on their points, 1,840 pieces. Comb: slices all standing on their points, 920 pieces.

chapters.title: Covered, chevron
chapters.promise: And the louvered cover.
narration: Covered chevron, and last, the louvered cover. Flip-flop: every other piece turned upside down, 800 pieces. Same hand: every piece lies like the frame, 480 pieces. Shimmed: full pieces flipped onto the slope, 820 pieces. Standing: slices standing on their points, 1,540 pieces. Comb: slices all standing on their points, 800 pieces. Louvered: slats tilted and lapped, 720 pieces.

chapters.title: Every fill, side by side
chapters.promise: Quarter scale.
narration: Every fill, side by side at quarter scale: 4 with pairs, 21 with the tool's patterns. Nothing shows through any of them. The least wood that closes every triangle completely is chevron, same hand: 1,038 feet, 52% solid. Rings leave a plug to cut at each centre.

chapters.title: The dial
chapters.promise: Solid or air.
narration: The overlap is a dial. Nest them tight at the corners, where the loads gather. Open them in the middle, where a cavity holds insulation. A bowtie touching at its points alone doesn't keep the weather out, so test the joint before you trust the least number.
equations: nested at the corners, open in the middle

chapters.title: The fridge with no compressor
chapters.promise: No compressor, no refrigerant, no moving parts: just water, a vacuum and a mineral.
narration: A molecular sieve is a zeolite: a mineral full of pores exactly the size of a water molecule. Put one in a sealed, air-free vessel beside a pan of water and it pulls the water's vapour in so hard that the water boils at room temperature, and boiling water gets cold. That is a refrigerator. When the zeolite is full, heat it and it gives the water back, ready to do it again.

chapters.title: The numbers we are working from
chapters.promise: Where every figure in this film comes from.
narration: Before anything is worked out, here is everything this film rests on: 7 numbers, 1 standard, 6 estimate. A claimed number is what the source said and has not been measured here. Every figure after this is arithmetic on these and on the dome's own computed numbers.
equations: water per kg of zeolite = 0.20 kg/kg  (estimate)
useful heat per square metre of collector = 3.0 kWh/m2/day  (estimate)

chapters.title: Water boils cold
chapters.promise: Take the air away and water boils at room temperature.
narration: Seal water in a vessel with the air pumped out and it boils at room temperature. Boiling takes heat, and it takes it from the water, so the water gets cold: every kilogram that boils off carries away 2,450 kilojoules. The only trick is to keep taking the vapour away, and that is the zeolite's job.

chapters.title: One bed, one day
chapters.promise: How much cold a bed of zeolite holds.
narration: A bed of 20.0 kilograms soaks up about 4.0 kilograms of water before it is full. Boiling that much water away pulls 2.7 kilowatt hours of heat out of whatever the cold side touches.

chapters.title: The sun resets it
chapters.promise: Heat drives it, not electricity.
narration: When the bed is full, heat it to about 200 degrees and it gives its water back, ready to go again. A solar collector does that. The price is heat: every day of cooling needs 6.8 kilowatt hours of it, because the cycle returns only 0.4 of cold for each unit of heat.

chapters.title: Where it fits the dome
chapters.promise: The seam module's desiccant drawer, grown up.
narration: In the dome this is the seam module's desiccant cartridge, grown up. The three-way gate already sends the channel's air through a silica drawer that comes out and goes in an oven. A zeolite bed pulls harder, gives its water back to the sun instead, and makes cold while it works. Run once a day it gathers 386 gallons of water a year, 5.1 times what the seam's thermoelectric plates condense.
equations: water it gathers a year = 386 gal

chapters.title: What it will not do
chapters.promise: The number that does not help.
narration: It is a daily batch, not an air conditioner: spread over the day it cools about 113 watts on average, a fraction of what a small window unit moves. And the heat has to come from somewhere: about 2.3 square metres of collector in good sun, on a dome whose whole shell is 550 square feet.

lessons.title: How Much Tree Closes a Dome

chapters.title: How Much Tree Closes a Dome
chapters.promise: One dome, every triangle closed with wedges: four trees, or seven, and you choose which.
narration: The dome's frame is 120 wedge members: 678 feet of wedge, cut from one log after another. Close every triangle with more wedges, laid in pairs with their points facing in, and the pairs can nest tight or open into a bowtie. Nested, a pair covers one wedge face; opened, two. That one choice moves the whole dome between 1,796 and 2,913 feet of wedge.

chapters.title: The numbers we are working from
chapters.promise: Where every figure in this film comes from.
narration: Before anything is worked out, here is everything this film rests on: 5 numbers, 1 standard, 4 estimate. A claimed number is what the source said and has not been measured here. Every figure after this is arithmetic on these and on the dome's own computed numbers.

chapters.title: The frame
chapters.promise: A tree and a half.
narration: A 12 inch log split 8 ways gives wedges with a face 4.59 inches wide. The frame takes 120 of them, 678 feet of wedge, and one 60 foot pine gives 480 feet.

chapters.title: Closing the triangles
chapters.promise: Pairs, points in.
narration: The triangles leave 428 square feet to close after the frame. Lay the wedges in pairs, points facing in. Nested tight, a pair covers one face; opened to a bowtie, two.

chapters.title: Your choice of trees
chapters.promise: The overlap is the dial.
narration: Bowtie pairs close the dome with 1,117 feet of infill; nested pairs take 2,235. Frame and all, that is 1,796 to 2,913 feet: 3.7 to 6.1 trees, before taper and kerf.

chapters.title: Where it fits the dome
chapters.promise: In the dome, this is the the tree, the log, the rip, yield and value.
narration: This is the whole timber bill of the wedge dome closed in wood: 1,796 to 2,913 feet of wedge against a frame of 678.

chapters.title: What it will not do
chapters.promise: The number that does not help.
narration: A bowtie touches only at its points: the 1,117 foot figure is a floor, not a weather-tight joint. And the area method runs about six per cent above the real pieces the Triangle Infill calculator cuts, because a triangle's corners take short pieces.
